abstract: It is well known that when an automatic learning algorithm is applied to a fixed corpus of data, the size of the corpus places an upper bound on the number of degrees of freedom that the model can contain if it is to generalize well. Because the amount of hardware in a neural network typically increases with the dimensionality of its inputs, it can be challenging to build a high-performance network for classifying large input patterns. In this paper, several techniques for addressing this problem are discussed in the context of an isolated word recognition task.

paragraphs: A neural classifier with high-dimensional inputs often requires many adjustable parameters and substantial hardware. With a fixed training corpus, that flexibility can exceed what the data support and weaken generalization. This paper studies ways to manage the connection between input size, model complexity, and available examples.

The authors discuss dimensionality reduction and prior knowledge in the context of isolated-word recognition. Reducing the representation’s dimensionality can lower the burden on the classifier, while prior structure can guide which distinctions it needs to represent. The application provides a concrete setting in which large input patterns must be classified from limited data.

The contribution is a treatment of representation and model design as part of the learning problem, rather than assuming that a larger network is always the right response to complex inputs. It highlights a practical constraint that links statistical and hardware efficiency: a compact, informed representation can make useful learning possible within both data and implementation limits.
summary.tldr: The paper examines dimensionality reduction and prior knowledge as ways to control network complexity in isolated-word recognition.

title: Dimensionality Reduction and Prior Knowledge in E-Set Recognition

abstract: The performance of seven minimization algorithms are compared on five neural network problems. These include a variable-step-size algorithm, conjugate gradient, and several methods with explicit analytic or numerical approximations to the Hessian.
originalAbstract: The performance of seven minimization algorithms are compared on five neural network problems. These include a variable-step-size algorithm, conjugate gradient, and several methods with explicit analytic or numerical approximations to the Hessian.
title: Time Trials on Second-Order and Variable-Learning-Rate Algorithms

abstract: This paper considers the problem of expressing predicate calculus in con(cid:173) nectionist networks that are based on energy minimization. Given a first(cid:173) order-logic knowledge base and a bound k, a symmetric network is con(cid:173) structed (like a Boltzman machine or a Hopfield network) that searches for a proof for a given query. If a resolution-based proof of length no longer than k exists, then the global minima of the energy function that is associated with the network represent such proofs. The network that is generated is of size cubic in the bound k and linear in the knowledge size. There are no restrictions on the type of logic formulas that can be represented. The network is inherently fault tolerant and can cope with inconsistency and nonmonotonicity.

paragraphs: This paper translates logical proof search into energy minimization in a symmetric neural network. Given a first-order knowledge base, a query, and a bound on proof length, the construction produces a network that searches for a proof. The network belongs to the same broad style as Hopfield networks or Boltzmann machines.

The central guarantee concerns the network's global energy minima. If a resolution proof exists within the chosen length bound, those minima represent such proofs. This connects a symbolic requirement—having a valid proof—to a numerical objective that a network can minimize. The guarantee specifies what globally minimal states mean; it does not itself assert that every search trajectory reaches one.

The constructed network grows cubically with the proof-length bound and linearly with the size of the knowledge base. The authors place no restrictions on the types of first-order formulas represented and describe the network as fault tolerant and able to handle inconsistency and nonmonotonicity. The result provides a concrete representation of bounded logical reasoning within a neural energy framework.
summary.tldr: A symmetric network encodes bounded first-order proof search so that global energy minima represent valid proofs when such proofs exist.

title: Constructing Proofs in Symmetric Networks

abstract: A figure-ground segregation network is proposed based on a novel boundary pair representation. Nodes in the network are bound(cid:173) ary segments obtained through local grouping. Each node is ex(cid:173) citatorily coupled with the neighboring nodes that belong to the same region, and inhibitorily coupled with the corresponding paired node. Gestalt grouping rules are incorporated by modulating con(cid:173) nections. The status of a node represents its probability being figural and is updated according to a differential equation. The system solves the figure-ground segregation problem through tem(cid:173) poral evolution. Different perceptual phenomena, such as modal and amodal completion, virtual contours, grouping and shape de(cid:173) composition are then explained through local diffusion. The system eliminates combinatorial optimization and accounts for many psy(cid:173) chophysical results with a fixed set of parameters.

paragraphs: Figure-ground perception requires deciding which image boundaries belong to foreground objects and which indicate background. This paper models that organization through the evolving state of a network. Its representation pairs boundary segments so that competing interpretations can interact locally.

Segments belonging to the same region excite one another, while paired alternatives inhibit one another. Gestalt grouping rules modify those connections, and differential equations update each segment’s probability of being figural. The desired organization emerges over time through local diffusion rather than an explicit combinatorial search over complete interpretations.

With a fixed parameter set, the model accounts for phenomena including completion, virtual contours, grouping, and shape decomposition. The contribution connects several perceptual effects to one dynamical mechanism. It suggests that local interactions among boundary interpretations can produce coherent global organization without requiring a separate hand-designed optimization procedure for each phenomenon.
summary.tldr: A dynamical network of paired boundary segments explains figure-ground organization and several completion effects through local interactions.

title: Perceptual Organization Based on Temporal Dynamics

abstract: It is desirable that a complex decision-making problem in an uncer(cid:173) tain world be adequately modeled by a Markov Decision Process (MDP) whose structural representation is adaptively designed by a parsimonious resources allocation process. Resources include time and cost of exploration, amount of memory and computational time allowed for the policy or value function representation. Concerned about making the best use of the available resources, we address the problem of efficiently estimating where adding extra resources is highly needed in order to improve the expected performance of the resulting policy. Possible application in reinforcement learning (RL) , when real-world exploration is highly costly, concerns the de(cid:173) tection of those areas of the state-space that need primarily to be explored in order to improve the policy. Another application con(cid:173) cerns approximation of continuous state-space stochastic control problems using adaptive discretization techniques for which highly efficient grid points allocation is mandatory to survive high dimen(cid:173) sionality. Maybe surprisingly these two problems can be formu(cid:173) lated under a common framework: for a given resource allocation, which defines a belief state over possible MDPs, find where adding new resources (thus decreasing the uncertainty of some parame(cid:173) ters -transition probabilities or rewards) will most likely increase the expected performance of the new policy. To do so, we use sam(cid:173) pling techniques for estimating the contribution of each parameter's probability distribution function (Pdf) to the expected loss of us(cid:173) ing an approximate policy (such as the optimal policy of the most probable MDP) instead of the true (but unknown) policy.

paragraphs: This paper asks where additional resources would most improve decision-making under uncertainty. Resources can include costly exploration, memory, computation, or a finer representation of the state space. The goal is to allocate them according to their expected effect on policy performance, rather than simply reducing uncertainty wherever it happens to be large.

The authors place exploration and adaptive discretization within a common Markov decision process framework. A current allocation defines beliefs over possible MDPs. Adding resources reduces uncertainty about some transition probabilities or rewards, so the central question becomes which uncertainty reduction is most likely to improve the resulting policy.

Sampling estimates how each parameter's probability distribution contributes to the expected loss from using an approximate policy instead of the true, unknown policy. One example of such an approximation is the optimal policy for the most probable MDP. This connects resource priorities to decision consequences and supplies a common basis for identifying valuable exploration regions or locations that merit additional grid points.
summary.tldr: A sampling-based framework estimates where reducing MDP uncertainty is most likely to improve policy performance.

title: Efficient Resources Allocation for Markov Decision Processes

abstract: Prediction suffix trees (PST) provide a popular and effective tool for tasks such as compression, classification, and language modeling. In this pa- per we take a decision theoretic view of PSTs for the task of sequence prediction. Generalizing the notion of margin to PSTs, we present an on- line PST learning algorithm and derive a loss bound for it. The depth of the PST generated by this algorithm scales linearly with the length of the input. We then describe a self-bounded enhancement of our learning al- gorithm which automatically grows a bounded-depth PST. We also prove an analogous mistake-bound for the self-bounded algorithm. The result is an efficient algorithm that neither relies on a-priori assumptions on the shape or maximal depth of the target PST nor does it require any param- eters. To our knowledge, this is the first provably-correct PST learning algorithm which generates a bounded-depth PST while being competi- tive with any fixed PST determined in hindsight.

paragraphs: Prediction suffix trees use portions of a sequence's recent history to support predictions. This paper studies them from a decision-theoretic perspective and extends the notion of a margin to this setting. The authors first introduce an online learning algorithm and derive a bound on its loss.

The initial algorithm produces a tree whose depth grows linearly with input length. The authors then introduce a self-bounded version that automatically grows a tree of bounded depth and prove a corresponding mistake bound. This addresses the tension between using longer histories for prediction and controlling how much historical context the learned structure retains.

The enhanced method requires neither parameters nor prior assumptions about the target tree's shape or maximum depth. Its guarantee compares it with any fixed prediction suffix tree selected in hindsight. The authors identify this combination of bounded learned depth and retrospective competitiveness as, to their knowledge, a first for a provably correct PST learner. The result connects selective memory growth with a formal prediction guarantee.
summary.tldr: A parameter-free online learner grows a bounded-depth prediction suffix tree while retaining a guarantee against any fixed tree chosen in hindsight.

title: The Power of Selective Memory: Self-Bounded Learning of Prediction Suffix Trees

abstract: Recurrent networks that perform a winner-take-all computation have been studied extensively. Although some of these studies include spik- ing networks, they consider only analog input rates. We present results of this winner-take-all computation on a network of integrate-and-ﬁre neurons which receives spike trains as inputs. We show how we can con- ﬁgure the connectivity in the network so that the winner is selected after a pre-determined number of input spikes. We discuss spiking inputs with both regular frequencies and Poisson-distributed rates. The robustness of the computation was tested by implementing the winner-take-all network on an analog VLSI array of 64 integrate-and-ﬁre neurons which have an innate variance in their operating parameters.

paragraphs: Winner-take-all networks perform a competitive computation that selects a winner among inputs. This paper studies that computation in a network of integrate-and-fire neurons receiving actual spike trains. The distinction matters because earlier studies, including some using spiking neurons, considered analog input rates rather than individual incoming spikes.

The authors show how to configure network connectivity so that a winner is selected after a predetermined number of input spikes. This links the decision process to the arrival of discrete events. They discuss both regularly timed inputs and inputs with Poisson-distributed rates, considering different forms of spike-train input within the same computational setting.

To test robustness, the network is implemented on an analog VLSI array containing 64 integrate-and-fire neurons. Those neurons have inherent variation in their operating parameters, so the hardware test exposes the computation to physical differences among units. The paper combines a connectivity-based account of spike-driven selection with an implementation used to examine robustness under that device variability.
summary.tldr: An integrate-and-fire winner-take-all network can be configured to select a winner after a predetermined number of incoming spikes.

title: Spiking Inputs to a Winner-take-all Network

abstract: We propose a non-linear generative model for human motion data that uses an undirected model with binary latent variables and real-valued "visible" variables that represent joint angles. The latent and visible variables at each time step receive directed connections from the visible variables at the last few time-steps. Such an architecture makes on-line inference efficient and allows us to use a simple approximate learning procedure. After training, the model finds a single set of parameters that simultaneously capture several different kinds of motion. We demonstrate the power of our approach by synthesizing various motion sequences and by performing on-line filling in of data lost during motion capture. Website: http://www.cs.toronto.edu/gwtaylor/publications/nips2006mhmublv/

paragraphs: This paper introduces a nonlinear generative model of human motion in which observed joint angles are represented by real-valued variables and hidden structure by binary variables. The aim is to capture several kinds of motion within one model, while supporting inference as a motion sequence unfolds over time.

At each time step, the hidden and observed variables form an undirected model. Both also receive directed connections from observed variables in the preceding few time steps. This architecture incorporates recent movement history into the current state. According to the authors, it enables efficient online inference and a simple approximate procedure for learning the model.

After training, a single parameter set captures several different motion types. The authors demonstrate the model by generating motion sequences and filling in missing motion-capture data online. These demonstrations show two uses of the same learned motion structure: synthesizing plausible sequences and reconstructing observations that were lost during capture. The contribution combines temporal conditioning with a shared latent representation of different movements.
summary.tldr: A motion model with binary hidden variables captures multiple movement types and supports sequence generation and online missing-data reconstruction.

title: Modeling Human Motion Using Binary Latent Variables

abstract: We describe a nonnegative variant of the "Sparse PCA" problem. The goal is to create a low dimensional representation from a collection of points which on the one hand maximizes the variance of the projected points and on the other uses only parts of the original coordinates, and thereby creating a sparse representation. What distinguishes our problem from other Sparse PCA formulations is that the projection involves only nonnegative weights of the original coordinates -- a desired quality in various fields, including economics, bioinformatics and computer vision. Adding nonnegativity contributes to sparseness, where it enforces a partitioning of the original coordinates among the new axes. We describe a simple yet efficient iterative coordinate-descent type of scheme which converges to a local optimum of our optimization criteria, giving good results on large real world datasets.

paragraphs: Principal component methods seek a smaller representation that preserves variation in the data. Sparse PCA additionally limits how many original coordinates contribute to that representation. This paper studies a version in which the projection weights must also be nonnegative, so a new coordinate combines selected inputs without negative contributions.

The objective balances retaining projected variance with using only parts of the original coordinate set. In the proposed formulation, nonnegativity further promotes sparsity by enforcing a partition of original coordinates among the new axes. This gives the representation a structure in which different axes use different portions of the input coordinates.

The authors develop a simple, efficient iterative method of the coordinate-descent type. It converges to a local optimum of their optimization criterion, which is a specific convergence result rather than a global-optimality guarantee. They report good results on large real-world datasets. The approach is motivated by settings such as economics, bioinformatics, and computer vision, where nonnegative projection weights are a desirable property.
summary.tldr: Nonnegative sparse PCA builds low-dimensional projections from selected input coordinates using an efficient method that converges locally.

title: Nonnegative Sparse PCA

abstract: The Diffusion Network(DN) is a stochastic recurrent network which has been shown capable of modeling the distributions of continuous-valued, continuous-time paths. However, the dynamics of the DN are governed by stochastic differential equations, making the DN unfavourable for simulation in a digital computer. This paper presents the implementation of the DN in analogue Very Large Scale Integration, enabling the DN to be simulated in real time. Moreover, the log-domain representation is applied to the DN, allowing the supply voltage and thus the power consumption to be reduced without limiting the dynamic ranges for diffusion processes. A VLSI chip containing a DN with two stochastic units has been designed and fabricated. The design of component circuits will be described, so will the simulation of the full system be presented. The simulation results demonstrate that the DN in VLSI is able to regenerate various types of continuous paths in real-time.

paragraphs: A Diffusion Network models distributions over paths that vary continuously in both time and value. Its behavior follows stochastic differential equations, making digital simulation inconvenient. This paper develops an analog circuit implementation intended to let the network's continuous stochastic dynamics run in real time.

The design uses a logarithmic representation of the network's variables. The stated benefit is that the supply voltage, and therefore power consumption, can be reduced without restricting the dynamic range of the diffusion processes. This connects the choice of mathematical representation directly to a practical hardware objective: representing a broad range of behavior under a lower supply voltage.

The authors designed and fabricated a chip containing two stochastic units and describe its component circuits. They also present simulations of the complete system, which regenerate several kinds of continuous paths in real time. The reported simulation result supports the feasibility of the analog approach, while the fabricated two-unit chip establishes the concrete scale of the implementation described.
summary.tldr: An analog, log-domain Diffusion Network design supports real-time path generation while allowing lower supply voltage without sacrificing dynamic range.

title: A Log-Domain Implementation of the Diffusion Network in Very Large Scale Integration

abstract: We present a novel class of actor-critic algorithms for actors consisting of sets of interacting modules. We present, analyze theoretically, and empirically evaluate an update rule for each module, which requires only local information: the module's input, output, and the TD error broadcast by a critic. Such updates are necessary when computation of compatible features becomes prohibitively difficult and are also desirable to increase the biological plausibility of reinforcement learning methods.
originalAbstract: We present a novel class of actor-critic algorithms for actors consisting of sets of interacting modules. We present, analyze theoretically, and empirically evaluate an update rule for each module, which requires only local information: the module's input, output, and the TD error broadcast by a critic. Such updates are necessary when computation of compatible features becomes prohibitively difficult and are also desirable to increase the biological plausibility of reinforcement learning methods.

paragraphs: This paper studies reinforcement-learning actors built from interacting modules. Rather than treating the actor as one indivisible decision-making component, it asks how each module can receive a useful learning update. The proposed coagent framework places these modular actors within an actor-critic approach, where a critic supplies a shared learning signal.

Each module's update requires only its own input, its own output, and the temporal-difference error broadcast by the critic. The rule therefore specifies a restricted information requirement for learning inside the actor. The authors present the rule, analyze it theoretically, and evaluate it empirically, making local module updates the central object of investigation.

The motivation is both computational and biological. Computing compatible features can become prohibitively difficult, creating a need for updates that use the available local information. Local updates with a broadcast critic signal are also desirable for making reinforcement-learning models more biologically plausible. The contribution is a class of algorithms designed around those information requirements for interacting modules.
summary.tldr: Coagent networks train interacting actor modules using only each module's input, output, and a critic's broadcast temporal-difference error.

title: Policy Gradient Coagent Networks

abstract: Inference in matrix-variate Gaussian models has major applications for multi- output prediction and joint learning of row and column covariances from matrix- variate data. Here, we discuss an approach for efﬁcient inference in such models that explicitly account for iid observation noise. Computational tractability can be retained by exploiting the Kronecker product between row and column covariance matrices. Using this framework, we show how to generalize the Graphical Lasso in order to learn a sparse inverse covariance between features while accounting for a low-rank confounding covariance between samples. We show practical utility on applications to biology, where we model covariances with more than 100,000 di- mensions. We ﬁnd greater accuracy in recovering biological network structures and are able to better reconstruct the confounders.

paragraphs: Matrix-valued data can contain dependencies both across rows and across columns. The paper studies Gaussian models that learn these two covariance structures while explicitly accounting for independent, identically distributed observation noise. This setting matters for predicting multiple outputs and for understanding relationships in data whose two axes both carry meaningful statistical structure.

The approach preserves computational tractability by exploiting the Kronecker product structure of the row and column covariance matrices. Within this framework, the authors generalize the Graphical Lasso to estimate a sparse inverse covariance among features while also modeling a low-rank confounding covariance among samples. This allows feature relationships and sample-level confounding to be considered within one model.

Biological applications demonstrate the framework with covariance models exceeding 100,000 dimensions. The authors report greater accuracy in recovering biological network structure and better reconstruction of the confounders. These findings support the practical value of incorporating sample dependencies alongside feature structure, while the structured covariance calculation makes the large modeled dimension computationally manageable.
summary.tldr: Structured Gaussian inference handles observation noise and sample confounding efficiently while improving biological network recovery in the reported applications.

title: Efficient inference in matrix-variate Gaussian models with \iid observation noise

abstract: In this paper, we study Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS) in zero-sum extensive-form games with perfect information and simultaneous moves. We present a general template of MCTS algorithms for these games, which can be instantiated by various selection methods. We formally prove that if a selection method is $\epsilon$-Hannan consistent in a matrix game and satisfies additional requirements on exploration, then the MCTS algorithm eventually converges to an approximate Nash equilibrium (NE) of the extensive-form game. We empirically evaluate this claim using regret matching and Exp3 as the selection methods on randomly generated and worst case games. We confirm the formal result and show that additional MCTS variants also converge to approximate NE on the evaluated games.
originalAbstract: In this paper, we study Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS) in zero-sum extensive-form games with perfect information and simultaneous moves. We present a general template of MCTS algorithms for these games, which can be instantiated by various selection methods. We formally prove that if a selection method is $\epsilon$-Hannan consistent in a matrix game and satisfies additional requirements on exploration, then the MCTS algorithm eventually converges to an approximate Nash equilibrium (NE) of the extensive-form game. We empirically evaluate this claim using regret matching and Exp3 as the selection methods on randomly generated and worst case games. We confirm the formal result and show that additional MCTS variants also converge to approximate NE on the evaluated games.

paragraphs: Monte Carlo tree search explores a game through repeated simulations, but its long-run behavior depends on how actions are selected. This paper studies games in which players can move simultaneously. Its setting is specifically zero-sum extensive-form games with perfect information, so the convergence claim is tied to that game class.

The authors give a general tree-search template that can use different selection methods. They prove a conditional result: if the selection method is epsilon-Hannan consistent in a matrix game and meets additional exploration requirements, the resulting search eventually approaches an approximate Nash equilibrium of the full game. The key connection is between controlled regret in local action selection and equilibrium behavior across the larger game tree.

Experiments instantiate the template with regret matching and Exp3 on randomly generated and worst-case games. The results support the formal convergence claim. Additional search variants also approach approximate equilibria in the evaluated games, but those observations are empirical. The paper therefore provides both a sufficient theoretical route to convergence and evidence about practical variants.
summary.tldr: Under specified regret and exploration conditions, Monte Carlo tree search converges to approximate Nash equilibria in simultaneous-move zero-sum games.

title: Convergence of Monte Carlo Tree Search in Simultaneous Move Games

abstract: We present the first provably sublinear time hashing algorithm for approximate \emph{Maximum Inner Product Search} (MIPS). Searching with (un-normalized) inner product as the underlying similarity measure is a known difficult problem and finding hashing schemes for MIPS was considered hard. While the existing Locality Sensitive Hashing (LSH) framework is insufficient for solving MIPS, in this paper we extend the LSH framework to allow asymmetric hashing schemes. Our proposal is based on a key observation that the problem of finding maximum inner products, after independent asymmetric transformations, can be converted into the problem of approximate near neighbor search in classical settings. This key observation makes efficient sublinear hashing scheme for MIPS possible. Under the extended asymmetric LSH (ALSH) framework, this paper provides an example of explicit construction of provably fast hashing scheme for MIPS. Our proposed algorithm is simple and easy to implement. The proposed hashing scheme leads to significant computational savings over the two popular conventional LSH schemes: (i) Sign Random Projection (SRP) and (ii) hashing based on $p$-stable distributions for $L_2$ norm (L2LSH), in the collaborative filtering task of item recommendations on Netflix and Movielens (10M) datasets.

Under the extended asymmetric LSH (ALSH) framework, this paper provides an example of explicit construction of provably fast hashing scheme for MIPS. Our proposed algorithm is simple and easy to implement. The proposed hashing scheme leads to significant computational savings over the two popular conventional LSH schemes: (i) Sign Random Projection (SRP) and (ii) hashing based on $p$-stable distributions for $L_2$ norm (L2LSH), in the collaborative filtering task of item recommendations on Netflix and Movielens (10M) datasets.

paragraphs: Maximum inner product search seeks items with the largest inner product with a query, without requiring vectors to be normalized. The paper addresses the difficulty of building fast hashing schemes for this similarity measure. It presents what the authors describe as the first provably sublinear-time hashing algorithm for approximate maximum inner product search.

The central change is to allow asymmetric hashing. Independent transformations convert the inner product search problem into approximate near-neighbor search in a classical setting. This expands the existing locality-sensitive hashing framework and makes it possible to construct an explicit scheme with a provable speed guarantee. The approximation concerns the search result; the sublinear guarantee concerns how search time scales.

The authors also report a simple implementation and evaluate it for collaborative-filtering recommendations on Netflix and Movielens datasets. Their scheme provides significant computational savings over sign random projection and L2 hashing based on p-stable distributions. The results connect the transformation-based argument to a practical retrieval task where inner products determine which items should be recommended.
summary.tldr: Asymmetric transformations enable provably sublinear approximate maximum inner product search through locality-sensitive hashing.

title: Asymmetric LSH (ALSH) for Sublinear Time Maximum Inner Product Search (MIPS)

abstract: We propose a robust and efficient approach to the problem of compressive phase retrieval in which the goal is to reconstruct a sparse vector from the magnitude of a number of its linear measurements. The proposed framework relies on constrained sensing vectors and a two-stage reconstruction method that consists of two standard convex programs that are solved sequentially.In recent years, various methods are proposed for compressive phase retrieval, but they have suboptimal sample complexity or lack robustness guarantees. The main obstacle has been that there is no straightforward convex relaxations for the type of structure in the target. Given a set of underdetermined measurements, there is a standard framework for recovering a sparse matrix, and a standard framework for recovering a low-rank matrix. However, a general, efficient method for recovering a jointly sparse and low-rank matrix has remained elusive.Deviating from the models with generic measurements, in this paper we show that if the sensing vectors are chosen at random from an incoherent subspace, then the low-rank and sparse structures of the target signal can be effectively decoupled. We show that a recovery algorithm that consists of a low-rank recovery stage followed by a sparse recovery stage will produce an accurate estimate of the target when the number of measurements is $\mathsf{O}(k\,\log\frac{d}{k})$, where $k$ and $d$ denote the sparsity level and the dimension of the input signal. We also evaluate the algorithm through numerical simulation.

paragraphs: Compressive phase retrieval reconstructs a sparse vector using only the magnitudes of linear measurements. The difficulty combines missing phase information with sparsity. In matrix formulations, this creates a target that is both low rank and sparse, a combination that is difficult to recover through a general efficient convex method.

The paper changes how measurements are constructed. Sensing vectors are sampled randomly from an incoherent subspace, allowing the low-rank and sparse aspects of the recovery problem to be separated. Reconstruction then proceeds through two standard convex programs: first low-rank recovery, followed by sparse recovery.

They also evaluate the algorithm numerically. The result demonstrates how a deliberate restriction on measurement vectors can make a difficult combined structure manageable through sequential recovery methods, while retaining a favorable measurement requirement.
summary.tldr: Structured random sensing separates low-rank and sparse recovery, enabling accurate compressive phase retrieval through two convex programs.

title: Efficient Compressive Phase Retrieval with Constrained Sensing Vectors

abstract: In addition to identifying the content within a single image, relating images and generating related images are critical tasks for image understanding. Recently, deep convolutional networks have yielded breakthroughs in producing image labels, annotations and captions, but have only just begun to be used for producing high-quality image outputs. In this paper we develop a novel deep network trained end-to-end to perform visual analogy making, which is the task of transforming a query image according to an example pair of related images. Solving this problem requires both accurately recognizing a visual relationship and generating a transformed query image accordingly. Inspired by recent advances in language modeling, we propose to solve visual analogies by learning to map images to a neural embedding in which analogical reasoning is simple, such as by vector subtraction and addition. In experiments, our model effectively models visual analogies on several datasets: 2D shapes, animated video game sprites, and 3D car models.

paragraphs: Visual analogy asks a system to inspect a related pair of images and apply the same relationship to a new query image. This requires more than identifying the objects present. The system must recognize how the example images relate and then generate an image expressing that relationship for the query.

The paper introduces a deep network trained end to end for this task. Its central idea is to map images into a learned neural embedding where relationships can be represented through simple operations such as vector subtraction and addition. The representation therefore serves two connected purposes: making the example transformation easy to express and supporting generation of the transformed query image.

Experiments demonstrate effective visual analogy modeling on datasets containing two-dimensional shapes, animated video game sprites, and three-dimensional car models. These findings support the usefulness of learning an image representation organized around relationships as well as content. The contribution brings recognition and image generation together within one model for transferring an observed visual relationship.
summary.tldr: An end-to-end network learns image embeddings where simple vector operations transfer visual relationships to new query images.

title: Deep Visual Analogy-Making

abstract: Autonomous agents optimize the reward function we give them. What they don't know is how hard it is for us to design a reward function that actually captures what we want. When designing the reward, we might think of some specific training scenarios, and make sure that the reward will lead to the right behavior in those scenarios. Inevitably, agents encounter new scenarios (e.g., new types of terrain) where optimizing that same reward may lead to undesired behavior. Our insight is that reward functions are merely observations about what the designer actually wants, and that they should be interpreted in the context in which they were designed. We introduce inverse reward design (IRD) as the problem of inferring the true objective based on the designed reward and the training MDP. We introduce approximate methods for solving IRD problems, and use their solution to plan risk-averse behavior in test MDPs. Empirical results suggest that this approach can help alleviate negative side effects of misspecified reward functions and mitigate reward hacking.

paragraphs: A reward function can encourage the intended behavior in familiar training situations yet produce unwanted behavior in new ones. This paper attributes part of that problem to how rewards are designed: a designer may check a limited set of scenarios without fully specifying what should happen everywhere.

Inverse reward design treats the written reward as evidence about the designer's true objective. It interprets that evidence together with the training Markov decision process, which describes the context in which the reward was created. The inference problem is therefore to recover information about the intended objective from both the reward and its design environment.

The authors introduce approximate methods for this inference and use their outputs to plan risk-averse behavior in test environments. Their empirical results suggest that the approach can reduce harmful side effects of misspecified rewards and mitigate reward hacking. The contribution is a way to carry uncertainty about design intent into planning, with evidence of benefits rather than a guarantee that reward misspecification is eliminated.
summary.tldr: Inverse reward design infers intended objectives from rewards and their training context to support risk-averse behavior in new environments.

title: Inverse Reward Design

abstract: We study the basic problem of learning overcomplete HMMs---those that have many hidden states but a small output alphabet. Despite having significant practical importance, such HMMs are poorly understood with no known positive or negative results for efficient learning. In this paper, we present several new results---both positive and negative---which help define the boundaries between the tractable-learning setting and the intractable setting. We show positive results for a large subclass of HMMs whose transition matrices are sparse, well-conditioned and have small probability mass on short cycles. We also show that learning is impossible given only a polynomial number of samples for HMMs with a small output alphabet and whose transition matrices are random regular graphs with large degree. We also discuss these results in the context of learning HMMs which can capture long-term dependencies.

paragraphs: An overcomplete hidden Markov model has many hidden states but only a small alphabet of observable outputs. That mismatch makes learning difficult because many internal configurations must be inferred from limited observable symbols. The paper develops positive and negative results that distinguish tractable cases from settings where data are insufficient.

The positive results apply to a large subclass whose transition matrices are sparse, well-conditioned, and assign little probability mass to short cycles. These structural requirements are part of the learning guarantee and cannot be dropped when interpreting the result.

Conversely, the authors show that a polynomial number of samples cannot suffice for certain models with small output alphabets and transition matrices formed by high-degree random regular graphs. They discuss implications for modeling long-term dependencies. The contribution is a map of learnability boundaries, rather than a single algorithm claimed to handle all overcomplete hidden Markov models.
summary.tldr: Structural assumptions determine when hidden Markov models with many hidden states can be learned.

title: Learning Overcomplete HMMs

abstract: Despite the success of single-agent reinforcement learning, multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) remains challenging due to complex interactions between agents. Motivated by decentralized applications such as sensor networks, swarm robotics, and power grids, we study policy evaluation in MARL, where agents with jointly observed state-action pairs and private local rewards collaborate to learn the value of a given policy. In this paper, we propose a double averaging scheme, where each agent iteratively performs averaging over both space and time to incorporate neighboring gradient information and local reward information, respectively. We prove that the proposed algorithm converges to the optimal solution at a global geometric rate. In particular, such an algorithm is built upon a primal-dual reformulation of the mean squared Bellman error minimization problem, which gives rise to a decentralized convex-concave saddle-point problem. To the best of our knowledge, the proposed double averaging primal-dual optimization algorithm is the first to achieve fast finite-time convergence on decentralized convex-concave saddle-point problems.

paragraphs: This paper studies how multiple agents can collaboratively evaluate a given policy when they jointly observe state-action pairs but receive private local rewards. The task is to estimate the policy's value through decentralized cooperation. Complex interactions between agents make this harder than evaluating a policy with a single learner.

The proposed algorithm combines two kinds of averaging. Averaging across neighboring agents incorporates gradient information from elsewhere in the network, while averaging over time incorporates local reward information. The authors derive this procedure by reformulating mean squared Bellman error minimization as a primal-dual problem, producing a decentralized convex-concave saddle-point formulation.

They prove that the resulting algorithm reaches the optimal solution at a global geometric rate. This provides a fast finite-time convergence result for the decentralized optimization problem underlying policy evaluation. The paper presents this as, to the authors' knowledge, the first such fast result for decentralized convex-concave saddle-point problems. Its contribution concerns evaluating a supplied policy under the stated information-sharing arrangement.
summary.tldr: A decentralized policy-evaluation algorithm averages information across agents and time and has a proven global geometric convergence rate.

title: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning via Double Averaging Primal-Dual Optimization

abstract: Communication could potentially be an effective way for multi-agent cooperation. However, information sharing among all agents or in predefined communication architectures that existing methods adopt can be problematic. When there is a large number of agents, agents cannot differentiate valuable information that helps cooperative decision making from globally shared information. Therefore, communication barely helps, and could even impair the learning of multi-agent cooperation. Predefined communication architectures, on the other hand, restrict communication among agents and thus restrain potential cooperation. To tackle these difficulties, in this paper, we propose an attentional communication model that learns when communication is needed and how to integrate shared information for cooperative decision making. Our model leads to efficient and effective communication for large-scale multi-agent cooperation. Empirically, we show the strength of our model in a variety of cooperative scenarios, where agents are able to develop more coordinated and sophisticated strategies than existing methods.

paragraphs: Communication can help cooperative agents, but broadcasting everything becomes problematic as the group grows. Useful information can be buried in irrelevant messages, while a fixed communication architecture can prevent helpful exchanges. This paper addresses both issues by learning how communication should support decisions.

The proposed attentional communication model learns when communication is needed and how to integrate the information that is shared. Its aim is efficient, effective cooperation among many agents, with communication adapted to the task rather than uniformly available or restricted by a predefined pattern.

Experiments span multiple cooperative scenarios and show agents developing more coordinated and sophisticated strategies than existing methods. The abstract does not specify agent counts, communication costs, or quantitative improvements. The supported conclusion is that learned selection and integration of messages improve cooperation in the tested settings; it is not a guarantee for every large multi-agent system.
summary.tldr: Learned attention decides when agents should communicate and how shared information should influence actions.

title: Learning Attentional Communication for Multi-Agent Cooperation

abstract: A large class of machine learning techniques requires the solution of optimization problems involving spectral functions of parametric matrices, e.g. log-determinant and nuclear norm. Unfortunately, computing the gradient of a spectral function is generally of cubic complexity, as such gradient descent methods are rather expensive for optimizing objectives involving the spectral function. Thus, one naturally turns to stochastic gradient methods in hope that they will provide a way to reduce or altogether avoid the computation of full gradients. However, here a new challenge appears: there is no straightforward way to compute unbiased stochastic gradients for spectral functions. In this paper, we develop unbiased stochastic gradients for spectral-sums, an important subclass of spectral functions. Our unbiased stochastic gradients are based on combining randomized trace estimators with stochastic truncation of the Chebyshev expansions. A careful design of the truncation distribution allows us to offer distributions that are variance-optimal, which is crucial for fast and stable convergence of stochastic gradient methods. We further leverage our proposed stochastic gradients to devise stochastic methods for objective functions involving spectral-sums, and rigorously analyze their convergence rate. The utility of our methods is demonstrated in numerical experiments.

title: Stochastic Chebyshev Gradient Descent for Spectral Optimization

abstract: As machine learning becomes more widely used in practice, we need new methods to build complex intelligent systems that integrate learning with existing software, and with domain knowledge encoded as rules. As a case study, we present such a system that learns to parse Newtonian physics problems in textbooks. This system, Nuts&Bolts, learns a pipeline process that incorporates existing code, pre-learned machine learning models, and human engineered rules. It jointly trains the entire pipeline to prevent propagation of errors, using a combination of labelled and unlabelled data. Our approach achieves a good performance on the parsing task, outperforming the simple pipeline and its variants. Finally, we also show how Nuts&Bolts can be used to achieve improvements on a relation extraction task and on the end task of answering Newtonian physics problems.

paragraphs: Practical intelligent systems often combine learned models with existing software and rules written by domain experts. Training such a system is difficult because mistakes made by one stage can affect later stages. This paper studies that challenge through parsing textbook problems about Newtonian physics, where understanding the text requires a coordinated processing pipeline.

The proposed system, Nuts&Bolts, integrates existing code, previously learned models, and human-engineered rules. It trains the pipeline jointly using both labeled and unlabeled examples, with the goal of preventing errors from propagating through separately trained components. The approach therefore treats learning as a system-wide problem while retaining useful components and domain knowledge already available.

On the parsing task, Nuts&Bolts outperforms a simple pipeline and its variants. The authors also demonstrate improvements in relation extraction and in the final task of answering Newtonian physics problems. These results connect better coordination inside the pipeline to better downstream outcomes, showing why joint learning can matter beyond the accuracy of any single processing stage.
summary.tldr: Nuts&Bolts jointly trains a pipeline combining models, software, and rules to improve physics-problem parsing and downstream answering.

title: Learning Pipelines with Limited Data and Domain Knowledge: A Study in Parsing Physics Problems

abstract: Reverse engineering of binary executables is a critical problem in the computer security domain. On the one hand, malicious parties may recover interpretable source codes from the software products to gain commercial advantages. On the other hand, binary decompilation can be leveraged for code vulnerability analysis and malware detection. However, efficient binary decompilation is challenging. Conventional decompilers have the following major limitations: (i) they are only applicable to specific source-target language pair, hence incurs undesired development cost for new language tasks; (ii) their output high-level code cannot effectively preserve the correct functionality of the input binary; (iii) their output program does not capture the semantics of the input and the reversed program is hard to interpret. To address the above problems, we propose Coda1, the first end-to-end neural-based framework for code decompilation. Coda decomposes the decompilation task into of two key phases: First, Coda employs an instruction type-aware encoder and a tree decoder for generating an abstract syntax tree (AST) with attention feeding during the code sketch generation stage. Second, Coda then updates the code sketch using an iterative error correction machine guided by an ensembled neural error predictor. By finding a good approximate candidate and then fixing it towards perfect, Coda achieves superior with performance compared to baseline approaches. We assess Coda’s performance with extensive experiments on various benchmarks. Evaluation results show that Coda achieves an average of 82% program recovery accuracy on unseen binary samples, where the state-of-the-art decompilers yield 0% accuracy. Furthermore, Coda outperforms the sequence-to-sequence model with attention by a margin of 70% program accuracy. Our work reveals the vulnerability of binary executables and imposes a new threat to the protection of Intellectual Property (IP) for software development.

title: Coda: An End-to-End Neural Program Decompiler

abstract: Reward Machines (RMs), originally proposed for specifying problems in Reinforcement Learning (RL), provide a structured, automata-based representation of a reward function that allows an agent to decompose problems into subproblems that can be efficiently learned using off-policy learning. Here we show that RMs can be learned from experience, instead of being specified by the user, and that the resulting problem decomposition can be used to effectively solve partially observable RL problems. We pose the task of learning RMs as a discrete optimization problem where the objective is to find an RM that decomposes the problem into a set of subproblems such that the combination of their optimal memoryless policies is an optimal policy for the original problem. We show the effectiveness of this approach on three partially observable domains, where it significantly outperforms A3C, PPO, and ACER, and discuss its advantages, limitations, and broader potential.

Here we show that RMs can be learned from experience, instead of being specified by the user, and that the resulting problem decomposition can be used to effectively solve partially observable RL problems. paragraphs: Reward machines represent a reinforcement learning reward function using an automaton, giving the task a structured decomposition into smaller problems. Those subproblems can be learned efficiently with off-policy methods. This paper shows how to learn reward machines from experience, removing the need for a user to specify that structure in advance.

The authors formulate the search for a reward machine as discrete optimization. The objective is to find a decomposition whose subproblems have optimal memoryless policies that combine into an optimal policy for the original task. This is especially relevant under partial observability, where choosing an action from the current observation alone may not capture the information needed for the whole problem.

Experiments in three partially observable domains show significant improvements over A3C, PPO, and ACER. The findings support learning useful task structure alongside behavior, rather than requiring the structure to be supplied beforehand. The contribution combines an explicit criterion for a useful decomposition with empirical evidence that learned reward machines can help solve the tested problems.
summary.tldr: Learning reward machines from experience provides task decompositions that improve reinforcement learning in three partially observable domains.

title: Learning Reward Machines for Partially Observable Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Many time series are effectively generated by a combination of deterministic continuous flows along with discrete jumps sparked by stochastic events. However, we usually do not have the equation of motion describing the flows, or how they are affected by jumps. To this end, we introduce Neural Jump Stochastic Differential Equations that provide a data-driven approach to learn continuous and discrete dynamic behavior, i.e., hybrid systems that both flow and jump. Our approach extends the framework of Neural Ordinary Differential Equations with a stochastic process term that models discrete events. We then model temporal point processes with a piecewise-continuous latent trajectory, where the discontinuities are caused by stochastic events whose conditional intensity depends on the latent state. We demonstrate the predictive capabilities of our model on a range of synthetic and real-world marked point process datasets, including classical point processes (such as Hawkes processes), awards on Stack Overflow, medical records, and earthquake monitoring.

paragraphs: Some time series evolve smoothly between events but change abruptly when an event occurs. Modeling either component alone misses part of that behavior. This paper develops a data-driven way to learn both the continuous motion and the jumps when the equations describing them are not already known.

Neural Jump Stochastic Differential Equations extend Neural Ordinary Differential Equations with a stochastic process term for discrete events. The resulting latent trajectory is continuous between events and can jump at event times. Event intensity depends on the latent state, connecting the system's current internal condition to the likelihood of another event occurring.

The authors use this construction to model temporal point processes and demonstrate predictive capabilities on synthetic and real marked-event datasets. Their evaluations include classical processes such as Hawkes processes, Stack Overflow awards, medical records, and earthquake monitoring. The contribution is a unified representation of evolving state and abrupt event-driven changes, with predictive demonstrations across several kinds of event sequences rather than a model confined to only continuous dynamics.
summary.tldr: Neural Jump Stochastic Differential Equations learn continuous dynamics together with random event-driven jumps for modeling temporal event sequences.

title: Neural Jump Stochastic Differential Equations

abstract: Behavioral cloning reduces policy learning to supervised learning by training a discriminative model to predict expert actions given observations. Such discriminative models are non-causal: the training procedure is unaware of the causal structure of the interaction between the expert and the environment. We point out that ignoring causality is particularly damaging because of the distributional shift in imitation learning. In particular, it leads to a counter-intuitive "causal misidentification" phenomenon: access to more information can yield worse performance. We investigate how this problem arises, and propose a solution to combat it through targeted interventions---either environment interaction or expert queries---to determine the correct causal model. We show that causal misidentification occurs in several benchmark control domains as well as realistic driving settings, and validate our solution against DAgger and other baselines and ablations.

paragraphs: Behavioral cloning teaches an agent to predict an expert's actions from observations. This turns imitation into supervised learning, but the predictor does not automatically distinguish causal relationships from correlations. The paper argues that this distinction becomes especially consequential when the agent's own behavior changes the observations it encounters.

The authors identify causal misidentification: a learner can use the wrong observed variables to explain expert behavior. Because imitation involves a shift between training and deployment distributions, those relationships can become unreliable. One striking consequence is that giving the learner more information can worsen its performance. Additional observations create more opportunities to rely on misleading associations.

The proposed solution uses targeted interventions, through interaction with the environment or questions to the expert, to identify the correct causal model. The paper demonstrates the problem in benchmark control tasks and realistic driving settings, then evaluates the intervention-based solution against DAgger and other comparisons. Its central message is that resolving causal ambiguity can be an essential part of learning to imitate.
summary.tldr: Imitation learners can perform worse with more information when they confuse correlation with causation; targeted interventions help resolve that confusion.

title: Causal Confusion in Imitation Learning

abstract: A panel dataset contains features or observations for multiple individuals over multiple time periods and regression problems with panel data are common in statistics and applied ML. When dealing with massive datasets, coresets have emerged as a valuable tool from a computational, storage and privacy perspective, as one needs to work with and share much smaller datasets. However, results on coresets for regression problems thus far have only been available for cross-sectional data ($N$ individuals each observed for a single time unit) or longitudinal data (a single individual observed for $T>1$ time units), but there are no results for panel data ($N>1$, $T>1$). This paper introduces the problem of coresets to panel data settings; we first define coresets for several variants of regression problems with panel data and then present efficient algorithms to construct coresets of size that are independent of $N$ and $T$, and only polynomially depend on $1/\varepsilon$ (where $\varepsilon$ is the error parameter) and the number of regression parameters. Our approach is based on the Feldman-Langberg framework in which a key step is to upper bound the “total sensitivity” that is roughly the sum of maximum influences of all individual-time pairs taken over all possible choices of regression parameters. Empirically, we assess our approach with a synthetic and a real-world datasets; the coreset sizes constructed using our approach are much smaller than the full dataset and coresets indeed accelerate the running time of computing the regression objective.

The paper develops coresets for regression in this setting: much smaller datasets designed to approximate the relevant regression problem. Previous coreset results covered either many individuals at a single time or one individual over many times, leaving the combined panel setting unaddressed.

Their coreset sizes are independent of both the number of individuals and the number of time periods. Tests on synthetic and real-world data produce coresets much smaller than the full datasets and speed up evaluation of the regression objective. These findings support the computational value of the theoretical size guarantees.
summary.tldr: The paper constructs panel-regression coresets whose sizes do not depend on the number of individuals or time periods.

title: Coresets for Regressions with Panel Data

abstract: L1 regularization has been broadly employed to pursue model sparsity. Despite the non-smoothness, people have developed efficient algorithms by leveraging the sparsity and convexity of the problems. In this paper, we propose a novel active incremental approach to further improve the efficiency of the solvers. We show that our method performs well even when the existing methods fail due to the low sparseness or high solution accuracy request. Theoretical analysis and experimental results on synthetic and real-world data sets validate the advantages of the method.

Despite the non-smoothness, people have developed efficient algorithms by leveraging the sparsity and convexity of the problems. In this paper, we propose a novel active incremental approach to further improve the efficiency of the solvers. We show that our method performs well even when the existing methods fail due to the low sparseness or high solution accuracy request. Theoretical analysis and experimental results on synthetic and real-world data sets validate the advantages of the method.

paragraphs: L1 regularization is widely used to encourage sparse models, in which many parameters are zero. Solving the resulting optimization problems requires dealing with a nonsmooth objective. Existing efficient algorithms exploit the problems’ convexity and sparsity, but the usefulness of those approaches can depend on how sparse the solution is and how accurately it must be computed.

Thunder introduces an active incremental approach to improve solver efficiency. The paper presents it as a coordinate-selection solver, placing the choice of coordinates to work on at the center of the method. Its aim is to improve computation for sparse learning, including demanding cases where existing methods struggle.

The authors report that the method performs well when solutions have relatively low sparsity or when high solution accuracy is required. They support its advantages with theoretical analysis and experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets. These findings matter because a solver’s practical usefulness depends on more than performance in strongly sparse, moderate-accuracy settings. Thunder targets efficiency across cases that challenge methods relying heavily on favorable sparsity.
summary.tldr: Thunder improves L1-regularized optimization with active incremental coordinate selection, including cases with limited sparsity or demanding accuracy requirements.

title: Thunder: a Fast Coordinate Selection Solver for Sparse Learning

abstract: In this paper, a rather general online problem called \emph{dynamic resource allocation with capacity constraints (DRACC)} is introduced and studied in the realm of posted price mechanisms. This problem subsumes several applications of stateful pricing, including but not limited to posted prices for online job scheduling and matching over a dynamic bipartite graph. As the existing online learning techniques do not yield vanishing-regret mechanisms for this problem, we develop a novel online learning framework defined over deterministic Markov decision processes with \emph{dynamic} state transition and reward functions. We then prove that if the Markov decision process is guaranteed to admit an oracle that can simulate any given policy from any initial state with bounded loss --- a condition that is satisfied in the DRACC problem --- then the online learning problem can be solved with vanishing regret. Our proof technique is based on a reduction to online learning with \emph{switching cost}, in which an online decision maker incurs an extra cost every time she switches from one arm to another. We formally demonstrate this connection and further show how DRACC can be used in our proposed applications of stateful pricing.

paragraphs: Posted prices can affect both immediate outcomes and the resources available for later decisions. This paper introduces dynamic resource allocation with capacity constraints, or DRACC, to study such stateful pricing problems. The formulation includes applications such as online job scheduling and matching in a changing bipartite graph.

To obtain vanishing regret, the authors develop an online learning framework over deterministic Markov decision processes whose transition and reward functions can change. Their guarantee requires an oracle that can simulate any specified policy from any starting state while incurring bounded loss. They show that DRACC satisfies this condition, connecting the general framework to the pricing applications.

The proof reduces the problem to online learning with switching costs, where changing the selected action incurs an additional cost. This connects the difficulty of managing state across decisions to an established form of online decision-making penalty. Under the oracle condition, the resulting framework achieves vanishing regret. The paper also formally develops the connection and shows how its resource-allocation formulation applies to the stated pricing problems.
summary.tldr: A reduction to online learning with switching costs yields vanishing regret for stateful pricing under a bounded-loss policy-simulation condition.

title: Stateful Posted Pricing with Vanishing Regret via Dynamic Deterministic Markov Decision Processes

abstract: Incorporating the natural document-sentence-word structure into hierarchical Bayesian modeling, we propose convolutional Poisson gamma dynamical systems (PGDS) that introduce not only word-level probabilistic convolutions, but also sentence-level stochastic temporal transitions. With word-level convolutions capturing phrase-level topics and sentence-level transitions capturing how the topic usages evolve over consecutive sentences, we aggregate the topic proportions of all sentences of a document as its feature representation. To consider not only forward but also backward sentence-level information transmissions, we further develop a bidirectional convolutional PGDS to incorporate the full contextual information to represent each sentence. For efficient inference, we construct a convolutional-recurrent inference network, which provides both sentence-level and document-level representations, and introduce a hybrid Bayesian inference scheme combining stochastic-gradient MCMC and amortized variational inference. Experimental results on a variety of document corpora demonstrate that the proposed models can extract expressive multi-level latent representations, including interpretable phrase-level topics and sentence-level temporal transitions as well as discriminative document-level features, achieving state-of-the-art document categorization performance while being memory and computation efficient.

paragraphs: This paper builds a probabilistic document model around the organization of words into sentences and sentences into documents. Word-level convolutions capture topics expressed through phrases, while stochastic transitions model how topic usage changes between consecutive sentences. Aggregating the topic proportions of individual sentences produces a representation of the whole document.

The bidirectional version lets information travel both forward and backward through the sentence sequence. Consequently, a sentence representation can incorporate context from sentences on either side. This extends the model beyond describing topic progression in only one direction while retaining representations at several levels of the document.

For efficient inference, the authors combine a convolutional-recurrent network with a hybrid of stochastic-gradient MCMC and amortized variational inference. Across multiple document collections, they report interpretable phrase topics and sentence transitions, along with document features useful for distinguishing categories. The models achieve state-of-the-art document categorization performance in the reported experiments while remaining efficient in memory and computation.
summary.tldr: A hierarchical probabilistic model combines phrase topics and bidirectional sentence transitions to learn interpretable, effective document representations.

title: Bidirectional Convolutional Poisson Gamma Dynamical Systems

abstract: Commonly used classification algorithms in machine learning, such as support vector machines, minimize a convex surrogate loss on training examples. In practice, these algorithms are surprisingly robust to errors in the training data. In this work, we identify a set of conditions on the data under which such surrogate loss minimization algorithms provably learn the correct classifier. This allows us to establish, in a unified framework, the robustness of these algorithms under various models on data as well as error. In particular, we show that if the data is linearly classifiable with a slightly non-trivial margin (i.e. a margin at least $C\div\sqrt{d}$ for $d$-dimensional unit vectors), and the class-conditional distributions are near isotropic and logconcave, then surrogate loss minimization has negligible error on the uncorrupted data even when a constant fraction of examples are adversarially mislabeled.

paragraphs: Classification algorithms such as support vector machines often learn by minimizing a convex surrogate loss. They can show substantial robustness to errors in training data, and this paper asks when that behavior has a mathematical guarantee. The authors identify conditions under which surrogate-loss minimization provably learns the correct classifier.

Their analysis provides a unified treatment of multiple data and error models. A specific result assumes that the data are linearly classifiable with a margin of at least C divided by the square root of the dimension, for unit-length input vectors. It also requires the class-conditional distributions to be near isotropic and logconcave. These distributional and separation conditions are part of the guarantee.

Under those conditions, surrogate-loss minimization has negligible error on uncorrupted data even if an adversary mislabels a constant fraction of the examples. The result supplies sufficient conditions for strong resistance to label corruption. Its significance is that adversarial training errors can coexist with reliable classification when the data have the stated geometric and distributional structure.
summary.tldr: Under stated margin and distributional conditions, surrogate-loss minimization tolerates a constant fraction of adversarially corrupted labels.

title: On the Error Resistance of Hinge-Loss Minimization

abstract: A vital aspect of human intelligence is the ability to compose increasingly complex concepts out of simpler ideas, enabling both rapid learning and adaptation of knowledge. In this paper we show that energy-based models can exhibit this ability by directly combining probability distributions. Samples from the combined distribution correspond to compositions of concepts. For example, given a distribution for smiling faces, and another for male faces, we can combine them to generate smiling male faces. This allows us to generate natural images that simultaneously satisfy conjunctions, disjunctions, and negations of concepts. We evaluate compositional generation abilities of our model on the CelebA dataset of natural faces and synthetic 3D scene images. We also demonstrate other unique advantages of our model, such as the ability to continually learn and incorporate new concepts, or infer compositions of concept properties underlying an image.

Its central idea is to combine probability distributions represented by energy-based models. Sampling from the resulting distribution then produces images corresponding to the combined concepts, connecting a mathematical operation on distributions to a visible change in generated content.

For example, distributions describing smiling faces and male faces can be combined to generate smiling male faces. The approach also supports conjunctions, disjunctions, and negations: combinations expressing that concepts occur together, that alternatives are allowed, or that a concept should be absent. This makes composition a direct part of the generation mechanism.

The authors evaluate these capabilities using natural faces from CelebA and synthetic three-dimensional scenes. They also demonstrate that the model can continually incorporate new concepts and infer combinations of concept properties underlying an image. These results support the use of energy-based models as a framework for both constructing visual concept combinations and reasoning about combinations already present in images.
summary.tldr: Energy-based models compose probability distributions to generate images satisfying combinations, alternatives, and negations of visual concepts.

title: Compositional Visual Generation with Energy Based Models

abstract: The information-theoretic framework of Russo and Zou (2016) and Xu and Raginsky (2017) provides bounds on the generalization error of a learning algorithm in terms of the mutual information between the algorithm's output and the training sample. In this work, we study the proposal, by Steinke and Zakynthinou (2020), to reason about the generalization error of a learning algorithm by introducing a super sample that contains the training sample as a random subset and computing mutual information conditional on the super sample. We first show that these new bounds based on the conditional mutual information are tighter than those based on the unconditional mutual information. We then introduce yet tighter bounds, building on the "individual sample" idea of Bu et al. (2019) and the "data dependent" ideas of Negrea et al. (2019), using disintegrated mutual information. Finally, we apply these bounds to the study of Langevin dynamics algorithm, showing that conditioning on the super sample allows us to exploit information in the optimization trajectory to obtain tighter bounds based on hypothesis tests.

paragraphs: Information-theoretic generalization bounds connect a learning algorithm's behavior on new data to how much information its output carries about its training sample. This paper sharpens that approach by considering a larger supersample from which the actual training sample is selected randomly. It measures mutual information conditional on that supersample.

The authors first show that these conditional-information bounds are tighter than corresponding bounds based on unconditional mutual information. They then obtain further improvements by combining reasoning about individual samples with data-dependent analysis, using disintegrated mutual information. The progression refines which information enters the bound, rather than treating all dependence between the output and dataset as a single undifferentiated quantity.

The paper applies these results to Langevin dynamics, a noisy iterative learning algorithm. Conditioning on the supersample makes it possible to use information from the optimization trajectory and derive tighter bounds through hypothesis tests. The contribution is therefore both a hierarchy of stronger generalization guarantees and a demonstration of how an algorithm's training path can improve its analysis.
summary.tldr: Conditional mutual information yields tighter generalization bounds and lets Langevin-dynamics analyses use information from the optimization trajectory.

title: Sharpened Generalization Bounds based on Conditional Mutual Information and an Application to Noisy, Iterative Algorithms

abstract: We study the online restless bandit problem, where the state of each arm evolves according to a Markov chain, and the reward of pulling an arm depends on both the pulled arm and the current state of the corresponding Markov chain. In this paper, we propose Restless-UCB, a learning policy that follows the explore-then-commit framework. In Restless-UCB, we present a novel method to construct offline instances, which only requires $O(N)$ time-complexity ($N$ is the number of arms) and is exponentially better than the complexity of existing learning policy. We also prove that Restless-UCB achieves a regret upper bound of $\tilde{O}((N+M^3)T^{2\over 3})$, where $M$ is the Markov chain state space size and $T$ is the time horizon. Compared to existing algorithms, our result eliminates the exponential factor (in $M,N$) in the regret upper bound, due to a novel exploitation of the sparsity in transitions in general restless bandit problems. As a result, our analysis technique can also be adopted to tighten the regret bounds of existing algorithms. Finally, we conduct experiments based on real-world dataset, to compare the Restless-UCB policy with state-of-the-art benchmarks. Our results show that Restless-UCB outperforms existing algorithms in regret, and significantly reduces the running time.
