paragraphs: The paper studies restless bandits, where each available arm has a state evolving according to a Markov chain. Pulling an arm produces a reward that depends on both the arm and its current state. Learning a good policy therefore requires handling changing state-dependent rewards as well as choosing which arm to pull.

Restless-UCB uses an explore-then-commit strategy. Its new construction of offline instances takes time linear in the number of arms, an exponential improvement over the existing learning-policy complexity described in the abstract. The authors also prove a regret bound scaling, up to logarithmic factors, as the number of arms plus the cube of the state-space size, multiplied by the time horizon to the two-thirds power.

The analysis exploits sparse transitions to remove an exponential dependence on arm count and state-space size from the regret bound. The authors state that this analytical technique can also sharpen bounds for existing algorithms. Experiments using a real-world dataset report lower regret and substantially shorter running times, supporting both the statistical and computational value of the approach.
summary.tldr: Restless-UCB exploits transition sparsity to improve regret bounds and reduce computation for learning with state-changing bandit arms.

title: Restless-UCB, an Efficient and Low-complexity Algorithm for Online Restless Bandits

abstract: Spiking neural networks (SNNs) are well suited for spatio-temporal learning and implementations on energy-efficient event-driven neuromorphic processors. However, existing SNN error backpropagation (BP) methods lack proper handling of spiking discontinuities and suffer from low performance compared with the BP methods for traditional artificial neural networks. In addition, a large number of time steps are typically required to achieve decent performance, leading to high latency and rendering spike-based computation unscalable to deep architectures. We present a novel Temporal Spike Sequence Learning Backpropagation (TSSL-BP) method for training deep SNNs, which breaks down error backpropagation across two types of inter-neuron and intra-neuron dependencies and leads to improved temporal learning precision. It captures inter-neuron dependencies through presynaptic firing times by considering the all-or-none characteristics of firing activities and captures intra-neuron dependencies by handling the internal evolution of each neuronal state in time. TSSL-BP efficiently trains deep SNNs within a much shortened temporal window of a few steps while improving the accuracy for various image classification datasets including CIFAR10.

paragraphs: Spiking neural networks represent activity through discrete firing events and are suited to event-driven neuromorphic processors. Training them is difficult because spikes are discontinuous and neural states evolve over time. Existing backpropagation methods described in the paper also need many time steps for useful performance, creating latency and making deep architectures harder to scale.

TSSL-BP separates error propagation into dependencies between neurons and dependencies within each neuron over time. For interactions between neurons, it uses presynaptic firing times while accounting for the all-or-none nature of spikes. For a neuron’s internal dependencies, it follows the evolution of that neuron’s state. This decomposition is designed to improve the precision of temporal learning.

The authors report that TSSL-BP trains deep spiking networks over temporal windows of only a few steps while improving accuracy on several image-classification datasets, including CIFAR10. The result addresses accuracy and temporal duration together. It supports explicitly handling both kinds of dependency as a way to make deep spiking-network training effective within shorter computation windows.
summary.tldr: TSSL-BP models dependencies between neurons and across time to train accurate deep spiking networks in only a few time steps.

title: Temporal Spike Sequence Learning via Backpropagation for Deep Spiking Neural Networks

abstract: In theory, the choice of ReLU(0) in [0, 1] for a neural network has a negligible influence both on backpropagation and training. Yet, in the real world, 32 bits default precision combined with the size of deep learning problems makes it a hyperparameter of training methods. We investigate the importance of the value of ReLU'(0) for several precision levels (16, 32, 64 bits), on various networks (fully connected, VGG, ResNet) and datasets (MNIST, CIFAR10, SVHN, ImageNet). We observe considerable variations of backpropagation outputs which occur around half of the time in 32 bits precision. The effect disappears with double precision, while it is systematic at 16 bits. For vanilla SGD training, the choice ReLU'(0) = 0 seems to be the most efficient. For our experiments on ImageNet the gain in test accuracy over ReLU'(0) = 1 was more than 10 points (two runs). We also evidence that reconditioning approaches as batch-norm or ADAM tend to buffer the influence of ReLU'(0)’s value. Overall, the message we convey is that algorithmic differentiation of nonsmooth problems potentially hides parameters that could be tuned advantageously.

paragraphs: ReLU has a corner at zero, so backpropagation must choose a derivative value there. Although that choice is theoretically expected to have negligible influence, this paper finds that finite numerical precision can make it consequential. The authors examine derivative choices across 16-, 32-, and 64-bit arithmetic, several network architectures, and multiple image datasets.

They observe substantial changes in backpropagation outputs around half the time at 32-bit precision. The effect is systematic at 16 bits and disappears at double precision in the reported investigation. This connects a seemingly minor implementation choice to the numerical setting in which a network actually trains, rather than treating ideal mathematical behavior as a complete description.

For vanilla SGD, choosing a zero derivative appears most effective in their experiments. On ImageNet, it exceeds the accuracy obtained with a derivative of one by more than ten points across two runs. Batch normalization and ADAM tend to soften the influence. The broader finding is that automatic differentiation of nonsmooth functions can contain hidden choices that may be useful to tune.
summary.tldr: Finite precision can make ReLU's derivative choice at zero materially affect backpropagation and training.

title: Numerical influence of ReLU’(0) on backpropagation

abstract: We study online convex optimization in the random order model, recently proposed by Garber et al. (2020), where the loss functions may be chosen by an adversary, but are then presented to the online algorithm in a uniformly random order. Focusing on the scenario where the cumulative loss function is (strongly) convex, yet individual loss functions are smooth but might be non-convex, we give algorithms that achieve the optimal bounds and significantly outperform the results of Garber et al. (2020), completely removing the dimension dependence and improve their scaling with respect to the strong convexity parameter. Our analysis relies on novel connections between algorithmic stability and generalization for sampling without-replacement analogous to those studied in the with-replacement i.i.d. setting, as well as on a refined average stability analysis of stochastic gradient descent.

paragraphs: This paper studies online optimization when an adversary may choose the loss functions, but those functions reach the learner in a uniformly random order. The learner must make decisions as losses arrive. Random ordering supplies useful structure without requiring the collection of losses itself to have been generated independently from a probability distribution.

The analysis focuses on settings where the cumulative loss is convex or strongly convex, even though individual losses need only be smooth and may be non-convex. The authors develop algorithms with optimal bounds, improving earlier results by eliminating dependence on dimension and obtaining better scaling with the strong-convexity parameter. These gains concern the stated random-order setting.

The proof connects algorithmic stability with generalization under sampling without replacement, alongside a refined average-stability analysis of stochastic gradient descent. Stability concerns how sensitive a learning procedure is to changes in its data. Establishing these connections helps explain how randomly ordered losses can yield strong guarantees even when individual losses lack convexity.
summary.tldr: The paper proves optimal dimension-independent bounds for random-order online optimization with convex cumulative loss and potentially non-convex individual losses.

title: Optimal Rates for Random Order Online Optimization

abstract: Recently, utilizing reinforcement learning (RL) to generate molecules with desired properties has been highlighted as a promising strategy for drug design. Molecular docking program -- a physical simulation that estimates protein-small molecule binding affinity -- can be an ideal reward scoring function for RL, as it is a straightforward proxy of the therapeutic potential. Still, two imminent challenges exist for this task. First, the models often fail to generate chemically realistic and pharmacochemically acceptable molecules. Second, the docking score optimization is a difficult exploration problem that involves many local optima and less smooth surface with respect to molecular structure. To tackle these challenges, we propose a novel RL framework that generates pharmacochemically acceptable molecules with large docking scores. Our method -- Fragment-based generative RL with Explorative Experience replay for Drug design (FREED) -- constrains the generated molecules to a realistic and qualified chemical space and effectively explores the space to find drugs by coupling our fragment-based generation method and a novel error-prioritized experience replay (PER). We also show that our model performs well on both de novo and scaffold-based schemes. Our model produces molecules of higher quality compared to existing methods while achieving state-of-the-art performance on two of three targets in terms of the docking scores of the generated molecules. We further show with ablation studies that our method, predictive error-PER (FREED(PE)), significantly improves the model performance.

Ablation studies also show significant performance improvements from the predictive-error replay variant, FREED(PE). These results concern generated-molecule quality and a simulated binding proxy; the stated contribution is a more effective way to search for promising molecular candidates using that feedback.
summary.tldr: FREED combines molecular fragments and error-prioritized replay to generate higher-quality molecules with strong docking scores.

title: Hit and Lead Discovery with Explorative RL and Fragment-based Molecule Generation

abstract: Understanding the structure of loss landscape of deep neural networks (DNNs) is obviously important. In this work, we prove an embedding principle that the loss landscape of a DNN "contains" all the critical points of all the narrower DNNs. More precisely, we propose a critical embedding such that any critical point, e.g., local or global minima, of a narrower DNN can be embedded to a critical point/affine subspace of the target DNN with higher degeneracy and preserving the DNN output function. Note that, given any training data, differentiable loss function and differentiable activation function, this embedding structure of critical points holds.This general structure of DNNs is starkly different from other nonconvex problems such as protein-folding.Empirically, we find that a wide DNN is often attracted by highly-degenerate critical points that are embedded from narrow DNNs. The embedding principle provides a new perspective to study the general easy optimization of wide DNNs and unravels a potential implicit low-complexity regularization during the training.Overall, our work provides a skeleton for the study of loss landscape of DNNs and its implication, by which a more exact and comprehensive understanding can be anticipated in the near future.

paragraphs: The paper proves a structural relationship between the loss landscapes of narrower and wider deep neural networks. A critical point is a parameter setting where the loss has no first-order change. The embedding principle says that critical points of narrower networks can be represented inside a wider target network while preserving the function computed by the network.

The proposed embedding maps a narrow network's critical point to a critical point or an affine subspace of critical points in the wider network, with greater degeneracy. The result holds for any training data when the loss and activation functions are differentiable. Thus, increasing width retains a structured collection of stationary configurations inherited from smaller networks.

Empirically, the authors find that wide networks are often attracted to highly degenerate critical points embedded from narrow networks. They suggest this offers a perspective on easy optimization and a possible implicit preference for low-complexity solutions during training. The embedding is proved; the proposed regularization interpretation remains a potential implication.
summary.tldr: A proved embedding principle shows how wider networks inherit narrower networks' critical points while preserving their output functions.

title: Embedding Principle of Loss Landscape of Deep Neural Networks

abstract: Hyperparameter (HP) tuning in deep learning is an expensive process, prohibitively so for neural networks (NNs) with billions of parameters.We show that, in the recently discovered Maximal Update Parametrization ($\mu$P), many optimal HPs remain stable even as model size changes. This leads to a new HP tuning paradigm we call *$\mu$Transfer*: parametrize the target model in $\mu$P, tune the HP indirectly on a smaller model, and *zero-shot transfer* them to the full-sized model, i.e., without directly tuning the latter at all.We verify $\mu$Transfer on Transformer and ResNet. For example, 1) by transferring pretraining HPs from a model of 13M parameters, we outperform published numbers of BERT-large (350M parameters), with a total tuning cost equivalent to pretraining BERT-large once; 2) by transferring from 40M parameters, we outperform published numbers of the 6.7B GPT-3 model, with tuning cost only 7% of total pretraining cost. A Pytorch implementation of our technique can be found at github.com/microsoft/mup. See arxiv.org for the full, up-to-date version of this work.

paragraphs: Hyperparameter tuning becomes expensive when each training run involves a very large neural network. This paper shows that, under Maximal Update Parametrization, or μP, many optimal hyperparameters remain stable as model size changes. That stability creates an opportunity to perform the search on a smaller and cheaper model.

The resulting method, μTransfer, parametrizes the target network in μP, tunes hyperparameters on a smaller network, and transfers them without directly tuning the full-sized model. The authors verify the approach on Transformers and ResNets. The claim concerns many hyperparameters under this parametrization, rather than every hyperparameter under arbitrary model scaling.

One demonstration transfers pretraining hyperparameters from a 13-million-parameter model and exceeds published BERT-large results, with total tuning cost equivalent to one BERT-large pretraining run. Another transfers from 40 million parameters and exceeds published results for the 6.7-billion-parameter GPT-3 model, with tuning costing 7% of total pretraining. These examples show how stable hyperparameters can translate into substantial savings while retaining strong performance.
summary.tldr: μTransfer tunes many hyperparameters on small μP-parametrized networks and transfers them to larger models without directly tuning the larger models.

title: Tuning Large Neural Networks via Zero-Shot Hyperparameter Transfer

abstract: In this paper, we present token labeling---a new training objective for training high-performance vision transformers (ViTs). Different from the standard training objective of ViTs that computes the classification loss on an additional trainable class token, our proposed one takes advantage of all the image patch tokens to compute the training loss in a dense manner. Specifically, token labeling reformulates the image classification problem into multiple token-level recognition problems and assigns each patch token with an individual location-specific supervision generated by a machine annotator. Experiments show that token labeling can clearly and consistently improve the performance of various ViT models across a wide spectrum. For a vision transformer with 26M learnable parameters serving as an example, with token labeling, the model can achieve 84.4% Top-1 accuracy on ImageNet. The result can be further increased to 86.4% by slightly scaling the model size up to 150M, delivering the minimal-sized model among previous models (250M+) reaching 86%. We also show that token labeling can clearly improve the generalization capability of the pretrained models on downstream tasks with dense prediction, such as semantic segmentation. Our code and model are publiclyavailable at https://github.com/zihangJiang/TokenLabeling.

paragraphs: This paper changes how vision transformers receive supervision during image classification. Standard training computes classification loss using an added class token. Token labeling also makes the image patch tokens contribute to the training objective, turning a single image recognition problem into multiple recognition problems tied to particular locations.

Each patch token receives its own location-specific target from a machine annotator. This gives training a denser signal: the model is supervised on representations of individual image regions, alongside the overall classification task. The approach matters because it uses the patch representations already present in a vision transformer as direct targets for learning.

The experiments report consistent improvements across various vision transformers. A model with 26 million parameters reaches 84.4% ImageNet Top-1 accuracy, while a 150-million-parameter model reaches 86.4%. The latter is smaller than the previously reported models exceeding 250 million parameters that reached 86%. The authors also report improved transfer to dense prediction tasks such as semantic segmentation, indicating benefits beyond the original classification setting.
summary.tldr: Token labeling trains vision transformers with supervision for individual image patches, improving classification and transfer to dense prediction tasks.

title: All Tokens Matter: Token Labeling for Training Better Vision Transformers

abstract: It has been recently observed that neural networks, unlike kernel methods, enjoy a reduced sample complexity when the distribution is isotropic (i.e., when the covariance matrix is the identity). We find that this sensitivity to the data distribution is not exclusive to neural networks, and the same phenomenon can be observed on the class of quadratic classifiers (i.e., the sign of a quadratic polynomial) with a nuclear-norm constraint. We demonstrate this by deriving an upper bound on the Rademacher Complexity that depends on two key quantities: (i) the intrinsic dimension, which is a measure of isotropy, and (ii) the largest eigenvalue of the second moment (covariance) matrix of the distribution. Our result improves the dependence on the dimension over the best previously known bound and precisely quantifies the relation between the sample complexity and the level of isotropy of the distribution.

paragraphs: The distribution of data can affect how many examples a classifier needs to generalize. This paper studies quadratic classifiers, which predict using the sign of a quadratic polynomial, under a nuclear-norm constraint. It shows that favorable sensitivity to isotropic data, previously observed for neural networks, also appears in this constrained class of classifiers.

The analysis derives an upper bound on Rademacher complexity, a quantity used to control generalization. The bound depends on two distributional properties: intrinsic dimension, used here as a measure of isotropy, and the largest eigenvalue of the second-moment matrix. This makes the shape of the data distribution an explicit part of the guarantee.

The result improves the dependence on dimension compared with the best previously known bound and quantifies how sample complexity relates to isotropy. Its significance is that the ambient number of coordinates does not tell the whole generalization story. For the studied nuclear-norm-constrained quadratic models, distributional structure provides a sharper account of the learning requirements.
summary.tldr: A sharper complexity bound explains how isotropy and intrinsic dimension affect generalization for nuclear-norm-constrained quadratic classifiers.

title: The Effect of the Intrinsic Dimension on the Generalization of Quadratic Classifiers

abstract: Federated learning (FL) has gain growing interests for its capability of learning from distributed data sources collectively without the need of accessing the raw data samples across different sources. So far FL research has mostly focused on improving the performance, how the algorithmic disparity will be impacted for the model learned from FL and the impact of algorithmic disparity on the utility inconsistency are largely unexplored. In this paper, we propose an FL framework to jointly consider performance consistency and algorithmic fairness across different local clients (data sources). We derive our framework from a constrained multi-objective optimization perspective, in which we learn a model satisfying fairness constraints on all clients with consistent performance. Specifically, we treat the algorithm prediction loss at each local client as an objective and maximize the worst-performing client with fairness constraints through optimizing a surrogate maximum function with all objectives involved. A gradient-based procedure is employed to achieve the Pareto optimality of this optimization problem. Theoretical analysis is provided to prove that our method can converge to a Pareto solution that achieves the min-max performance with fairness constraints on all clients. Comprehensive experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the superiority that our approach over baselines and its effectiveness in achieving both fairness and consistency across all local clients.

paragraphs: Federated learning lets multiple clients train a shared model without exchanging their raw data. Strong overall performance, however, does not itself describe whether the model works consistently across clients or satisfies fairness requirements within them. This paper makes those concerns explicit parts of the learning objective.

The authors formulate training as constrained optimization with several objectives, one prediction loss for each client. They focus on improving the worst-performing client while imposing fairness constraints on every client. A surrogate maximum function brings all client objectives into the optimization, and a gradient-based procedure seeks a Pareto solution: a tradeoff where improving one objective cannot come without worsening another.

The theoretical analysis establishes that the method can converge to a Pareto solution achieving the stated min-max performance criterion under the fairness constraints. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets report advantages over baselines in both fairness and performance consistency. The contribution is a framework that treats client-level disparities as training requirements rather than leaving them outside the optimization problem.
summary.tldr: A constrained federated learning framework improves worst-client performance while enforcing fairness requirements across clients.

title: Addressing Algorithmic Disparity and Performance Inconsistency in Federated Learning

abstract: We consider the problem of estimating a linear time-invariant (LTI) dynamical system from a single trajectory via streaming algorithms, which is encountered in several applications including reinforcement learning (RL) and time-series analysis. While the LTI system estimation problem is well-studied in the {\em offline} setting, the practically important streaming/online setting has received little attention. Standard streaming methods like stochastic gradient descent (SGD) are unlikely to work since streaming points can be highly correlated. In this work, we propose a novel streaming algorithm, SGD with Reverse Experience Replay (SGD-RER), that is inspired by the experience replay (ER) technique popular in the RL literature. SGD-RER divides data into small buffers and runs SGD backwards on the data stored in the individual buffers. We show that this algorithm exactly deconstructs the dependency structure and obtains information theoretically optimal guarantees for both parameter error and prediction error. Thus, we provide the first -- to the best of our knowledge -- optimal SGD-style algorithm for the classical problem of linear system identification with a first order oracle. Furthermore, SGD-RER can be applied to more general settings like sparse LTI identification with known sparsity pattern, and non-linear dynamical systems. Our work demonstrates that the knowledge of data dependency structure can aid us in designing statistically and computationally efficient algorithms which can ``decorrelate'' streaming samples.

paragraphs: Estimating a dynamical system from a single evolving trajectory creates a dependency problem: successive observations can be strongly correlated. This paper studies streaming estimation of linear time-invariant systems, where data arrive sequentially. Such dependence makes ordinary streaming stochastic gradient descent a problematic approach, despite the extensive study of offline system estimation.

The proposed algorithm, SGD with Reverse Experience Replay, divides observations into small buffers and processes each buffer backward with stochastic gradient descent. The ordering is the key intervention. The authors show that reversing the data within buffers deconstructs the dependency structure, allowing a first-order streaming method to obtain information-theoretically optimal guarantees for both parameter estimation and prediction error.

The paper also describes applications to sparse linear systems with a known sparsity pattern and to nonlinear dynamical systems. The optimal guarantees stated for the central linear-system problem should be distinguished from these broader applications. Overall, the work shows how knowledge of temporal dependence can guide the order of updates and improve the statistical and computational efficiency of streaming learning.
summary.tldr: Processing small buffers backward enables a streaming SGD method to attain optimal estimation and prediction guarantees for linear system identification.

title: Streaming Linear System Identification with Reverse Experience Replay

abstract: \textit{Off-policy evaluation} (OPE) aims to estimate the performance of hypothetical policies using data generated by a different policy. Because of its huge potential impact in practice, there has been growing research interest in this field. There is, however, no real-world public dataset that enables the evaluation of OPE, making its experimental studies unrealistic and irreproducible. With the goal of enabling realistic and reproducible OPE research, we present \textit{Open Bandit Dataset}, a public logged bandit dataset collected on a large-scale fashion e-commerce platform, ZOZOTOWN. Our dataset is unique in that it contains a set of \textit{multiple} logged bandit datasets collected by running different policies on the same platform. This enables experimental comparisons of different OPE estimators for the first time. We also develop Python software called \textit{Open Bandit Pipeline} to streamline and standardize the implementation of batch bandit algorithms and OPE. Our open data and software will contribute to fair and transparent OPE research and help the community identify fruitful research directions. We provide extensive benchmark experiments of existing OPE estimators using our dataset and software. The results open up essential challenges and new avenues for future OPE research.

paragraphs: Off-policy evaluation estimates how a policy would perform using records generated by a different policy. The paper addresses the difficulty of evaluating these estimates with realistic, reproducible public data. It introduces the Open Bandit Dataset, collected on the large fashion e-commerce platform ZOZOTOWN.

The key feature is that the resource includes multiple logged datasets produced by running different policies on the same platform. This gives researchers a shared basis for experimentally comparing off-policy estimators. The collection directly addresses the authors’ concern that the absence of suitable public real-world data had made studies difficult to reproduce and disconnected from realistic settings.

The authors use the data and software for extensive experiments with existing estimators, reporting that the results reveal important challenges and research opportunities. Together, the resources support more transparent comparisons through shared observations, implementation tools, and benchmark experiments.
summary.tldr: Open Bandit combines real e-commerce logs from multiple policies with shared software for reproducible off-policy evaluation.

title: Open Bandit Dataset and Pipeline: Towards Realistic and Reproducible Off-Policy Evaluation

abstract: Although deep learning methods have achieved advanced video object recognition performance in recent years, perceiving heavily occluded objects in a video is still a very challenging task. To promote the development of occlusion understanding, we collect a large-scale dataset called OVIS for video instance segmentation in the occluded scenario. OVIS consists of 296k high-quality instance masks and 901 occluded scenes. While our human vision systems can perceive those occluded objects by contextual reasoning and association, our experiments suggest that current video understanding systems cannot. On the OVIS dataset, all baseline methods encounter a significant performance degradation of about 80\% in the heavily occluded object group, which demonstrates that there is still a long way to go in understanding obscured objects and videos in a complex real-world scenario. To facilitate the research on new paradigms for video understanding systems, we launched a challenge basing on the OVIS dataset. The submitted top-performing algorithms have achieved much higher performance than our baselines. In this paper, we will introduce the OVIS dataset and further dissect it by analyzing the results of baselines and submitted methods. The OVIS dataset and challenge information can be found at \url{http://songbai.site/ovis}.

paragraphs: OVIS targets a persistent difficulty in video understanding: recognizing and separating individual objects when other objects heavily obscure them. The paper introduces a dataset for video instance segmentation under these conditions, containing 901 occluded scenes and 296,000 instance masks. These annotations provide a substantial resource for evaluating object segmentation where visibility is limited.

The authors motivate the task through the contrast between human contextual reasoning and the behavior of tested video systems. On OVIS, every evaluated baseline suffers a performance degradation of about 80% in the heavily occluded object group. This result identifies severe occlusion as a substantial weakness for those methods, even amid broader progress in video object recognition.

The accompanying challenge draws submissions whose strongest algorithms perform much better than the original baselines. The paper analyzes both sets of results to examine the dataset and the methods used on it. OVIS thus provides evidence of a difficult failure case and a shared testing ground where improved approaches to obscured objects can be compared.
summary.tldr: OVIS exposes large baseline performance losses under heavy occlusion while its challenge submissions demonstrate substantial improvement over those baselines.

title: Occluded Video Instance Segmentation: Dataset and ICCV 2021 Challenge

abstract: Sortition is a form of democracy built on random selection of representatives. Two of the key arguments in favor of sortition are that it provides representation (a random panel reflects the composition of the population) and fairness (everyone has a chance to participate). Uniformly random selection is perfectly fair, but is it representative? Towards answering this question, we introduce the notion of a representation metric on the space of individuals, and assume that the cost of an individual for a panel is determined by the $q$-th closest representative; the representation of a (random) panel is measured by the ratio between the (expected) sum of costs of the optimal panel for the individuals and that of the given panel. For $k/2 < q \le k-\Omega(k)$, where $k$ is the panel size, we show that uniform random selection is indeed representative by establishing a constant lower bound on this ratio. By contrast, for $q \leq k/2$, no random selection algorithm that is almost fair can give such a guarantee. We therefore consider relaxed fairness guarantees and develop a new random selection algorithm that sheds light on the tradeoff between representation and fairness.

paragraphs: Randomly selecting representatives gives everyone an equal chance to participate, but equal selection chances do not automatically establish how well a panel represents people. This paper formalizes that distinction using a representation metric between individuals. Each person's cost depends on their q-th closest panel member, making the choice of q central to the analysis.

Panel quality is assessed through a ratio comparing the optimal panel's aggregate cost with that of the selected panel, using expectations for random selection. For a panel of size k, uniform selection receives a constant representation guarantee when k/2 < q ≤ k−Ω(k). Thus, the positive result applies to a particular range of this representation parameter.

For q ≤ k/2, the authors prove that no almost-fair random selection algorithm can provide such a guarantee. They then relax the fairness requirement and develop another selection algorithm to explore the tradeoff. The findings show that whether random selection combines fairness and representation depends on the formal notion of representation and how strictly fairness must be maintained.
summary.tldr: Random selection's ability to be both fair and representative depends on how representation is measured and how much fairness may be relaxed.

title: Is Sortition Both Representative and Fair?

abstract: We consider the problem of building a reinforcement learning (RL) agent that can both accomplish non-trivial tasks, like winning a real-time strategy game, and strictly follow high-level language commands from humans, like “attack”, even if a command is sub-optimal. We call this novel yet important problem, Grounded Reinforcement Learning (GRL). Compared with other language grounding tasks, GRL is particularly non-trivial and cannot be simply solved by pure RL or behavior cloning (BC). From the RL perspective, it is extremely challenging to derive a precise reward function for human preferences since the commands are abstract and the valid behaviors are highly complicated and multi-modal. From the BC perspective, it is impossible to obtain perfect demonstrations since human strategies in complex games are typically sub-optimal. We tackle GRL via a simple, tractable, and practical constrained RL objective and develop an iterative RL algorithm, REinforced demonstration Distillation (RED), to obtain a strong GRL policy. We evaluate the policies derived by RED, BC and pure RL methods on a simplified real-time strategy game, MiniRTS. Experiment results and human studies show that the RED policy is able to consistently follow human commands and achieve a higher win rate than the baselines. We release our code and present more examples at https://sites.google.com/view/grounded-rl.

This paper defines Grounded Reinforcement Learning around that combination: accomplishing a demanding task while following high-level language commands. Success therefore involves both task performance and responsiveness to human direction.

The authors explain why either ordinary reinforcement learning or behavior cloning alone is inadequate for this problem. Abstract commands can permit many complicated behaviors, making precise reward design difficult. Demonstrations also reflect human strategies that may be suboptimal. The proposed approach uses a constrained reinforcement learning objective and an iterative algorithm called REinforced demonstration Distillation, or RED, to learn a policy for this combined goal.

Evaluation uses the simplified real-time strategy game MiniRTS, comparing RED with behavior cloning and pure reinforcement learning. Experiments and human studies find that RED consistently follows commands while achieving a higher win rate than those baselines. The results demonstrate the approach's value in that game setting, where command adherence and competitive performance must be handled together.
summary.tldr: RED combines constrained reinforcement learning with demonstration distillation to follow human commands and improve win rates in MiniRTS.

title: Grounded Reinforcement Learning: Learning to Win the Game under Human Commands

abstract: In many real-world scenarios, data to train machine learning models becomes available over time. Unfortunately, these models struggle to continually learn new concepts without forgetting what has been learnt in the past. This phenomenon is known as catastrophic forgetting and it is difficult to prevent due to practical constraints. For instance, the amount of data that can be stored or the computational resources that can be used might be limited. Moreover, applications increasingly rely on large pre-trained neural networks, such as pre-trained Transformers, since compute or data might not be available in sufficiently large quantities to practitioners to train from scratch. In this paper, we devise a method to incrementally train a model on a sequence of tasks using pre-trained Transformers and extending them with Adapters. Different than the existing approaches, our method is able to scale to a large number of tasks without significant overhead and allows sharing information across tasks. On both image and text classification tasks, we empirically demonstrate that our method maintains a good predictive performance without retraining the model or increasing the number of model parameters over time. The resulting model is also significantly faster at inference time compared to Adapter-based state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Learning tasks one after another creates a practical problem: a model can lose earlier knowledge as it learns new concepts. Storing old data or repeatedly training a large model may be too expensive. This paper addresses continual learning in the increasingly common setting where practitioners begin with a pretrained Transformer instead of training a network from scratch.

The proposed method extends pretrained Transformers with Adapters and trains incrementally across a sequence of tasks. Its design supports information sharing between tasks while scaling to many tasks without significant overhead. The important resource goal is to avoid making the model continually larger as the task sequence grows, while still allowing it to acquire new capabilities.

Experiments on image and text classification show that the method maintains good predictive performance without retraining the model or increasing its parameter count over time. The resulting model also performs inference significantly faster than the compared leading Adapter-based methods. These findings support a practical combination of continued learning, bounded model size, and faster prediction across the evaluated task sequences.
summary.tldr: A Transformer-and-Adapter method learns successive tasks with a fixed parameter count, shared information, and faster inference in image and text experiments.

title: Memory Efficient Continual Learning with Transformers

abstract: We consider three central problems in optimization: the restricted assignment load-balancing problem, the Steiner tree network design problem, and facility location clustering. We consider the online setting, where the input arrives over time, and irrevocable decisions must be made without knowledge of the future. For all these problems, any online algorithm must incur a cost that is approximately $\log |I|$ times the optimal cost in the worst-case, where $|I|$ is the length of the input. But can we go beyond the worst-case? In this work we give algorithms that perform substantially better when a $p$-fraction of the input is given as a sample: the algorithm use this sample to \emph{learn} a good strategy to use for the rest of the input.

paragraphs: Online algorithms make decisions as inputs arrive, without seeing what will come next. When those decisions cannot be reversed, early choices can make the final solution expensive. This paper studies that difficulty in three optimization problems: restricted assignment load balancing, Steiner tree network design, and facility location clustering.

For each problem, worst-case analysis imposes a substantial barrier: an online algorithm can be forced to pay roughly a logarithmic factor in input length more than the optimum. The authors ask whether that pessimistic comparison can improve when the algorithm receives partial information about the input before handling the remaining decisions.

Their algorithms use a sample containing a p-fraction of the input to learn a strategy for the rest. Under this sample-informed setup, they achieve substantially better performance than the worst-case benchmark described for ordinary online algorithms. The contribution is therefore conditional on access to that sample. It shows how limited advance information can become actionable guidance across several online optimization problems, without requiring the entire future input to be available.
summary.tldr: Access to a sample of future input enables substantially better algorithms for three classic online optimization problems.

title: Learning from a Sample in Online Algorithms

abstract: We study two basic statistical tasks in non-interactive local differential privacy (LDP): *learning* and *refutation*: learning requires finding a concept that best fits an unknown target function (from labelled samples drawn from a distribution), whereas refutation requires distinguishing between data distributions that are well-correlated with some concept in the class, versus distributions where the labels are random. Our main result is a complete characterization of the sample complexity of agnostic PAC learning for non-interactive LDP protocols. We show that the optimal sample complexity for any concept class is captured by the approximate $\gamma_2$ norm of a natural matrix associated with the class. Combined with previous work, this gives an *equivalence* between agnostic learning and refutation in the agnostic setting.

paragraphs: This paper compares two statistical tasks under noninteractive local differential privacy. Learning seeks a concept that best matches an unknown target from labeled examples. Refutation asks a different question: whether the labels have meaningful correlation with some concept in the class or instead behave like random labels.

The main result characterizes the sample complexity of agnostic PAC learning in this privacy setting. Agnostic learning looks for the best available fit without requiring the target to belong to the chosen concept class. The authors show that the optimal number of samples is captured by the approximate gamma-two norm of a matrix naturally associated with that class. This gives a mathematical quantity for describing the learning difficulty of any concept class within the stated setting.

Combining this characterization with earlier work establishes an equivalence between agnostic learning and refutation. The significance is that finding a fitting concept and detecting whether meaningful fit exists are linked at the level of statistical difficulty. The equivalence concerns the agnostic, noninteractive local-privacy setting studied in the paper.
summary.tldr: A matrix norm characterizes agnostic learning sample complexity under noninteractive local privacy and establishes an equivalence with refutation.

title: On Learning and Refutation in Noninteractive Local Differential Privacy

abstract: While large pretrained foundation models (FMs) have shown remarkable zero-shot classification robustness to dataset-level distribution shifts, their robustness to subpopulation or group shifts is relatively underexplored. We study this problem, and find that foundation models such as CLIP may not be robust to various group shifts. Across 9 robustness benchmarks, zero-shot classification with their embeddings results in gaps of up to 80.7 percentage points (pp) between average and worst-group accuracy. Unfortunately, existing methods to improve robustness require retraining, which can be prohibitively expensive on large foundation models. We also find that efficient ways to improve model inference (e.g. via adapters, lightweight networks that transform FM embeddings) do not consistently improve and can sometimes *hurt* group robustness compared to zero-shot. We therefore develop an adapter training strategy to effectively and efficiently improve FM group robustness. Our motivating observation is that while poor robustness results from groups in the same class being embedded far apart in the foundation model "embedding space," standard adapter training may not actually bring these points closer together. We thus propose contrastive adapting, which contrastively trains adapters to bring sample embeddings close to both their ground-truth class embeddings and same-class sample embeddings. Across the 9 robustness benchmarks, contrastive adapting consistently improves group robustness, raising worst-group accuracy by 8.5 to 56.0 pp over zero-shot. Our approach is also efficient, doing so without any FM finetuning and only a fixed set of FM embeddings. On popular benchmarks such as Waterbirds and CelebA, this leads to worst-group accuracy comparable to state-of-the-art methods, while only training <1% of the model parameters.

title: Contrastive Adapters for Foundation Model Group Robustness

abstract: We consider the problem of allocating a distribution of items to $n$ recipients where each recipient has to be allocated a fixed, pre-specified fraction of all items, while ensuring that each recipient does not experience too much envy. We show that this problem can be formulated as a variant of the semi-discrete optimal transport (OT) problem, whose solution structure in this case has a concise representation and a simple geometric interpretation. Unlike existing literature that treats envy-freeness as a hard constraint, our formulation allows us to \emph{optimally} trade off efficiency and envy continuously. Additionally, we study the statistical properties of the space of our OT based allocation policies by showing a polynomial bound on the number of samples needed to approximate the optimal solution from samples. Our approach is suitable for large-scale fair allocation problems such as the blood donation matching problem, and we show numerically that it performs well on a prior realistic data simulator.

paragraphs: The paper studies allocation when every recipient must receive a fixed, prespecified fraction of a distribution of items. Alongside those quotas, an allocation should limit envy between recipients. The challenge is to balance allocation efficiency with envy while respecting the required shares, rather than treating complete envy-freeness as the only acceptable outcome.

The authors formulate the problem as a variant of semi-discrete optimal transport. In this formulation, the solution has a compact representation and a simple geometric interpretation. It permits a continuous, optimal trade-off between efficiency and envy, providing a way to vary the balance within a single allocation framework.

The paper also analyzes how these allocation policies can be learned from samples. It establishes a polynomial bound on the number of samples needed to approximate the optimal solution. Numerical results using an existing realistic simulator support the approach for large-scale fair allocation, with blood donation matching as a motivating application. The contribution combines a structured optimization formulation with statistical and simulation-based evidence.
summary.tldr: An optimal transport formulation continuously balances allocation efficiency and envy while respecting fixed recipient shares.

title: Optimal Efficiency-Envy Trade-Off via Optimal Transport

abstract: Recent work has shown that a simple, fast method called Simple Graph Convolution (SGC) (Wu et al., 2019), which eschews deep learning, is competitive with deep methods like graph convolutional networks (GCNs) (Kipf & Welling, 2017) in common graph machine learning benchmarks. The use of graph data in SGC implicitly assumes the common but not universal graph characteristic of homophily, wherein nodes link to nodes which are similar. Here we confirm that SGC is indeed ineffective for heterophilous (i.e., non-homophilous) graphs via experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets. We propose Adaptive Simple Graph Convolution (ASGC), which we show can adapt to both homophilous and heterophilous graph structure. Like SGC, ASGC is not a deep model, and hence is fast, scalable, and interpretable; further, we can prove performance guarantees on natural synthetic data models. Empirically, ASGC is often competitive with recent deep models at node classification on a benchmark of real-world datasets. The SGC paper questioned whether the complexity of graph neural networks is warranted for common graph problems involving homophilous networks; our results similarly suggest that, while deep learning often achieves the highest performance, heterophilous structure alone does not necessitate these more involved methods.

Many graphs instead exhibit heterophily, where connections do not follow that pattern. This paper confirms through synthetic and real-data experiments that the original simple method is ineffective on heterophilous graphs.

The authors propose Adaptive Simple Graph Convolution, which can adjust to both homophilous and heterophilous structure. Their narrower conclusion is that heterophily alone does not make a complex deep architecture necessary: adapting a simpler graph method can already address an important source of mismatch between an algorithm and graph structure.
summary.tldr: Adaptive Simple Graph Convolution handles both homophily and heterophily while often competing with deep models on node classification.

title: Simplified Graph Convolution with Heterophily

abstract: Deep learning models have shown their vulnerability when dealing with adversarial attacks. Existing attacks almost perform on low-level instances, such as pixels and super-pixels, and rarely exploit semantic clues. For face recognition attacks, existing methods typically generate the l_p-norm perturbations on pixels, however, resulting in low attack transferability and high vulnerability to denoising defense models. In this work, instead of performing perturbations on the low-level pixels, we propose to generate attacks through perturbing on the high-level semantics to improve attack transferability. Specifically, a unified flexible framework, Adversarial Attributes (Adv-Attribute), is designed to generate inconspicuous and transferable attacks on face recognition, which crafts the adversarial noise and adds it into different attributes based on the guidance of the difference in face recognition features from the target. Moreover, the importance-aware attribute selection and the multi-objective optimization strategy are introduced to further ensure the balance of stealthiness and attacking strength. Extensive experiments on the FFHQ and CelebA-HQ datasets show that the proposed Adv-Attribute method achieves the state-of-the-art attacking success rates while maintaining better visual effects against recent attack methods.

paragraphs: Face-recognition attacks often modify individual pixels under a constraint on perturbation size. The authors identify two weaknesses of these approaches: attacks may transfer poorly between recognition models, and denoising defenses may remove their effect. They investigate whether changing higher-level facial attributes can produce attacks that remain visually inconspicuous while transferring more effectively.

Adv-Attribute introduces adversarial changes through semantic attributes. Differences between the recognition features of a face and those of a target guide these changes. The framework also selects attributes according to their importance and uses multiple optimization objectives to balance attack strength against how noticeable the resulting image changes are.

Experiments on FFHQ and CelebA-HQ report state-of-the-art attack success rates together with better visual results than recent attack methods. These findings support the paper's central proposal that semantic attributes are a useful space for constructing face-recognition attacks. The contribution joins attack effectiveness and visual subtlety in one framework, with the reported evidence coming from the two evaluated datasets.
summary.tldr: Adv-Attribute modifies semantic facial attributes to produce visually subtle attacks with strong reported success and transferability.

title: Adv-Attribute: Inconspicuous and Transferable Adversarial Attack on Face Recognition

abstract: Few-shot semantic segmentation aims to segment the target objects in query under the condition of a few annotated support images. Most previous works strive to mine more effective category information from the support to match with the corresponding objects in query. However, they all ignored the category information gap between query and support images. If the objects in them show large intra-class diversity, forcibly migrating the category information from the support to the query is ineffective. To solve this problem, we are the first to introduce an intermediate prototype for mining both deterministic category information from the support and adaptive category knowledge from the query. Specifically, we design an Intermediate Prototype Mining Transformer (IPMT) to learn the prototype in an iterative way. In each IPMT layer, we propagate the object information in both support and query features to the prototype and then use it to activate the query feature map. By conducting this process iteratively, both the intermediate prototype and the query feature can be progressively improved. At last, the final query feature is used to yield precise segmentation prediction. Extensive experiments on both PASCAL-5i and COCO-20i datasets clearly verify the effectiveness of our IPMT and show that it outperforms previous state-of-the-art methods by a large margin. Code is available at https://github.com/LIUYUANWEI98/IPMT

paragraphs: Few-shot semantic segmentation identifies target-object pixels in a query image using only a few annotated support images. A difficulty arises when objects from the same class look very different across support and query images. Information extracted from the support may then be a poor match for the object that must actually be segmented.

The proposed Intermediate Prototype Mining Transformer addresses this gap with a representation that draws information from both sides. The support supplies category information grounded in its annotations, while the query contributes information adapted to its own appearance. Each transformer layer updates this intermediate prototype using support and query features, then uses the prototype to activate the query feature map.

Repeating this exchange progressively refines both the prototype and the query representation before producing the segmentation. The authors report that the method substantially outperforms previous state-of-the-art approaches on PASCAL-5i and COCO-20i. The findings support the value of adapting category information jointly with the query, especially for the support–query appearance differences that motivate the design.
summary.tldr: IPMT repeatedly combines support and query information into an intermediate prototype to improve few-shot segmentation.

title: Intermediate Prototype Mining Transformer for Few-Shot Semantic Segmentation

abstract: Multitask learning is a powerful framework that enables one to simultaneously learn multiple related tasks by sharing information between them. Quantifying uncertainty in the estimated tasks is of pivotal importance for many downstream applications, such as online or active learning. In this work, we provide novel confidence intervals for multitask regression in the challenging agnostic setting, i.e., when neither the similarity between tasks nor the tasks' features are available to the learner. The obtained intervals do not require i.i.d. data and can be directly applied to bound the regret in online learning. Through a refined analysis of the multitask information gain, we obtain new regret guarantees that, depending on a task similarity parameter, can significantly improve over treating tasks independently. We further propose a novel online learning algorithm that achieves such improved regret without knowing this parameter in advance, i.e., automatically adapting to task similarity. As a second key application of our results, we introduce a novel multitask active learning setup where several tasks must be simultaneously optimized, but only one of them can be queried for feedback by the learner at each round. For this problem, we design a no-regret algorithm that uses our confidence intervals to decide which task should be queried. Finally, we empirically validate our bounds and algorithms on synthetic and real-world (drug discovery) data.
originalAbstract: Multitask learning is a powerful framework that enables one to simultaneously learn multiple related tasks by sharing information between them. Quantifying uncertainty in the estimated tasks is of pivotal importance for many downstream applications, such as online or active learning. In this work, we provide novel confidence intervals for multitask regression in the challenging agnostic setting, i.e., when neither the similarity between tasks nor the tasks' features are available to the learner. The obtained intervals do not require i.i.d. data and can be directly applied to bound the regret in online learning. Through a refined analysis of the multitask information gain, we obtain new regret guarantees that, depending on a task similarity parameter, can significantly improve over treating tasks independently. We further propose a novel online learning algorithm that achieves such improved regret without knowing this parameter in advance, i.e., automatically adapting to task similarity. As a second key application of our results, we introduce a novel multitask active learning setup where several tasks must be simultaneously optimized, but only one of them can be queried for feedback by the learner at each round. For this problem, we design a no-regret algorithm that uses our confidence intervals to decide which task should be queried. Finally, we empirically validate our bounds and algorithms on synthetic and real-world (drug discovery) data.

paragraphs: Learning related tasks together can be useful, but deciding what to do next also requires knowing how uncertain each prediction is. This paper develops confidence intervals for multitask regression in an agnostic setting where the learner lacks both task similarity information and task features. The intervals also do not require independent, identically distributed data.

The authors use these uncertainty bounds to analyze online learning. Their regret guarantees can improve substantially over learning tasks independently, depending on how similar the tasks are. They also propose an algorithm that adapts to this similarity without knowing its value beforehand. This connects the potential benefit of information sharing to an implementable learning procedure.

A second application considers active learning across several tasks when only one task can be queried for feedback each round. The proposed no-regret algorithm uses the confidence intervals to choose which task to query while pursuing all tasks simultaneously. Synthetic and drug-discovery experiments validate the bounds and algorithms, supporting uncertainty estimation as a tool for coordinating limited feedback across related problems.
summary.tldr: New multitask confidence bounds enable online and active-learning algorithms that adapt to unknown task similarity.

title: Multitask Learning with No Regret: from Improved Confidence Bounds to Active Learning

abstract: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) facilitates the alignment of large language models with human preferences, significantly enhancing the quality of interactions between humans and models. InstructGPT implements RLHF through several stages, including Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), reward model training, and Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO). However, PPO is sensitive to hyperparameters and requires multiple models in its standard implementation, making it hard to train and scale up to larger parameter counts.In contrast, we propose a novel learning paradigm called RRHF, which scores sampled responses from different sources via a logarithm of conditional probabilities and learns to align these probabilities with human preferences through ranking loss.RRHF can leverage sampled responses from various sources including the model responses from itself, other large language model responses, and human expert responses to learn to rank them.RRHF only needs 1 to 2 models during tuning and can efficiently align language models with human preferences robustly without complex hyperparameter tuning. Additionally, RRHF can be considered an extension of SFT and reward model training while being simpler than PPO in terms of coding, model counts, and hyperparameters. We evaluate RRHF on the Helpful and Harmless dataset, demonstrating comparable alignment performance with PPO by reward model score and human labeling.Extensive experiments show that the performance of RRHF is highly related to sampling quality which suggests RRHF is a best-of-$n$ learner.

paragraphs: Aligning language models with human preferences often involves supervised fine-tuning, reward modeling, and Proximal Policy Optimization. The paper identifies PPO's sensitivity to hyperparameters and need for multiple models as obstacles to training and scaling. RRHF offers a simpler learning approach that turns preference alignment into a response-ranking problem.

RRHF scores candidate responses using their conditional log probabilities and applies a ranking loss so those scores agree with human preferences. Candidates may come from the model itself, other language models, or human experts. Tuning requires only one or two models, and the authors describe the method as an extension of supervised fine-tuning and reward-model training with less implementation and tuning complexity than PPO.

On the Helpful and Harmless dataset, RRHF achieves alignment comparable to PPO according to reward-model scores and human labels. Experiments also show a strong relationship between performance and the quality of sampled responses. This suggests a best-of-n learning behavior: the candidate pool matters substantially because ranking learns from the quality of the alternatives supplied.
summary.tldr: RRHF aligns response probabilities with human preference rankings, matching PPO on the reported evaluation with a simpler tuning setup.

title: RRHF: Rank Responses to Align Language Models with Human Feedback

abstract: The meteoric rise in the adoption of deep neural networks as computational models of vision has inspired efforts to ``align” these models with humans. One dimension of interest for alignment includes behavioral choices, but moving beyond characterizing choice patterns to capturing temporal aspects of visual decision-making has been challenging. Here, we sketch a general-purpose methodology to construct computational accounts of reaction times from a stimulus-computable, task-optimized model. Specifically, we introduce a novel metric leveraging insights from subjective logic theory summarizing evidence accumulation in recurrent vision models. We demonstrate that our metric aligns with patterns of human reaction times for stimulus manipulations across four disparate visual decision-making tasks spanning perceptual grouping, mental simulation, and scene categorization. This work paves the way for exploring the temporal alignment of model and human visual strategies in the context of various other cognitive tasks toward generating testable hypotheses for neuroscience. Links to the code and data can be found on the project page: https://serre-lab.github.io/rnn_rts_site/.

paragraphs: A vision model can make choices similar to a person’s without explaining how long that person takes to decide. This paper examines that temporal dimension of alignment. It develops a methodology for deriving a reaction-time measure from a model that processes visual stimuli and has been optimized for a task.

The proposed metric draws on subjective logic theory to summarize evidence accumulation in recurrent vision models. Recurrence provides a sequence of internal processing steps, giving the method something to analyze beyond the final choice. The goal is to connect the model’s evolving evidence with patterns of decision timing, making reaction time part of the computational account of visual behavior.

The authors demonstrate alignment with human reaction-time patterns under stimulus manipulations across four tasks, spanning perceptual grouping, mental simulation, and scene categorization. These findings support using the metric to study temporal similarities between model and human strategies. The proposed broader value is a route toward testable neuroscience hypotheses in additional cognitive tasks, rather than an established explanation of timing across all visual behavior.
summary.tldr: An evidence-accumulation metric from recurrent vision models aligns with human reaction-time patterns across four visual tasks.

title: Computing a human-like reaction time metric from stable recurrent vision models

abstract: Federated learning (FL) has emerged as a powerful scheme to facilitate the collaborative learning of models amongst a set of agents holding their own private data. Although the agents benefit from the global model trained on shared data, by participating in federated learning, they may also incur costs (related to privacy and communication) due to data sharing. In this paper, we model a collaborative FL framework, where every agent attempts to achieve an optimal trade-off between her learning payoff and data sharing cost. We show the existence of Nash equilibrium (NE) under mild assumptions on agents' payoff and costs. Furthermore, we show that agents can discover the NE via best response dynamics. However, some of the NE may be bad in terms of overall welfare for the agents, implying little incentive for some fraction of the agents to participate in the learning. To remedy this, we design a budget-balanced mechanism involving payments to the agents, that ensures that any $p$-mean welfare function of the agents' utilities is maximized at NE. In addition, we introduce a FL protocol FedBR-BG that incorporates our budget-balanced mechanism, utilizing best response dynamics. Our empirical validation on MNIST and CIFAR-10 substantiates our theoretical analysis. We show that FedBR-BG outperforms the basic best-response-based protocol without additional incentivization, the standard federated learning protocol FedAvg, as well as a recent baseline MWFed in terms of achieving superior $p$-mean welfare.

This paper treats each participant as an agent choosing a trade-off between learning benefits and those costs. Under mild assumptions on payoffs and costs, it proves that a Nash equilibrium exists and can be discovered through best-response dynamics.

An equilibrium can still leave participants collectively poorly served, with some having little incentive to contribute. The authors therefore design a budget-balanced payment mechanism that makes equilibrium maximize a chosen p-mean welfare function of participant utilities. This connects individual decision-making to an explicit collective objective, addressing the gap between stable behavior and desirable outcomes.

The mechanism is incorporated into FedBR-BG, a federated-learning protocol that uses best-response updates. Experiments on MNIST and CIFAR-10 support the theoretical analysis: FedBR-BG achieves better p-mean welfare than an unincentivized best-response protocol, FedAvg, and MWFed. The stated improvement concerns participant welfare, reflecting how the protocol balances learning payoffs and participation costs in the modeled collaboration.
summary.tldr: A budget-balanced incentive mechanism aligns federated-learning equilibria with participant welfare and improves reported p-mean welfare.

title: Incentives in Federated Learning: Equilibria, Dynamics, and Mechanisms for Welfare Maximization

abstract: Elastic geophysical properties (such as P- and S-wave velocities) are of great importance to various subsurface applications like CO$_2$ sequestration and energy exploration (e.g., hydrogen and geothermal). Elastic full waveform inversion (FWI) is widely applied for characterizing reservoir properties. In this paper, we introduce $\mathbf{\mathbb{E}^{FWI}}$, a comprehensive benchmark dataset that is specifically designed for elastic FWI. $\mathbf{\mathbb{E}^{FWI}}$ encompasses 8 distinct datasets that cover diverse subsurface geologic structures (flat, curve, faults, etc). The benchmark results produced by three different deep learning methods are provided. In contrast to our previously presented dataset (pressure recordings) for acoustic FWI (referred to as OpenFWI), the seismic dataset in $\mathbf{\mathbb{E}^{FWI}}$ has both vertical and horizontal components. Moreover, the velocity maps in $\mathbf{\mathbb{E}^{FWI}}$ incorporate both P- and S-wave velocities. While the multicomponent data and the added S-wave velocity make the data more realistic, more challenges are introduced regarding the convergence and computational cost of the inversion. We conduct comprehensive numerical experiments to explore the relationship between P-wave and S-wave velocities in seismic data. The relation between P- and S-wave velocities provides crucial insights into the subsurface properties such as lithology, porosity, fluid content, etc. We anticipate that $\mathbf{\mathbb{E}^{FWI}}$ will facilitate future research on multiparameter inversions and stimulate endeavors in several critical research topics of carbon-zero and new energy exploration. All datasets, codes and relevant information can be accessed through our website at https://efwi-lanl.github.io/

paragraphs: Elastic full waveform inversion uses seismic information to characterize subsurface properties, including P-wave and S-wave velocities. These properties matter for applications such as carbon dioxide storage and energy exploration. This paper introduces EFWI, a benchmark collection designed specifically for learning and evaluating elastic inversion across varied geological structures.

The collection contains eight datasets, including structures with flat layers, curves, and faults, and supplies benchmark results from three deep learning methods. Compared with the authors' earlier acoustic OpenFWI dataset, its seismic observations include both horizontal and vertical components. Its target velocity maps also contain both P-wave and S-wave velocities, adding another physical quantity to recover.

These additions make the data more realistic while increasing difficulties with inversion convergence and computational cost. Numerical experiments investigate how P-wave and S-wave velocities relate in the seismic data, a relationship relevant to properties such as lithology, porosity, and fluid content. The benchmark is intended to support future multiparameter inversion research, including work connected to carbon-zero and new-energy applications.
summary.tldr: EFWI provides eight elastic seismic inversion datasets with multicomponent observations, P- and S-wave targets, and deep learning benchmarks.

title: $\mathbf{\mathbb{E}^{FWI}}$: Multiparameter Benchmark Datasets for Elastic Full Waveform Inversion of Geophysical Properties

abstract: As machine learning agents act more autonomously in the world, they will increasingly interact with each other. Unfortunately, in many social dilemmas like the one-shot Prisoner’s Dilemma, standard game theory predicts that ML agents will fail to cooperate with each other. Prior work has shown that one way to enable cooperative outcomes in the one-shot Prisoner’s Dilemma is to make the agents mutually transparent to each other, i.e., to allow them to access one another’s source code (Rubinstein, 1998; Tennenholtz, 2004) – or weights in the case of ML agents. However, full transparency is often unrealistic, whereas partial transparency is commonplace. Moreover, it is challenging for agents to learn their way to cooperation in the full transparency setting. In this paper, we introduce a more realistic setting in which agents only observe a single number indicating how similar they are to each other. We prove that this allows for the same set of cooperative outcomes as the full transparency setting. We also demonstrate experimentally that cooperation can be learned using simple ML methods.

paragraphs: Autonomous learning agents may face social dilemmas in which standard game-theoretic reasoning predicts a failure to cooperate. Earlier work showed that access to one another's source code or model weights can enable cooperation in the one-shot Prisoner's Dilemma. However, full transparency can be unrealistic, and learning cooperative behavior in that setting can be difficult.

This paper studies a more limited information channel: each agent sees a single number describing how similar it is to the other agent. The authors prove that their similarity-based setting permits the same set of cooperative outcomes as the full-transparency setting. Thus, within the proposed framework, the available cooperative outcomes can be preserved despite the much narrower observation.

The paper also demonstrates experimentally that simple machine-learning methods can learn cooperation in this setting. The theoretical result concerns which outcomes are possible, while the experiments address whether learning can reach cooperative behavior. Together, they show how partial information about another agent can provide a basis for cooperation without requiring access to its complete implementation.
summary.tldr: In the proposed setting, a single similarity signal permits the same cooperative outcomes as full transparency, and simple learning methods can learn cooperation.

title: Similarity-based cooperative equilibrium

abstract: Training generative adversarial networks (GANs) with limited data is challenging because the discriminator is prone to overfitting. Previously proposed differentiable augmentation demonstrates improved data efficiency of training GANs. However, the augmentation implicitly introduces undesired invariance to augmentation for the discriminator since it ignores the change of semantics in the label space caused by data transformation, which may limit the representation learning ability of the discriminator and ultimately affect the generative modeling performance of the generator. To mitigate the negative impact of invariance while inheriting the benefits of data augmentation, we propose a novel augmentation-aware self-supervised discriminator that predicts the augmentation parameter of the augmented data. Particularly, the prediction targets of real data and generated data are required to be distinguished since they are different during training. We further encourage the generator to adversarially learn from the self-supervised discriminator by generating augmentation-predictable real and not fake data. This formulation connects the learning objective of the generator and the arithmetic $-$ harmonic mean divergence under certain assumptions. We compare our method with state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods using the class-conditional BigGAN and unconditional StyleGAN2 architectures on data-limited CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, FFHQ, LSUN-Cat, and five low-shot datasets. Experimental results demonstrate significant improvements of our method over SOTA methods in training data-efficient GANs.
