paragraphs: With little training data, a GAN's discriminator can overfit. Data augmentation helps, but the paper identifies a potential drawback: a discriminator that ignores which transformation was applied can acquire unwanted invariance. When transformations change label meaning, that invariance may weaken the representations that guide the generator.

The proposed discriminator therefore predicts augmentation parameters as an additional self-supervised task. It distinguishes the prediction targets for real and generated examples, preserving the difference between those sources during training. The generator learns adversarially to produce examples whose transformations are predictable and whose discriminator targets correspond to real data.

Under certain assumptions, the authors connect the generator's objective to the arithmetic–harmonic mean divergence. They also evaluate the approach with class-conditional BigGAN and unconditional StyleGAN2 across several limited-data and low-shot datasets. The reported significant improvements over leading methods support retaining information about transformations, rather than automatically discarding it, as a useful way to strengthen GAN training when examples are scarce.
summary.tldr: Teaching a GAN discriminator to recognize augmentations improves generation in the evaluated limited-data settings.

title: Augmentation-Aware Self-Supervision for Data-Efficient GAN Training

abstract: In visual-based Reinforcement Learning (RL), agents often struggle to generalize well to environmental variations in the state space that were not observed during training. The variations can arise in both task-irrelevant features, such as background noise, and task-relevant features, such as robot configurations, that are related to the optimal decisions. To achieve generalization in both situations, agents are required to accurately understand the impact of changed features on the decisions, i.e., establishing the true associations between changed features and decisions in the policy model. However, due to the inherent correlations among features in the state space, the associations between features and decisions become entangled, making it difficult for the policy to distinguish them. To this end, we propose Saliency-Guided Features Decorrelation (SGFD) to eliminate these correlations through sample reweighting. Concretely, SGFD consists of two core techniques: Random Fourier Functions (RFF) and the saliency map. RFF is utilized to estimate the complex non-linear correlations in high-dimensional images, while the saliency map is designed to identify the changed features. Under the guidance of the saliency map, SGFD employs sample reweighting to minimize the estimated correlations related to changed features, thereby achieving decorrelation in visual RL tasks. Our experimental results demonstrate that SGFD can generalize well on a wide range of test environments and significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in handling both task-irrelevant variations and task-relevant variations.

paragraphs: Visual reinforcement learning agents can struggle when their environment looks different from the training setting. Some changes, such as background noise, should not affect decisions. Others, such as robot configurations, can change which action is appropriate. The paper argues that correlations between visual features entangle their relationships with decisions, making these two situations difficult for a policy to handle correctly.

Saliency-Guided Features Decorrelation, or SGFD, addresses this problem through sample reweighting. Random Fourier Functions estimate complex nonlinear correlations in high-dimensional images, while a saliency map identifies changed features. The method then adjusts sample weights to reduce estimated correlations involving those features. This targets the dependencies that can obscure how environmental changes should influence behavior.

Experiments across a broad set of test environments show strong generalization and significant improvements over the compared state-of-the-art methods. The reported benefits cover both task-irrelevant and task-relevant variation. That distinction matters because successful adaptation requires sensitivity to meaningful changes as well as resilience to distracting ones.
summary.tldr: SGFD reweights training samples to reduce correlations involving changed visual features, improving RL generalization to relevant and irrelevant variations.

title: Learning Generalizable Agents via Saliency-guided Features Decorrelation

abstract: We establish the first mathematically rigorous link between Bayesian, variational Bayesian, and ensemble methods. A key step towards this it to reformulate the non-convex optimisation problem typically encountered in deep learning as a convex optimisation in the space of probability measures. On a technical level, our contribution amounts to studying generalised variational inference through the lense of Wasserstein gradient flows. The result is a unified theory of various seemingly disconnected approaches that are commonly used for uncertainty quantification in deep learning---including deep ensembles and (variational) Bayesian methods. This offers a fresh perspective on the reasons behind the success of deep ensembles over procedures based on parameterised variational inference, and allows the derivation of new ensembling schemes with convergence guarantees. We showcase this by proposing a family of interacting deep ensembles with direct parallels to the interactions of particle systems in thermodynamics, and use our theory to prove the convergence of these algorithms to a well-defined global minimiser on the space of probability measures.

paragraphs: Deep ensembles and Bayesian methods both address uncertainty in neural networks, but their mathematical descriptions can make them look unrelated. This paper develops a rigorous connection between them by changing the object being optimized. Instead of working only with individual network parameters, it considers probability distributions over those parameters.

The central move reformulates the usual nonconvex optimization problem as a convex problem in the space of probability measures. The authors study generalized variational inference through Wasserstein gradient flows, providing a common framework for ensembles, Bayesian inference, and variational Bayesian inference. This perspective also offers an explanation for the success of deep ensembles relative to approaches using parameterized variational distributions.

The framework leads to new ensembles whose members interact, with parallels to interacting particles in thermodynamics. The authors prove convergence of these algorithms to a well-defined global minimizer in the space of probability measures. The location of that guarantee matters: it concerns the distribution-level formulation that makes the connection possible.
summary.tldr: A distribution-level optimization framework connects deep ensembles with Bayesian methods and yields interacting ensembles with convergence guarantees.

title: A Rigorous Link between Deep Ensembles and (Variational) Bayesian Methods

abstract: We study the consistency of surrogate risks for robust binary classification.It is common to learn robust classifiers by adversarial training, which seeks to minimize the expected $0$-$1$ loss when each example can be maliciously corrupted within a small ball.We give a simple and complete characterization of the set of surrogate loss functions that are \emph{consistent}, i.e., that can replace the $0$-$1$ loss without affecting the minimizing sequences of the original adversarial risk, for any data distribution.We also prove a quantitative version of adversarial consistency for the $\rho$-margin loss.Our results reveal that the class of adversarially consistent surrogates is substantially smaller than in the standard setting, where many common surrogates are known to be consistent.

paragraphs: Robust binary classification seeks correct decisions even when an adversary can alter each input within a small neighborhood. Its natural objective counts classification errors under those perturbations. Training commonly substitutes another loss for this zero-one objective, raising a theoretical question: does optimizing the replacement still lead toward the intended robust classification objective?

The paper gives a complete characterization of surrogate losses that satisfy adversarial consistency for any data distribution. Here, consistency concerns minimizing sequences: progressively optimizing the surrogate must preserve the relevant connection to minimizing the original adversarial risk. The result identifies exactly which replacement losses meet this distribution-independent requirement in the setting studied.

The authors also prove a quantitative consistency result for the rho-margin loss, strengthening the qualitative relationship for that particular surrogate. Their characterization shows that adversarially consistent losses form a substantially smaller class than consistent losses in ordinary classification. Consequently, a surrogate’s established suitability without adversarial perturbations does not by itself establish its suitability for robust learning. The contribution clarifies the mathematical requirements behind choosing a replacement objective for adversarial training.
summary.tldr: The paper completely characterizes distribution-independent adversarially consistent surrogate losses and shows they are more restricted than ordinary consistent losses.

title: The Adversarial Consistency of Surrogate Risks for Binary Classification

abstract: Object-centric learning aims to represent visual data with a set of object entities (a.k.a. slots), providing structured representations that enable systematic generalization.Leveraging advanced architectures like Transformers, recent approaches have made significant progress in unsupervised object discovery.In addition, slot-based representations hold great potential for generative modeling, such as controllable image generation and object manipulation in image editing.However, current slot-based methods often produce blurry images and distorted objects, exhibiting poor generative modeling capabilities.In this paper, we focus on improving slot-to-image decoding, a crucial aspect for high-quality visual generation.We introduce SlotDiffusion -- an object-centric Latent Diffusion Model (LDM) designed for both image and video data.Thanks to the powerful modeling capacity of LDMs, SlotDiffusion surpasses previous slot models in unsupervised object segmentation and visual generation across six datasets.Furthermore, our learned object features can be utilized by existing object-centric dynamics models, improving video prediction quality and downstream temporal reasoning tasks.Finally, we demonstrate the scalability of SlotDiffusion to unconstrained real-world datasets such as PASCAL VOC and COCO, when integrated with self-supervised pre-trained image encoders.

paragraphs: Object-centric learning represents a scene through a collection of object entities called slots. These structured representations offer possibilities for controlled generation and object manipulation, but existing slot-based methods can decode them into blurry images or distorted objects. SlotDiffusion addresses this bottleneck by focusing on how object representations are converted back into visual content.

The method is an object-centric latent diffusion model for images and videos. It uses the modeling capacity of latent diffusion to improve slot-to-image decoding. Across six datasets, the authors report better unsupervised object segmentation and visual generation than previous slot models. The results link stronger visual decoding with improvements in both generated output and the discovery of objects.

The learned object features can also be used by existing object-centric dynamics models, improving video prediction and downstream temporal reasoning in the reported evaluations. When combined with self-supervised pretrained image encoders, SlotDiffusion also scales to unconstrained real-world datasets such as PASCAL VOC and COCO. This integration condition matters: the stated real-world scalability is demonstrated with those pretrained encoders as part of the system.
summary.tldr: SlotDiffusion improves object-based image and video modeling with latent diffusion, benefiting segmentation, generation, and temporal tasks.

title: SlotDiffusion: Object-Centric Generative Modeling with Diffusion Models

abstract: Pruning schemes have been widely used in practice to reduce the complexity of trained models with a massive number of parameters. In fact, several practical studies have shown that if the pruned model is fine-tuned with some gradient-based updates it generalizes well to new samples. Although the above pipeline, which we refer to as pruning + fine-tuning, has been extremely successful in lowering the complexity of trained models, there is very little known about the theory behind this success. In this paper we address this issue by investigating the pruning + fine-tuning framework on the overparameterized matrix sensing problem with the ground truth denoted $U_\star \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times r}$ and the overparameterized model $U \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times k}$ with $k \gg r$. We study the approximate local minima of the mean square error, augmented with a smooth version of a group Lasso regularizer, $\sum_{i=1}^{k} \lVert Ue_i \rVert_2 $. In particular, we provably show that pruning all the columns below a certain explicit $\ell_2$-norm threshold results in a solution $U_{\text{prune}}$ which has the minimum number of columns $r$, yet close to the ground truth in training loss. Moreover, in the subsequent fine-tuning phase, gradient descent initialized at $U_{\text{prune}}$ converges at a linear rate to its limit. While our analysis provides insights into the role of regularization in pruning, we also show that running gradient descent in the absence of regularization results in models which {are not suitable for greedy pruning}, i.e., many columns could have their $\ell_2$ norm comparable to that of the maximum. Lastly, we show that our results also extend for the training and pruning of two-layer neural networks with quadratic activation functions. To the best of our knowledge, our results provide the first rigorous insights on why greedy pruning + fine-tuning leads to smaller models which also generalize well.

paragraphs: Pruning followed by additional training often produces smaller models that still generalize well, but explaining that success theoretically is difficult. This paper studies the process in matrix sensing, where the trained representation has many more columns than the ground-truth representation needs. It analyzes approximate local minima of squared error with a smoothed group Lasso penalty.

The penalty acts on entire columns. The authors prove that removing columns whose norms fall below an explicit threshold leaves exactly the minimum required number of columns, while keeping training loss close to the ground-truth solution. Starting gradient descent from this pruned representation then gives linear convergence to its limit during fine-tuning.

The analysis also explains why regularization matters for this pruning rule. Without it, gradient descent can produce many columns with comparable norms, making small-column removal unsuitable. The results extend to two-layer neural networks with quadratic activations. These findings provide rigorous support for pruning and fine-tuning in the studied settings, showing how regularization can make redundant structure identifiable through a simple magnitude threshold.
summary.tldr: For matrix sensing, group Lasso makes norm-based pruning recover the required model size and supports provably effective fine-tuning.

title: Greedy Pruning with Group Lasso Provably Generalizes for Matrix Sensing

abstract: As extreme weather events become more frequent, understanding their impact on human health becomes increasingly crucial. However, the utilization of Earth Observation to effectively analyze the environmental context in relation to health remains limited. This limitation is primarily due to the lack of fine-grained spatial and temporal data in public and population health studies, hindering a comprehensive understanding of health outcomes. Additionally, obtaining appropriate environmental indices across different geographical levels and timeframes poses a challenge. For the years 2019 (pre-COVID) and 2020 (COVID), we collected spatio-temporal indicators for all Lower Layer Super Output Areas in England. These indicators included: i) 111 sociodemographic features linked to health in existing literature, ii) 43 environmental point features (e.g., greenery and air pollution levels), iii) 4 seasonal composite satellite images each with 11 bands, and iv) prescription prevalence associated with five medical conditions (depression, anxiety, diabetes, hypertension, and asthma), opioids and total prescriptions. We combined these indicators into a single MedSat dataset, the availability of which presents an opportunity for the machine learning community to develop new techniques specific to public health. These techniques would address challenges such as handling large and complex data volumes, performing effective feature engineering on environmental and sociodemographic factors, capturing spatial and temporal dependencies in the models, addressing imbalanced data distributions, developing novel computer vision methods for health modeling based on satellite imagery, ensuring model explainability, and achieving generalization beyond the specific geographical region.

MedSat addresses this need by combining environmental, sociodemographic, satellite, and prescription indicators for every Lower Layer Super Output Area in England. Its coverage includes 2019 and 2020, providing data from before and during COVID.

The dataset contains 111 sociodemographic features, 43 environmental point features such as greenery and air pollution, and four seasonal satellite composites with 11 bands each. They identify challenges involving complex data, feature engineering, spatial and temporal relationships, imbalance, explainability, and geographic generalization. Satellite-based health modeling is another proposed direction. The paper's contribution is the integrated data resource that enables these investigations, rather than a reported causal finding about environmental exposure or a demonstrated health-prediction method.
summary.tldr: MedSat combines England-wide prescription, environmental, sociodemographic, and satellite data to support public-health machine learning.

title: MedSat: A Public Health Dataset for England Featuring Medical Prescriptions and Satellite Imagery

abstract: To address the challenges of sim-to-real gap and sample efficiency in reinforcement learning (RL), this work studies distributionally robust Markov decision processes (RMDPs) --- optimize the worst-case performance when the deployed environment is within an uncertainty set around some nominal MDP. Despite recent efforts, the sample complexity of RMDPs has remained largely undetermined. While the statistical implications of distributional robustness in RL have been explored in some specific cases, the generalizability of the existing findings remains unclear, especially in comparison to standard RL. Assuming access to a generative model that samples from the nominal MDP, we examine the sample complexity of RMDPs using a class of generalized $L_p$ norms as the 'distance' function for the uncertainty set, under two commonly adopted $sa$-rectangular and $s$-rectangular conditions. Our results imply that RMDPs can be more sample-efficient to solve than standard MDPs using generalized $L_p$ norms in both $sa$- and $s$-rectangular cases, potentially inspiring more empirical research. We provide a near-optimal upper bound and a matching minimax lower bound for the $sa$-rectangular scenarios. For $s$-rectangular cases, we improve the state-of-the-art upper bound and also derive a lower bound using $L_\infty$ norm that verifies the tightness.

paragraphs: Distributionally robust reinforcement learning optimizes performance against the worst environment within a specified uncertainty set around a nominal model. This offers a way to account for differences between training and deployment environments. The paper asks how many samples are needed to solve these robust problems, particularly when uncertainty is measured using generalized Lp norms.

The analysis assumes access to a generative model that can sample from the nominal Markov decision process. It considers two common structures for the uncertainty set, called state-action rectangular and state rectangular. Within these settings, the results imply that robust problems can require fewer samples than standard reinforcement learning problems. This is a possibility established under the analyzed setup, rather than a universal advantage of robustness.

For state-action rectangular uncertainty, the paper gives a near-optimal upper bound and a matching minimax lower bound. For state rectangular uncertainty, it improves the existing upper bound and establishes tightness through a lower bound using the L-infinity norm. These results clarify the statistical cost of robustness and identify settings where established complexity bounds can be sharpened.
summary.tldr: The paper sharpens sample-complexity bounds for robust reinforcement learning with generalized Lp uncertainty and shows it can be more sample-efficient than standard RL.

title: Near-Optimal Distributionally Robust Reinforcement Learning with General $L_p$ Norms

abstract: Subset selection tasks, such as anomaly detection and compound selection in AI-assisted drug discovery, are crucial for a wide range of applications. Learning subset-valued functions with neural networks has achieved great success by incorporating permutation invariance symmetry into the architecture. However, existing neural set architectures often struggle to either capture comprehensive information from the superset or address complex interactions within the input. Additionally, they often fail to perform in scenarios where superset sizes surpass available memory capacity. To address these challenges, we introduce the novel concept of the Identity Property, which requires models to integrate information from the originating set, resulting in the development of neural networks that excel at performing effective subset selection from large supersets. Moreover, we present the Hierarchical Representation of Neural Subset Selection (HORSE), an attention-based method that learns complex interactions and retains information from both the input set and the optimal subset supervision signal. Specifically, HORSE enables the partitioning of the input ground set into manageable chunks that can be processed independently and then aggregated, ensuring consistent outcomes across different partitions. Through extensive experimentation, we demonstrate that HORSE significantly enhances neural subset selection performance by capturing more complex information and surpasses state-of-the-art methods in handling large-scale inputs by a margin of up to 20%.

paragraphs: HORSE addresses selecting a useful subset from a large collection, a problem that appears in anomaly detection and compound selection for drug discovery. Neural set models account for the fact that reordering a collection should not change its meaning. However, the paper argues that existing architectures can miss information about the full collection or complex interactions among its elements.

The authors introduce an Identity Property requiring models to incorporate information from the set that a subset comes from. Their attention-based HORSE method learns interactions while retaining information from both the input collection and supervision specifying the optimal subset. This connects decisions about selected elements to the broader set containing them.

HORSE also supports dividing a collection into chunks that can be processed independently and then combined, with consistent results across different partitions. This addresses inputs larger than available memory. Experiments report improved subset selection and gains of up to 20% over state-of-the-art methods for large inputs, supporting the combination of richer set representations and manageable chunk-based processing.
summary.tldr: HORSE improves large-scale subset selection by preserving whole-set information while allowing consistent processing in manageable chunks.

title: HORSE: Hierarchical Representation for Large-Scale Neural Subset Selection

abstract: We develop a framework for analyzing the training and learning rate dynamics on a large class of high-dimensional optimization problems, which we call the high line, trained using one-pass stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with adaptive learning rates. We give exact expressions for the risk and learning rate curves in terms of a deterministic solution to a system of ODEs. We then investigate in detail two adaptive learning rates -- an idealized exact line search and AdaGrad-Norm -- on the least squares problem. When the data covariance matrix has strictly positive eigenvalues, this idealized exact line search strategy can exhibit arbitrarily slower convergence when compared to the optimal fixed learning rate with SGD. Moreover we exactly characterize the limiting learning rate (as time goes to infinity) for line search in the setting where the data covariance has only two distinct eigenvalues. For noiseless targets, we further demonstrate that the AdaGrad-Norm learning rate converges to a deterministic constant inversely proportional to the average eigenvalue of the data covariance matrix, and identify a phase transition when the covariance density of eigenvalues follows a power law distribution. We provideour code for evaluation at https://github.com/amackenzie1/highline2024.

paragraphs: Adaptive learning rates change the size of optimization updates during training, but their long-run behavior can be difficult to analyze. The high line framework studies one-pass stochastic gradient descent on a broad class of high-dimensional problems. It expresses risk and learning-rate trajectories through deterministic ordinary differential equations.

The paper examines idealized exact line search and AdaGrad-Norm in least squares. When the data covariance has strictly positive eigenvalues, exact line search can converge arbitrarily more slowly than SGD using the optimal fixed learning rate. For covariance matrices with only two distinct eigenvalues, the authors exactly characterize the limiting line-search learning rate.

For noiseless targets, the AdaGrad-Norm learning rate converges to a deterministic constant inversely proportional to the covariance’s average eigenvalue. The analysis also identifies a phase transition when the eigenvalue density follows a power law. These results connect adaptive training dynamics to the data’s covariance structure and show, under the stated conditions, that choosing a learning rate adaptively need not improve convergence.
summary.tldr: The high line framework characterizes adaptive SGD dynamics and shows conditions where idealized line search can be arbitrarily slower than an optimal fixed rate.

title: The High Line: Exact Risk and Learning Rate Curves of Stochastic Adaptive Learning Rate Algorithms

abstract: Investigating the marginal causal effect of an intervention on an outcome from complex data remains challenging due to the inflexibility of employed models and the lack of complexity in causal benchmark datasets, which often fail to reproduce intricate real-world data patterns. In this paper we introduce Frugal Flows, a likelihood-based machine learning model that uses normalising flows to flexibly learn the data-generating process, while also directly targeting the marginal causal quantities inferred from observational data. We provide a novel algorithm for fitting a model to observational data with a parametrically specified causal distribution, and propose that these models are exceptionally well suited for synthetic data generation to validate causal methods. Unlike existing data generation methods, Frugal Flows generate synthetic data that closely resembles the empirical dataset, while also automatically and exactly satisfying a user-defined average treatment effect. To our knowledge, Frugal Flows are the first generative model to both learn flexible data representations and also \textit{exactly} parameterise quantities such as the average treatment effect and the degree of unobserved confounding. We demonstrate the above with experiments on both simulated and real-world datasets.

paragraphs: Frugal Flows addresses a difficulty in studying causal effects: models can be too inflexible, and synthetic benchmarks can be too simple to reflect real data. The paper introduces a likelihood-based generative model using normalizing flows to learn complex data patterns while directly representing marginal causal quantities of interest.

Its fitting algorithm uses observational data together with a parametrically specified causal distribution. For synthetic data generation, the model aims to resemble the empirical dataset while exactly satisfying a user-chosen average treatment effect. This combines flexible modeling of the observed data with explicit control over the causal quantity that a downstream method is supposed to estimate.

The authors also describe exact parameterization of the degree of unobserved confounding, and report experiments using simulated and real-world datasets. They present Frugal Flows as, to their knowledge, the first generative model combining flexible representations with exact parameterization of such causal quantities. This capability makes the approach useful for validating causal methods against controlled targets while retaining richer data structure.
summary.tldr: Frugal Flows learns flexible data distributions while exactly specifying causal quantities such as a user-defined average treatment effect.

title: Marginal Causal Flows for Validation and Inference

abstract: A critical question about Large Language Models (LLMs) is whether their apparent deficiency in mathematical reasoning is inherent, or merely a result of insufficient exposure to high-quality mathematical data. To explore this, we developed an automated method for generating high-quality, supervised mathematical datasets. The method carefully mutates existing math problems, ensuring both diversity and validity of the newly generated problems. This is achieved by a neuro-symbolic data generation framework combining the intuitive informalization strengths of LLMs, and the precise symbolic reasoning of math solvers along with projected Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling in the highly-irregular symbolic space.Empirical experiments demonstrate the high quality of data generated by the proposed method, and that the LLMs, specifically LLaMA-2 and Mistral, when realigned with the generated data, surpass their state-of-the-art counterparts.

paragraphs: The paper investigates whether language models’ mathematical weaknesses may partly reflect insufficient high-quality training data. It develops an automated method for producing supervised mathematical datasets by modifying existing problems. The aim is to create diverse new examples while preserving mathematical validity, making expansion of the dataset more than a matter of changing surface wording.

The framework combines language models with symbolic math solvers. Language models contribute their ability to express mathematical content informally, while solvers provide precise symbolic reasoning. Projected Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling is used to explore the irregular space of symbolic problems. These components divide the work between language production, mathematical correctness, and variation among generated examples.

Experiments report that the resulting data are high quality. LLaMA-2 and Mistral models realigned with these datasets outperform their state-of-the-art counterparts. This supports the importance of mathematical data quality and exposure for the evaluated models. It does not settle the broader question of whether every mathematical reasoning deficiency is caused by inadequate data, but provides evidence that this generation strategy can improve performance.
summary.tldr: Combining language models, symbolic solvers, and structured sampling produces math training data that improves LLaMA-2 and Mistral reasoning performance.

title: Neuro-Symbolic Data Generation for Math Reasoning

abstract: In model inversion attacks (MIAs), adversaries attempt to recover private training data by exploiting access to a well-trained target model. Recent advancements have improved MIA performance using a two-stage generative framework. This approach first employs a generative adversarial network to learn a fixed distributional prior, which is then used to guide the inversion process during the attack. However, in this paper, we observed a phenomenon that such a fixed prior would lead to a low probability of sampling actual private data during the inversion process due to the inherent distribution gap between the prior distribution and the private data distribution, thereby constraining attack performance. To address this limitation, we propose increasing the density around high-quality pseudo-private data—recovered samples through model inversion that exhibit characteristics of the private training data—by slightly tuning the generator. This strategy effectively increases the probability of sampling actual private data that is close to these pseudo-private data during the inversion process. After integrating our method, the generative model inversion pipeline is strengthened, leading to improvements over state-of-the-art MIAs. This paves the way for new research directions in generative MIAs.

paragraphs: Model inversion attacks try to recover private training data through access to a trained model. A common generative approach first learns a prior distribution with a generative adversarial network and then uses it to guide the attack. This paper identifies a problem with keeping that prior fixed: it may poorly match the private-data distribution.

That mismatch can make actual private examples unlikely to be sampled during inversion. The proposed method uses high-quality recovered examples, called pseudo-private data, as guidance for slightly tuning the generator. These examples exhibit characteristics of the private training data. Adjusting the generator increases probability density around them and makes nearby actual private data more likely to be sampled.

Integrating this adjustment into generative inversion improves attack performance over state-of-the-art methods. The finding highlights the importance of adapting the generative prior during the attack rather than treating it as a finished component. Successful partial reconstructions can help reshape subsequent sampling, strengthening the inversion pipeline through information already obtained from the target model.
summary.tldr: Tuning a generator around promising recovered examples improves model inversion by reducing mismatch with the private-data distribution.

title: Pseudo-Private Data Guided Model Inversion Attacks

abstract: While originally developed for continuous control problems, Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) has emerged as the work-horse of a variety of reinforcement learning (RL) applications, including the fine-tuning of generative models. Unfortunately, PPO requires multiple heuristics to enable stable convergence (e.g. value networks, clipping), and is notorious for its sensitivity to the precise implementation of these components. In response, we take a step back and ask what a *minimalist* RL algorithm for the era of generative models would look like. We propose REBEL, an algorithm that cleanly reduces the problem of policy optimization to regressing the *relative reward* between two completions to a prompt in terms of the policy, enabling strikingly lightweight implementation. In theory, we prove that fundamental RL algorithms like Natural Policy Gradient can be seen as variants of REBEL, which allows us to match the strongest known theoretical guarantees in terms of convergence and sample complexity in the RL literature. REBEL can also cleanly incorporate offline data and be extended to handle the intransitive preferences we frequently see in practice. Empirically, we find that REBEL provides a unified approach to language modeling and image generation with stronger or similar performance as PPO and DPO, all while being simpler to implement and more computationally efficient than PPO. When fine-tuning Llama-3-8B-Instruct, REBEL achieves strong performance in AlpacaEval 2.0, MT-Bench, and Open LLM Leaderboard. Implementation of REBEL can be found at <https://github.com/ZhaolinGao/REBEL>, and models trained by REBEL can be found at <https://huggingface.co/Cornell-AGI>.
originalAbstract: While originally developed for continuous control problems, Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) has emerged as the work-horse of a variety of reinforcement learning (RL) applications, including the fine-tuning of generative models. Unfortunately, PPO requires multiple heuristics to enable stable convergence (e.g. value networks, clipping), and is notorious for its sensitivity to the precise implementation of these components. In response, we take a step back and ask what a *minimalist* RL algorithm for the era of generative models would look like. We propose REBEL, an algorithm that cleanly reduces the problem of policy optimization to regressing the *relative reward* between two completions to a prompt in terms of the policy, enabling strikingly lightweight implementation. In theory, we prove that fundamental RL algorithms like Natural Policy Gradient can be seen as variants of REBEL, which allows us to match the strongest known theoretical guarantees in terms of convergence and sample complexity in the RL literature. REBEL can also cleanly incorporate offline data and be extended to handle the intransitive preferences we frequently see in practice. Empirically, we find that REBEL provides a unified approach to language modeling and image generation with stronger or similar performance as PPO and DPO, all while being simpler to implement and more computationally efficient than PPO. When fine-tuning Llama-3-8B-Instruct, REBEL achieves strong performance in AlpacaEval 2.0, MT-Bench, and Open LLM Leaderboard. Implementation of REBEL can be found at <https://github.com/ZhaolinGao/REBEL>, and models trained by REBEL can be found at <https://huggingface.co/Cornell-AGI>.

paragraphs: Optimizing generative models with reinforcement learning often involves PPO, whose stability depends on implementation choices such as value networks and clipping. REBEL seeks a simpler formulation. It turns policy optimization into a regression problem involving the reward difference between two completions of the same prompt, expressed through the policy.

This relative comparison gives the algorithm a lightweight implementation while retaining connections to established reinforcement learning methods. The authors show theoretically that Natural Policy Gradient and other fundamental algorithms can be viewed as REBEL variants, allowing them to match strong existing convergence and sample-complexity guarantees. The framework also accommodates offline data and extensions for intransitive preferences.

Experiments cover language modeling and image generation, reporting performance similar to or stronger than PPO and DPO, with simpler implementation and greater computational efficiency than PPO. Fine-tuning Llama-3-8B-Instruct also produces strong results across the listed language evaluations. The contribution is a common optimization formulation that combines practical simplicity with theoretical links to established policy-learning algorithms.
summary.tldr: REBEL reduces policy optimization to regression on relative rewards, offering theoretical guarantees and competitive generative-model results with a simpler implementation.

title: REBEL: Reinforcement Learning via Regressing Relative Rewards

abstract: We develop a novel measurement framework based on Gaussian process coregionalization model to address a long-lasting debate in psychometrics: whether psychological features like personality share a common structure across the population or vary uniquely for individuals. We propose idiographic personality Gaussian process (IPGP), an intermediate model that accommodates both shared trait structure across individuals and "idiographic" deviations. IPGP leverages the Gaussian process coregionalization model to conceptualize responses of grouped survey batteries but adjusted to non-Gaussian ordinal data, and exploits stochastic variational inference for latent factor estimation. Using both synthetic data and a novel survey, we show that IPGP improves both prediction of actual responses and estimation of intrapersonal response patterns compared to existing benchmarks. In the survey study, IPGP also identifies unique clusters of personality taxonomies, displaying great potential in advancing individualized approaches to psychological diagnosis.

paragraphs: Personality measurement faces a longstanding question: should psychological traits have one common structure across people, or should each individual have a distinct structure? The idiographic personality Gaussian process, or IPGP, takes an intermediate position. It represents shared trait organization while also allowing person-specific deviations from that organization.

The model builds on Gaussian process coregionalization to describe related responses across grouped survey batteries. It adapts this construction to ordinal responses, where answer categories have an order but are not treated as Gaussian measurements. Stochastic variational inference estimates the latent factors used to characterize these response patterns.

Using synthetic data and a new survey, the authors report better prediction of observed answers and better estimation of within-person response patterns than existing benchmarks. The survey analysis also identifies distinct clusters of personality taxonomies. These results support a measurement approach that preserves population-level structure while accommodating individual variation, with potential relevance to individualized psychological diagnosis rather than an established diagnostic outcome.
summary.tldr: IPGP models shared personality structure alongside individual deviations, improving survey-response prediction and within-person pattern estimation.

title: Idiographic Personality Gaussian Process for Psychological Assessment

abstract: Recent work on studying memorization in self-supervised learning (SSL) suggests that even though SSL encoders are trained on millions of images, they still memorize individual data points. While effort has been put into characterizing the memorized data and linking encoder memorization to downstream utility, little is known about where the memorization happens inside SSL encoders. To close this gap, we propose two metrics for localizing memorization in SSL encoders on a per-layer (LayerMem) and per-unit basis (UnitMem). Our localization methods are independent of the downstream task, do not require any label information, and can be performed in a forward pass. By localizing memorization in various encoder architectures (convolutional and transformer-based) trained on diverse datasets with contrastive and non-contrastive SSL frameworks, we find that (1) while SSL memorization increases with layer depth, highly memorizing units are distributed across the entire encoder, (2) a significant fraction of units in SSL encoders experiences surprisingly high memorization of individual data points, which is in contrast to models trained under supervision, (3) atypical (or outlier) data points cause much higher layer and unit memorization than standard data points, and (4) in vision transformers, most memorization happens in the fully-connected layers. Finally, we show that localizing memorization in SSL has the potential to improve fine-tuning and to inform pruning strategies.

paragraphs: Self-supervised vision encoders can memorize individual images even when trained on millions of examples. This paper investigates where that memorization occurs inside the network. It introduces LayerMem and UnitMem to measure memorization at the level of whole layers and individual units, without labels or a specified downstream task and using a forward pass.

The authors examine convolutional and transformer encoders trained with different datasets and self-supervised frameworks. They find that memorization increases with depth, while strongly memorizing units occur throughout the network. A substantial fraction of units shows high memorization of individual examples, contrasting with supervised models. Atypical examples produce much stronger memorization than standard examples.

For vision transformers, most memorization is found in fully connected layers. Together, these observations separate a broad depth trend from the locations of particular memorizing units. The authors also show that localization has potential to improve fine-tuning and guide pruning. The contribution makes memorization more spatially specific within an encoder, which can help inform decisions about how the model is adapted or reduced.
summary.tldr: LayerMem and UnitMem locate memorization inside self-supervised vision encoders, revealing patterns relevant to fine-tuning and pruning.

title: Localizing Memorization in SSL Vision Encoders

abstract: Scalable oversight protocols aim to enable humans to accurately supervise superhuman AI. In this paper we study debate, where two AI's compete to convince a judge; consultancy, where a single AI tries to convince a judge that asks questions;and compare to a baseline of direct question-answering, where the judge just answers outright without the AI.We use large language models (LLMs) as both AI agents and as stand-ins for human judges, taking the judge models to be weaker than agent models. We benchmark on a diverse range of asymmetries between judges and agents, extending previous work on a single extractive QA task with information asymmetry, to also include mathematics, coding, logic and multimodal reasoning asymmetries. We find that debate outperforms consultancy across all tasks when the consultant is randomly assigned to argue for the correct/incorrect answer. Comparing debate to direct question answering, the results depend on the type of task: in extractive QA tasks with information asymmetry debate outperforms direct question answering, but in other tasks without information asymmetry the results are mixed.Previous work assigned debaters/consultants an answer to argue for. When we allow them to instead choose which answer to argue for, we find judges are less frequently convinced by the wrong answer in debate than in consultancy.Further, we find that stronger debater models increase judge accuracy, though more modestly than in previous studies.

paragraphs: This paper studies whether weaker language models can judge stronger models more accurately through structured interaction. It compares debate between two agents, consultancy with one agent answering a judge's questions, and direct answering by the judge. Weaker models serve as stand-ins for human judges across information, mathematical, coding, logical, and multimodal reasoning asymmetries.

When consultants are randomly assigned to defend correct or incorrect answers, debate outperforms consultancy across all evaluated tasks. Its advantage over direct answering is more conditional. Debate helps in extractive question answering where agents and judges have unequal information, but results are mixed on other tasks without that information asymmetry.

When agents choose their own answers to defend, judges are less often persuaded by an incorrect answer in debate than in consultancy. Stronger debaters also improve judge accuracy, though the gains are more modest than in earlier studies. These findings support debate relative to consultancy in the tested settings, while showing that its value over a judge working alone depends on the task and information available.
summary.tldr: Debate improves weaker judges' decisions relative to consultancy in the tested settings, but its advantage over direct answering depends on the task.

title: On scalable oversight with weak LLMs judging strong LLMs

abstract: Federated learning works by aggregating locally computed gradients from multiple clients, thus enabling collaborative training without sharing private client data. However, prior work has shown that the data can actually be recovered by the server using so-called gradient inversion attacks. While these attacks perform well when applied on images, they are limited in the text domain and only permit approximate reconstruction of small batches and short input sequences. In this work, we propose DAGER, the first algorithm to recover whole batches of input text exactly. DAGER leverages the low-rank structure of self-attention layer gradients and the discrete nature of token embeddings to efficiently check if a given token sequence is part of the client data. We use this check to exactly recover full batches in the honest-but-curious setting without any prior on the data for both encoder and decoder-based architectures using exhaustive heuristic search and a greedy approach, respectively. We provide an efficient GPU implementation of DAGER and show experimentally that it recovers full batches of size up to 128 on large language models (LLMs), beating prior attacks in speed (20x at same batch size), scalability (10x larger batches), and reconstruction quality (ROUGE-1/2 > 0.99).

paragraphs: Federated learning keeps client data local while sharing gradients for collaborative training. Those gradients can nevertheless reveal the underlying examples. Previous text reconstruction attacks were limited to approximate recovery of small batches and short sequences. DAGER is presented as an algorithm capable of exactly recovering entire batches of input text.

The method combines two properties: self-attention gradients have a low-rank structure, and token embeddings come from a discrete set. Together, these enable a check for whether a candidate token sequence belongs to the client data. DAGER uses an exhaustive heuristic search for encoder architectures and a greedy approach for decoder architectures. Its setting assumes an honest-but-curious server and requires no prior information about the data.

Reported comparisons show 20-fold higher speed at the same batch size, support for batches ten times larger, and ROUGE-1/2 above 0.99. These findings demonstrate substantial text leakage through shared gradients under the studied setting, despite keeping the original examples on clients.
summary.tldr: DAGER exploits self-attention gradient structure and discrete token embeddings to recover full text batches from shared gradients.

title: DAGER: Exact Gradient Inversion for Large Language Models

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities in various tasks using the in-context learning (ICL) paradigm. However, their effectiveness is often compromised by inherent bias, leading to prompt brittleness—sensitivity to design settings such as example selection, order, and prompt formatting. Previous studies have addressed LLM bias through external adjustment of model outputs, but the internal mechanisms that lead to such bias remain unexplored. Our work delves into these mechanisms, particularly investigating how feedforward neural networks (FFNs) and attention heads result in the bias of LLMs. By Interpreting the contribution of individual FFN vectors and attention heads, we identify the biased LLM components that skew LLMs' prediction toward specific labels. To mitigate these biases, we introduce UniBias, an inference-only method that effectively identifies and eliminates biased FFN vectors and attention heads. Extensive experiments across 12 NLP datasets demonstrate that UniBias significantly enhances ICL performance and alleviates prompt brittleness of LLMs.

paragraphs: In-context learning lets a language model perform tasks using examples supplied in its prompt. Its effectiveness can change with example selection, example order, or formatting. UniBias investigates internal biases behind this prompt brittleness, focusing on components that push predictions toward particular labels.

The authors examine the contributions of individual feedforward-network vectors and attention heads. By interpreting those contributions, they identify components associated with skewed label predictions. UniBias then identifies and eliminates biased vectors and heads during inference. This places the intervention inside the model's computation, extending beyond the external output adjustments discussed in prior work.

Experiments across twelve natural-language-processing datasets show significant improvements in in-context learning performance and reduced prompt brittleness. The reported findings concern label preferences and sensitivity to prompt design in these tasks. They support the idea that examining individual internal components can reveal useful intervention points for making predictions more reliable across different ways of presenting examples and instructions.
summary.tldr: UniBias removes internal components associated with label bias during inference, improving in-context learning and reducing prompt sensitivity.

title: UniBias: Unveiling and Mitigating LLM Bias through Internal Attention and FFN Manipulation

abstract: Symmetry detection has been shown to improve various machine learning tasks. In the context of continuous symmetry detection, current state of the art experiments are limited to the detection of affine transformations. Under the manifold assumption, we outline a framework for discovering continuous symmetry in data beyond the affine transformation group. We also provide a similar framework for discovering discrete symmetry. We experimentally compare our method to an existing method known as LieGAN and show that our method is competitive at detecting affine symmetries for large sample sizes and superior than LieGAN for small sample sizes. We also show our method is able to detect continuous symmetries beyond the affine group and is generally more computationally efficient than LieGAN.

paragraphs: Symmetry discovery seeks transformations that preserve meaningful structure in data. Such knowledge can improve machine-learning tasks, but the paper notes that existing continuous-symmetry experiments have largely focused on affine transformations. The authors develop a framework intended to reach beyond that transformation family.

The framework assumes the data have an underlying manifold structure. Under this assumption, it supports discovery of continuous symmetries beyond the affine group. The paper also supplies a related framework for discrete symmetries, extending the scope of the proposed approach to another kind of structure-preserving transformation.

Experiments compare the method with LieGAN. For affine symmetry detection, the proposed method is competitive when many samples are available and performs better with small sample sizes. It also detects continuous symmetries outside the affine group and is generally more computationally efficient than LieGAN. The findings therefore address both breadth and practicality: the framework captures a broader class of transformations while showing favorable sample-size and computational behavior in the reported comparisons.
summary.tldr: Under a manifold assumption, the proposed framework discovers continuous symmetries beyond affine transformations and compares favorably with LieGAN.

title: Symmetry Discovery Beyond Affine Transformations

abstract: Existing parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods have achieved significant success on vision transformers (ViTs) adaptation by improving parameter efficiency. However, the exploration of enhancing inference efficiency during adaptation remains underexplored. This limits the broader application of pre-trained ViT models, especially when the model is computationally extensive. In this paper, we propose Dynamic Tuning (DyT), a novel approach to improve both parameter and inference efficiency for ViT adaptation. Specifically, besides using the lightweight adapter modules, we propose a token dispatcher to distinguish informative tokens from less important ones, allowing the latter to dynamically skip the original block, thereby reducing the redundant computation during inference. Additionally, we explore multiple design variants to find the best practice of DyT. Finally, inspired by the mixture-of-experts (MoE) mechanism, we introduce an enhanced adapter to further boost the adaptation performance. We validate DyT across various tasks, including image/video recognition and semantic segmentation. For instance, DyT achieves superior performance compared to existing PEFT methods while evoking only 71% of their FLOPs on the VTAB-1K benchmark.

paragraphs: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning reduces how many parameters must be adapted for a new task, but a large vision Transformer can still be expensive to run afterward. This paper addresses that remaining inference cost. Dynamic Tuning, or DyT, aims to make adaptation efficient both in the parameters it changes and in the computation required when using the model.

DyT combines lightweight adapters with a token dispatcher. The dispatcher distinguishes informative tokens from less important ones and allows the latter to skip the original processing block dynamically. This reduces redundant inference computation. The authors examine several design variants and introduce an enhanced adapter inspired by mixture-of-experts methods to improve adaptation performance further.

Evaluation spans image recognition, video recognition, and semantic segmentation. On VTAB-1K, DyT outperforms the compared parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods while using 71% of their FLOPs. The result illustrates why adaptation efficiency has two separate dimensions: a method can keep trainable parameters small while also deciding where the adapted model needs to spend computation.
summary.tldr: DyT combines lightweight adapters with dynamic token skipping to improve both parameter efficiency and inference efficiency when adapting vision Transformers.

title: Dynamic Tuning Towards Parameter and Inference Efficiency for ViT Adaptation

abstract: Training generative models with differential privacy (DP) typically involves injecting noise into gradient updates or adapting the discriminator's training procedure. As a result, such approaches often struggle with hyper-parameter tuning and convergence. We consider the \emph{slicing privacy mechanism} that injects noise into random low-dimensional projections of the private data, and provide strong privacy guarantees for it. These noisy projections are used for training generative models.To enable optimizing generative models using this DP approach, we introduce the \emph{smoothed-sliced $f$-divergence} and show it enjoys statistical consistency. Moreover, we present a kernel-based estimator for this divergence, circumventing the need for adversarial training. Extensive numerical experiments demonstrate that our approach can generate synthetic data of higher quality compared with baselines. Beyond performance improvement, our method, by sidestepping the need for noisy gradients, offers data scientists the flexibility to adjust generator architecture and hyper-parameters, run the optimization over any number of epochs, and even restart the optimization process---all without incurring additional privacy costs.

Moreover, we present a kernel-based estimator for this divergence, circumventing the need for adversarial training. paragraphs: Differentially private generative training often adds noise to gradient updates or modifies discriminator training. These choices can complicate convergence and hyperparameter tuning. This paper studies a different location for the privacy mechanism: random low-dimensional projections of the private data, to which noise is added before they are used for training.

The authors establish strong privacy guarantees for this slicing mechanism. They introduce a smoothed-sliced f-divergence as an optimization objective and prove its statistical consistency. A kernel-based estimator makes that objective usable without adversarial training. The generator can therefore learn through a comparison based on the noisy projections rather than a discriminator-based procedure.

Numerical experiments report higher-quality synthetic data than the evaluated baselines. A further benefit is flexibility after the private projections have been produced: researchers can change the generator architecture, adjust hyperparameters, run additional epochs, or restart optimization without additional privacy costs. This connects the privacy guarantee to a reusable training resource and allows more freedom in optimizing the generator.
summary.tldr: Noisy data projections enable private generative training with flexible optimization and no additional privacy cost for tuning or restarting training.

title: Privacy without Noisy Gradients: Slicing Mechanism for Generative Model Training

abstract: In coded aperture snapshot spectral imaging (CASSI), the captured measurement entangles spatial and spectral information, posing a severely ill-posed inverse problem for hyperspectral images (HSIs) reconstruction. Moreover, the captured radiance inherently depends on scene illumination, making it difficult to recover the intrinsic spectral reflectance that remains invariant to lighting conditions. To address these challenges, we propose a chromaticity-intensity decomposition framework, which disentangles an HSI into a spatially smooth intensity map and a spectrally variant chromaticity cube. The chromaticity encodes lighting-invariant reflectance, enriched with high-frequency spatial details and local spectral sparsity. Building on this decomposition, we develop CIDNet—a Chromaticity-Intensity Decomposition unfolding network within a dual-camera CASSI system. CIDNet integrates a hybrid spatial-spectral Transformer tailored to reconstruct fine-grained and sparse spectral chromaticity and a degradation-aware, spatially-adaptive noise estimation module that captures anisotropic noise across iterative stages. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world CASSI datasets demonstrate that our method achieves superior performance in both spectral and chromaticity fidelity. Code is released at: \url{https://github.com/xiaodongwo/CIDNet}.

paragraphs: Snapshot spectral imaging compresses spatial and wavelength information into measurements that are difficult to reverse into a hyperspectral image. Lighting adds another complication because measured radiance changes with illumination. This paper introduces a decomposition intended to separate that intensity variation from the spectral reflectance information of the scene.

The framework splits the image into a spatially smooth intensity map and a chromaticity cube containing spectral variation, fine spatial detail, and local spectral sparsity. The authors build CIDNet around this decomposition within a dual-camera imaging system. Its spatial-spectral Transformer reconstructs chromaticity, while a spatially adaptive noise estimator accounts for direction-dependent noise across iterative reconstruction stages.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world coded aperture snapshot spectral imaging datasets show superior spectral and chromaticity fidelity. These results support the value of giving intensity and chromaticity distinct roles in reconstruction. The method connects a representation of lighting-invariant reflectance with a network designed for fine spectral detail and changing noise conditions, addressing both the structure of the desired image and the degradation in its measurements.
summary.tldr: CIDNet separates intensity from chromaticity to improve hyperspectral reconstruction and recover more faithful spectral reflectance information.

title: Spectral Compressive Imaging via Chromaticity-Intensity Decomposition

abstract: Visual navigation is a fundamental problem in embodied AI, yet practical deployments demand long-horizon planning capabilities to address multi-objective tasks. A major bottleneck is data scarcity: policies learned from limited data often overfit and fail to generalize OOD. Existing neural network-based agents typically increase architectural complexity that paradoxically become counterproductive in the small-sample regime. This paper introduce NeuRO, a integrated learning-to-optimize framework that tightly couples perception networks with downstream task-level robust optimization. Specifically, NeuRO addresses core difficulties in this integration: (i) it transforms noisy visual predictions under data scarcity into convex uncertainty sets using Partially Input Convex Neural Networks (PICNNs) with conformal calibration, which directly parameterize the optimization constraints; and (ii) it reformulates planning under partial observability as a robust optimization problem, enabling uncertainty-aware policies that transfer across environments. Extensive experiments on both unordered and sequential multi-object navigation tasks demonstrate that NeuRO establishes SoTA performance, particularly in generalization to unseen environments. Our work thus presents a significant advancement for developing robust, generalizable autonomous agents.

paragraphs: Visual navigation becomes difficult when an agent must plan over many steps, satisfy multiple objectives, and learn from limited data. NeuRO addresses this by tightly connecting visual perception with robust optimization at the level of the navigation task.

The framework converts noisy visual predictions into convex uncertainty sets using partially input convex neural networks and conformal calibration. Those sets directly define constraints for the downstream optimization. It also formulates planning with partial observability as a robust optimization problem. This gives the planner an explicit representation of uncertainty to use when selecting actions.

Experiments cover multi-object navigation tasks with both unordered and sequential objectives. The authors report state-of-the-art performance, particularly when transferring to unseen environments. These results support integrating uncertainty from perception into planning as a route to better generalization. The approach’s main contribution is the connection between what the vision system can infer and what the task optimizer can safely rely on under uncertainty.
summary.tldr: NeuRO turns uncertain visual predictions into optimization constraints, improving multi-object navigation and generalization to unseen environments in reported experiments.

title: Seeing through Uncertainty: Robust Task-Oriented Optimization in Visual Navigation

abstract: Recent advancements in text-guided image editing have achieved notable success by leveraging natural language prompts for fine-grained semantic control. However, certain editing semantics are challenging to specify precisely using textual descriptions alone. A practical alternative involves learning editing semantics from paired source-target examples. Existing exemplar-based editing methods still rely on text prompts describing the change within paired examples or learning implicit text-based editing instructions. In this paper, we introduce PairEdit, a novel visual editing method designed to effectively learn complex editing semantics from a limited number of image pairs or even a single image pair, without using any textual guidance. We propose a target noise prediction that explicitly models semantic variations within paired images through a guidance direction term. Moreover, we introduce a content-preserving noise schedule to facilitate more effective semantic learning. We also propose optimizing distinct LoRAs to disentangle the learning of semantic variations from content. Extensive qualitative and quantitative evaluations demonstrate that PairEdit successfully learns intricate semantics while significantly improving content consistency compared to baseline methods. Code is available at https://github.com/xudonmao/PairEdit.

title: PairEdit: Learning Semantic Variations for Exemplar-based Image Editing

abstract: The attention mechanism is a core component of the Transformer architecture. Various methods have been developed to compute attention scores, including multi-head attention (MHA), multi-query attention, group-query attention and so on. We further analyze the MHA and observe that its performance improves as the number of attention heads increases, provided the hidden size per head remains sufficiently large. Therefore, increasing both the head count and hidden size per head with minimal parameter overhead can lead to significant performance gains at a low cost. Motivated by this insight, we introduce Simulated Attention Score (SAS), which **maintains a compact model size while simulating a larger number of attention heads and hidden feature dimension per head.** This is achieved by projecting a low-dimensional head representation into a higher-dimensional space, effectively increasing attention capacity without increasing parameter count. Beyond the head representations, we further extend the simulation approach to feature dimension of the key and query embeddings, enhancing expressiveness by mimicking the behavior of a larger model while preserving the original model size. **To control the parameter cost, we also propose Parameter-Efficient Attention Aggregation (PEAA).** Comprehensive experiments on a variety of datasets and tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed SAS method, achieving significant improvements over different attention variants.

Experiments across multiple datasets and tasks report significant improvements over different attention variants. The central idea is to separate the size of the learned representation from the larger attention computation it can simulate. The reported findings support this approach as a way to improve expressiveness while preserving model size, grounded in the observed relationship between head count and per-head capacity.
summary.tldr: SAS simulates more attention heads and larger feature dimensions through compact representations, improving attention performance without enlarging the model.

title: SAS: Simulated Attention Score

abstract: Data Shapley values provide a principled approach for quantifying the contribution of individual training examples to machine learning models. However, computing these values often requires computational complexity that is exponential in the data size, and this has led researchers to pursue efficient algorithms tailored to specific machine learning models. Building on the prior success of the Shapley valuation for $K$-nearest neighbor (KNN) models, in this paper, we introduce a localized data Shapley framework that significantly accelerates the valuation of data points. Our approach leverages the distance-based local structure in the data space to decompose the global valuation problem into smaller, localized computations. Our primary contribution is an efficient valuation algorithm for a threshold-based KNN variant and shows that it provides provable speedups over the baseline under mild assumptions. Extensive experiments on real-life datasets demonstrate that our methods achieve a substantial speedup compared to previous approaches.

Its central idea is to make valuation local.

The proposed framework uses distance-based structure to divide a global valuation problem into smaller computations. This connects the valuation procedure to the local relationships that nearest-neighbor algorithms already use. The main algorithm targets a threshold-based nearest-neighbor variant, giving the authors a specific setting in which to develop and analyze the acceleration.

Under assumptions described as mild, the paper proves speedups over its baseline. Experiments on real-world datasets also show substantial reductions in computation compared with previous approaches. The contribution is a way to use local data structure to accelerate principled valuation, with both theoretical and empirical support in the studied nearest-neighbor setting. The formal speedup remains conditional on the stated assumptions.
summary.tldr: Localized Data Shapley accelerates nearest-neighbor data valuation by decomposing global computations using distance-based local structure.

title: Localized Data Shapley: Accelerating Valuation for Nearest Neighbor Algorithms

abstract: This work tackles the fundamental challenges in Federated Learning (FL) posed by arbitrary client participation and data heterogeneity, prevalent characteristics in practical FL settings. It is well-established that popular FedAvg-style algorithms struggle with exact convergence and can suffer from slow convergence rates since a decaying learning rate is required to mitigate these scenarios. To address these issues, we introduce the concept of stochastic matrix and the corresponding time-varying graphs as a novel modeling tool to accurately capture the dynamics of arbitrary client participation and the local update procedure. Leveraging this approach, we offer a fresh perspective on designing FL algorithms, provide a rigorous quantitative analysis of the limitations inherent in the FedAvg algorithm, and present FOCUS, Federated Optimization with Exact Convergence via Push-pull Strategy, a provably convergent algorithm designed to effectively overcome the previously mentioned two challenges. More specifically, we provide a rigorous proof demonstrating that FOCUS achieves exact convergence with a linear rate regardless of the arbitrary client participation, establishing it as the first work to demonstrate this significant result.

These two features make optimization difficult: popular FedAvg-style methods can struggle to converge exactly and may need decreasing learning rates that slow progress. This paper studies how to model those dynamics and design an algorithm that handles them more effectively.

This mathematical description captures how information moves through the learning process. It supports a quantitative analysis of FedAvg’s limitations and provides the foundation for FOCUS, an algorithm built around a push-pull strategy for federated optimization.

The central result is a proof that FOCUS achieves exact convergence at a linear rate despite arbitrary client participation in the analyzed setting. Exact convergence concerns reaching the optimization target, while a linear rate describes geometric reduction of error. The contribution establishes that variable participation and heterogeneous data can be addressed together without accepting the convergence shortcomings identified for FedAvg-style methods.
summary.tldr: FOCUS uses a graph-based push-pull formulation to establish exact, linear convergence under arbitrary client participation.

title: Exact and Linear Convergence for Federated Learning under Arbitrary Client Participation is Attainable

abstract: AlphaZero has achieved remarkable success in complex decision-making problems through self-play and neural network training. However, its self-play process remains inefficient due to limited exploration of high-uncertainty positions, the overlooked runner-up decisions in Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS), and high variance in value labels. To address these challenges, we propose and evaluate uncertainty-guided exploration by branching from high-uncertainty positions using our proposed Label Change Rate (LCR) metric, which is further refined by a Bayesian inference framework. Our proposed approach leverages runner-up MCTS decisions to create multiple variations, and ensembles value labels across these variations to reduce variance. We investigate three key design parameters for our branching strategy: where to branch, how many variations to branch, and which move to play in the new branch. Our empirical findings indicate that branching with 10 variations per game provides the best performance-exploration balance. Overall, our end-to-end results show an improved sample efficiency over the baseline by 58.5\% on 9x9 Go in the early stage of training and by 47.3\% on 19x19 Go in the late stage of training.

This paper targets inefficient exploration of uncertain positions, neglected runner-up decisions, and noisy value-training labels. It expands self-play by branching into additional game variations at selected positions.

A proposed Label Change Rate metric identifies uncertainty, with a Bayesian inference framework refining that signal. The method uses runner-up Monte Carlo Tree Search decisions to generate alternative continuations, then ensembles value labels across those variations to reduce variance. These findings support directing additional self-play toward uncertainty while extracting more stable learning targets from alternative continuations.
summary.tldr: Branching self-play at uncertain positions and combining labels across variations improves AlphaZero's reported sample efficiency on Go.

title: Uncertainty-Guided Exploration for Efficient AlphaZero Training

abstract: We study channel simulation and distributed matching, two fundamental problems with several applications to machine learning, using a recently introduced generalization of the standard rejection sampling (RS) algorithm known as Ensemble Rejection Sampling (ERS). For channel simulation, we propose a new coding scheme based on ERS that achieves a near-optimal coding rate. In this process, we demonstrate that standard RS can also achieve a near-optimal coding rate and generalize the result of Braverman and Garg (2014) to the continuous alphabet setting. Next, as our main contribution, we present a distributed matching lemma for ERS, which serves as the rejection sampling counterpart to the Poisson Matching Lemma (PML) introduced by Li and Anantharam (2021). Our result also generalizes a recent work on importance matching lemma (Phan et al, 2024) and, to our knowledge, is the first result on distributed matching in the family of rejection sampling schemes where the matching probability is close to PML. We demonstrate the practical significance of our approach over prior works by applying it to distributed compression. The effectiveness of our proposed scheme is validated through experiments involving synthetic Gaussian sources and distributed image compression using the MNIST dataset.
