paragraphs: The paper describes density modeling through invertible transformations that turn a structured probability distribution into a uniform one. It calls such a transformation a density destructor because it removes the original distribution’s structure. This perspective unifies earlier approaches, including Gaussianization and autoregressive density models, within a common mathematical interface.

A useful property is that the original density equals the absolute Jacobian determinant of its destructor. The determinant describes how the transformation locally changes volume, linking the transformation directly to probability density. This also connects shallow and deep models: each layer of a deep density model can itself be understood as a shallow density.

The framework is intended to make existing methods easier to combine, compare, and improve systematically. Using its connection to shallow densities, the authors introduce a destructor based on tree densities and another that uses pixel locality for images. They illustrate the framework on a two-dimensional dataset, MNIST, and CIFAR-10, presenting both a unifying viewpoint and concrete constructions.
summary.tldr: Invertible transformations to a uniform density unify deep density models and motivate new tree-based and image-specific components.

title: Deep Density Destructors

abstract: Machine translation is a popular test bed for research in neural sequence-to-sequence models but despite much recent research, there is still a lack of understanding of these models. Practitioners report performance degradation with large beams, the under-estimation of rare words and a lack of diversity in the final translations. Our study relates some of these issues to the inherent uncertainty of the task, due to the existence of multiple valid translations for a single source sentence, and to the extrinsic uncertainty caused by noisy training data. We propose tools and metrics to assess how uncertainty in the data is captured by the model distribution and how it affects search strategies that generate translations. Our results show that search works remarkably well but that the models tend to spread too much probability mass over the hypothesis space. Next, we propose tools to assess model calibration and show how to easily fix some shortcomings of current models. We release both code and multiple human reference translations for two popular benchmarks.

paragraphs: A source sentence can have several valid translations, so uncertainty is part of the translation task itself. Noisy training examples add another source of uncertainty. This paper examines how these two sources relate to familiar problems in neural translation, including worse performance with larger search beams, underestimated rare words, and limited diversity among generated translations.

The authors develop tools and metrics for examining how a model distributes probability across possible translations and how that distribution interacts with search. Their results indicate that search performs remarkably well, while the models tend to disperse too much probability across the space of candidate outputs. This finding directs attention toward the learned distribution when diagnosing translation problems.

The study also introduces tools for assessing calibration: whether the model’s confidence appropriately reflects its behavior. The authors show ways to correct some calibration shortcomings and release code alongside multiple human translations for two benchmarks. Together, these contributions make uncertainty something that can be examined directly when evaluating both translation models and their decoding procedures.
summary.tldr: The study links translation problems to uncertainty and finds that models spread probability too broadly even when search works well.

title: Analyzing Uncertainty in Neural Machine Translation

abstract: The sparse inverse covariance estimation problem is commonly solved using an $\ell_{1}$-regularized Gaussian maximum likelihood estimator known as “graphical lasso”, but its computational cost becomes prohibitive for large data sets. A recently line of results showed{–}under mild assumptions{–}that the graphical lasso estimator can be retrieved by soft-thresholding the sample covariance matrix and solving a maximum determinant matrix completion (MDMC) problem. This paper proves an extension of this result, and describes a Newton-CG algorithm to efficiently solve the MDMC problem. Assuming that the thresholded sample covariance matrix is sparse with a sparse Cholesky factorization, we prove that the algorithm converges to an $\epsilon$-accurate solution in $O(n\log(1/\epsilon))$ time and $O(n)$ memory. The algorithm is highly efficient in practice: we solve the associated MDMC problems with as many as 200,000 variables to 7-9 digits of accuracy in less than an hour on a standard laptop computer running MATLAB.

paragraphs: Sparse inverse covariance estimation is often performed with graphical lasso, but its computational cost can become prohibitive at large scale. This paper builds on results connecting that estimator to a different route: soft-threshold the sample covariance matrix, then solve a maximum determinant matrix completion problem. The earlier connection holds under mild assumptions.

The authors extend this connection and introduce a Newton-CG algorithm for the resulting completion problem. Their efficiency guarantee assumes that the thresholded covariance matrix is sparse and also has a sparse Cholesky factorization. Under that structure, the algorithm reaches accuracy epsilon in O(n log(1/epsilon)) time using O(n) memory.

The practical results demonstrate the scale this approach can reach. The authors solve associated completion problems with up to 200,000 variables to seven to nine digits of accuracy in under an hour on a standard laptop running MATLAB. The significance is a computational route to large problems whose efficiency is explicitly tied to the sparsity structure used by the algorithm.
summary.tldr: A thresholding and matrix-completion approach enables efficient sparse inverse covariance estimation under specified sparsity assumptions.

title: Large-Scale Sparse Inverse Covariance Estimation via Thresholding and Max-Det Matrix Completion

abstract: The tasks that an agent will need to solve often are not known during training. However, if the agent knows which properties of the environment are important then, after learning how its actions affect those properties, it may be able to use this knowledge to solve complex tasks without training specifically for them. Towards this end, we consider a setup in which an environment is augmented with a set of user defined attributes that parameterize the features of interest. We propose a method that learns a policy for transitioning between “nearby” sets of attributes, and maintains a graph of possible transitions. Given a task at test time that can be expressed in terms of a target set of attributes, and a current state, our model infers the attributes of the current state and searches over paths through attribute space to get a high level plan, and then uses its low level policy to execute the plan. We show in 3D block stacking, grid-world games, and StarCraft that our model is able to generalize to longer, more complex tasks at test time by composing simpler learned policies.

paragraphs: An agent may encounter tasks after training that it has never practiced directly. This paper studies how learning the effects of actions on important environmental properties can support such tasks. Its setup provides user-defined attributes describing the features of interest, so goals can be expressed in terms of those attributes.

The method learns a policy for moving between nearby attribute configurations and records possible transitions in a graph. At test time, it infers the attributes of the current state and searches the graph for a route to the target configuration. This route supplies a high-level plan, while the learned policy carries out its individual transitions.

The key idea is to reuse short, learned behaviors as components of longer plans. Experiments in block stacking, grid-world games, and StarCraft show generalization to longer and more complex tasks through this composition. The stated setup requires that a test-time task be expressible as a target set of attributes, tying the planning capability to the properties supplied for the environment.
summary.tldr: An agent plans through a graph of user-defined attributes, composing learned local policies to solve longer tasks at test time.

title: Composable Planning with Attributes

abstract: We propose a novel combination of optimization tools with learning theory bounds in order to analyze the sample complexity of optimal kernel sum classifiers. This contrasts the typical learning theoretic results which hold for all (potentially suboptimal) classifiers. Our work also justifies assumptions made in prior work on multiple kernel learning. As a byproduct of our analysis, we also provide a new form of Rademacher complexity for hypothesis classes containing only optimal classifiers.
originalAbstract: We propose a novel combination of optimization tools with learning theory bounds in order to analyze the sample complexity of optimal kernel sum classifiers. This contrasts the typical learning theoretic results which hold for all (potentially suboptimal) classifiers. Our work also justifies assumptions made in prior work on multiple kernel learning. paragraphs: Learning-theory bounds often cover every classifier in a hypothesis class, including choices that do not optimize the learning objective. This paper instead analyzes the sample complexity of optimal kernel sum classifiers. The distinction makes optimality part of the statistical analysis, allowing the argument to use information about how the classifier was selected.

The authors combine optimization tools with learning-theory bounds to carry out this analysis. Their approach focuses on classifiers formed through kernel sums and uses their optimality to study statistical efficiency. This ties the optimization problem to the question of how much data learning requires, rather than treating the entire candidate class as an undifferentiated collection.

The analysis also justifies assumptions used in earlier work on multiple kernel learning. As a further result, the paper introduces a form of Rademacher complexity for hypothesis classes containing only optimal classifiers. That provides a complexity measure aligned with the paper’s central idea: statistical guarantees can account explicitly for the restriction to optimized solutions.
summary.tldr: Combining optimization and learning theory yields sample-complexity analysis and a Rademacher-complexity formulation specifically for optimal kernel sum classifiers.

title: Optimality Implies Kernel Sum Classifiers are Statistically Efficient

abstract: Attention based Transformer architecture has enabled significant advances in the field of natural language processing. In addition to new pre-training techniques, recent improvements crucially rely on working with a relatively larger embedding dimension for tokens. Unfortunately, this leads to models that are prohibitively large to be employed in the downstream tasks. In this paper we identify one of the important factors contributing to the large embedding size requirement. In particular, our analysis highlights that the scaling between the number of heads and the size of each head in the current architecture gives rise to a low-rank bottleneck in attention heads, causing this limitation. We further validate this in our experiments. As a solution we propose to set the head size of an attention unit to input sequence length, and independent of the number of heads, resulting in multi-head attention layers with provably more expressive power. We empirically show that this allows us to train models with a relatively smaller embedding dimension and with better performance scaling.

paragraphs: Transformer improvements often come with larger token embeddings, which increase model size and can make downstream use difficult. This paper identifies one factor behind that pressure: the relationship between the number of attention heads and the size of each head. The standard scaling creates a low-rank bottleneck that limits what individual heads can represent.

The authors analyze this bottleneck and validate it experimentally. Their proposed change sets an attention head's size to the input sequence length and makes that size independent of the number of heads. This separates two architectural choices whose usual coupling can restrict the expressive capacity of the attention layer.

The revised multi-head attention layers have provably greater expressive power. Experiments also show that models using the change can train with smaller embedding dimensions and better performance scaling. The result identifies an architectural source of size pressure and offers a targeted remedy; it establishes both a representational advantage and an empirical opportunity to reduce embedding size, without asserting that embedding size is governed by this factor alone.
summary.tldr: Decoupling attention-head size from head count addresses a low-rank bottleneck and enables smaller embeddings with improved empirical scaling.

title: Low-Rank Bottleneck in Multi-head Attention Models

abstract: Since hardware resources are limited, the objective of training deep learning models is typically to maximize accuracy subject to the time and memory constraints of training and inference. We study the impact of model size in this setting, focusing on Transformer models for NLP tasks that are limited by compute: self-supervised pretraining and high-resource machine translation. We first show that even though smaller Transformer models execute faster per iteration, wider and deeper models converge in significantly fewer steps. Moreover, this acceleration in convergence typically outpaces the additional computational overhead of using larger models. Therefore, the most compute-efficient training strategy is to counterintuitively train extremely large models but stop after a small number of iterations. This leads to an apparent trade-off between the training efficiency of large Transformer models and the inference efficiency of small Transformer models. However, we show that large models are more robust to compression techniques such as quantization and pruning than small models. Consequently, one can get the best of both worlds: heavily compressed, large models achieve higher accuracy than lightly compressed, small models.

paragraphs: Choosing model size involves both training and inference costs. This paper studies that choice for Transformers in compute-limited self-supervised pretraining and high-resource machine translation. It finds that although smaller models execute individual training iterations faster, wider and deeper models converge in substantially fewer steps.

In the studied settings, this reduction in steps typically outweighs the additional computation per step. The resulting strategy is to train very large models for a relatively small number of iterations. This changes how training efficiency is assessed: the cost of an iteration must be considered together with how many iterations are needed to achieve useful accuracy.

Large models appear to create an inference disadvantage, but the paper also finds that they tolerate quantization and pruning better than small models. Heavily compressed large models achieve higher accuracy than lightly compressed small models. Together, the findings support training large and then compressing as a way to combine efficient training with efficient inference in the examined Transformer workloads.
summary.tldr: In the studied Transformer workloads, training larger models briefly and then compressing them combines favorable training efficiency with strong inference accuracy.

title: Train Big, Then Compress: Rethinking Model Size for Efficient Training and Inference of Transformers

abstract: While sorting is an important procedure in computer science, the argsort operator - which takes as input a vector and returns its sorting permutation - has a discrete image and thus zero gradients almost everywhere. This prohibits end-to-end, gradient-based learning of models that rely on the argsort operator. A natural way to overcome this problem is to replace the argsort operator with a continuous relaxation. Recent work has shown a number of ways to do this, but the relaxations proposed so far are computationally complex. In this work we propose a simple continuous relaxation for the argsort operator which has the following qualities: it can be implemented in three lines of code, achieves state-of-the-art performance, is easy to reason about mathematically - substantially simplifying proofs - and is faster than competing approaches. We open source the code to reproduce all of the experiments and results.

paragraphs: The argsort operation returns the permutation that puts a vector's entries in sorted order. Its output is discrete, so its gradients are zero almost everywhere. This creates an obstacle when a model needs to learn through a sorting decision using ordinary end-to-end gradient-based training.

SoftSort replaces that discrete operation with a continuous relaxation. Such a replacement provides a way to incorporate sorting-related behavior into differentiable models. The paper's emphasis is simplicity: the proposed relaxation can be implemented in three lines of code and has mathematical structure that makes it easier to reason about and substantially simplifies proofs.

The authors report state-of-the-art performance and faster computation than competing approaches. These findings matter because a relaxation has to be both useful for learning and practical to compute; a complicated substitute can make sorting-based models harder to build and analyze. SoftSort brings implementation simplicity, mathematical tractability, and empirical competitiveness together in one operator. The authors also release code for reproducing their experiments and results.
summary.tldr: SoftSort offers a simple continuous approximation to argsort that supports gradient-based learning and runs faster than competing approaches.

title: SoftSort: A Continuous Relaxation for the argsort Operator

abstract: We investigate the combination of actor-critic reinforcement learning algorithms with a uniform large-scale experience replay and propose solutions for two ensuing challenges: (a) efficient actor-critic learning with experience replay (b) the stability of off-policy learning where agents learn from other agents behaviour. To this end we analyze the bias-variance tradeoffs in V-trace, a form of importance sampling for actor-critic methods. Based on our analysis, we then argue for mixing experience sampled from replay with on-policy experience, and propose a new trust region scheme that scales effectively to data distributions where V-trace becomes unstable. We provide extensive empirical validation of the proposed solutions on DMLab-30 and further show the benefits of this setup in two training regimes for Atari: (1) a single agent is trained up until 200M environment frames per game (2) a population of agents is trained up until 200M environment frames each and may share experience. We demonstrate state-of-the-art data efficiency among model-free agents in both regimes.

To this end we analyze the bias-variance tradeoffs in V-trace, a form of importance sampling for actor-critic methods. Based on our analysis, we then argue for mixing experience sampled from replay with on-policy experience, and propose a new trust region scheme that scales effectively to data distributions where V-trace becomes unstable. We provide extensive empirical validation of the proposed solutions on DMLab-30 and further show the benefits of this setup in two training regimes for Atari: (1) a single agent is trained up until 200M environment frames per game (2) a population of agents is trained up until 200M environment frames each and may share experience. We demonstrate state-of-the-art data efficiency among model-free agents in both regimes.

paragraphs: Experience replay lets reinforcement learning agents reuse collected interactions, but combining large replay stores with actor-critic learning introduces efficiency and stability challenges. These become especially relevant when one agent learns from another agent’s behavior. This paper studies uniform large-scale replay with that shared-experience setting in view.

The authors analyze the bias-variance trade-off in V-trace, an importance-sampling method used for actor-critic learning. Their analysis motivates mixing replayed experience with fresh on-policy experience. They also propose a trust region scheme that works effectively with data distributions where V-trace becomes unstable. Together, these changes address both useful reuse of past data and stability when the behavior producing that data differs.

The proposed solutions receive extensive evaluation on DMLab-30. Atari experiments examine a single agent and a population whose members can share experience, with each agent trained for up to 200 million environment frames per game. The authors report state-of-the-art data efficiency among model-free agents in both regimes, supporting replay and experience sharing when paired with appropriate learning safeguards.
summary.tldr: Mixing replay with on-policy experience and adding a trust region improves the efficiency and stability of actor-critic learning with shared experience.

title: Off-Policy Actor-Critic with Shared Experience Replay

abstract: Recent papers have demonstrated that ensemble stumps and trees could be vulnerable to small input perturbations, so robustness verification and defense for those models have become an important research problem. However, due to the structure of decision trees, where each node makes decision purely based on one feature value, all the previous works only consider the $\ell_\infty$ norm perturbation. To study robustness with respect to a general $\ell_p$ norm perturbation, one has to consider the correlation between perturbations on different features, which has not been handled by previous algorithms. In this paper, we study the problem of robustness verification and certified defense with respect to general $\ell_p$ norm perturbations for ensemble decision stumps and trees. For robustness verification of ensemble stumps, we prove that complete verification is NP-complete for $p\in(0, \infty)$ while polynomial time algorithms exist for $p=0$ or $\infty$. For $p\in(0, \infty)$ we develop an efficient dynamic programming based algorithm for sound verification of ensemble stumps. For ensemble trees, we generalize the previous multi-level robustness verification algorithm to $\ell_p$ norm. We demonstrate the first certified defense method for training ensemble stumps and trees with respect to $\ell_p$ norm perturbations, and verify its effectiveness empirically on real datasets.

paragraphs: Tree ensembles can change their predictions under small input perturbations. This paper extends robustness verification and certified defense beyond infinity-norm perturbations to general p-norm constraints. The difficulty is that these constraints require accounting for relationships among perturbations across features, even though individual tree nodes make decisions using one feature at a time.

For ensembles of decision stumps, the authors prove that complete verification is NP-complete for finite positive p, while polynomial-time algorithms exist for p equal to zero or infinity. They develop an efficient dynamic programming method for sound verification in the finite-positive-p setting. Sound verification supplies valid certificates without claiming complete verification of every case.

For ensembles of larger trees, the paper extends an existing multilevel verification algorithm to general p-norm perturbations. It also introduces what the authors describe as the first certified defense for training these ensembles under such perturbations, with empirical validation on real datasets. The contribution combines a computational difficulty result with verification and training methods that address the broader perturbation setting.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes the difficulty of general p-norm robustness verification and develops sound verification and certified training methods for tree ensembles.

title: On Lp-norm Robustness of Ensemble Decision Stumps and Trees

abstract: When tasks change over time, meta-transfer learning seeks to improve the efficiency of learning a new task via both meta-learning and transfer-learning. While the standard attention has been effective in a variety of settings, we question its effectiveness in improving meta-transfer learning since the tasks being learned are dynamic and the amount of context can be substantially smaller. In this paper, using a recently proposed meta-transfer learning model, Sequential Neural Processes (SNP), we first empirically show that it suffers from a similar underfitting problem observed in the functions inferred by Neural Processes. However, we further demonstrate that unlike the meta-learning setting, the standard attention mechanisms are not effective in meta-transfer setting. To resolve, we propose a new attention mechanism, Recurrent Memory Reconstruction (RMR), and demonstrate that providing an imaginary context that is recurrently updated and reconstructed with interaction is crucial in achieving effective attention for meta-transfer learning. Furthermore, incorporating RMR into SNP, we propose Attentive Sequential Neural Processes-RMR (ASNP-RMR) and demonstrate in various tasks that ASNP-RMR significantly outperforms the baselines.

paragraphs: Meta-transfer learning combines learning across tasks with transferring prior knowledge as tasks change over time. This paper examines Sequential Neural Processes, or SNP, in that setting and empirically finds underfitting in the functions they infer. It also finds that standard attention mechanisms do not provide the same effective remedy seen in the meta-learning setting.

The authors propose Recurrent Memory Reconstruction, or RMR, to make attention useful when tasks are dynamic and available context can be small. RMR supplies an imaginary context that is recurrently updated and reconstructed through interaction. The key change is therefore the context available to attention, with an evolving memory supporting the learning process.

Combining RMR with SNP produces Attentive Sequential Neural Processes-RMR. Across various tasks, this model significantly outperforms the evaluated baselines. The experiments support the importance of recurrently reconstructed context for effective attention in the studied meta-transfer setting, while showing why simply adding a standard attention mechanism did not resolve the observed underfitting problem.
summary.tldr: Recurrently reconstructed imaginary context makes attention effective for Sequential Neural Processes and improves performance across tested changing-task settings.

title: Robustifying Sequential Neural Processes

abstract: We present Graph Random Neural Features (GRNF), a novel embedding method from graph-structured data to real vectors based on a family of graph neural networks. The embedding naturally deals with graph isomorphism and preserves the metric structure of the graph domain, in probability. In addition to being an explicit embedding method, it also allows us to efficiently and effectively approximate graph metric distances (as well as complete kernel functions); a criterion to select the embedding dimension trading off the approximation accuracy with the computational cost is also provided. GRNF can be used within traditional processing methods or as a training-free input layer of a graph neural network. The theoretical guarantees that accompany GRNF ensure that the considered graph distance is metric, hence allowing to distinguish any pair of non-isomorphic graphs.

paragraphs: Graph Random Neural Features, or GRNF, converts graphs into real-valued vectors using a family of graph neural networks. The aim is to make graph data usable by vector-based methods while retaining meaningful structural differences. The representation also handles graph isomorphism, so alternative descriptions of the same graph structure are treated appropriately.

The method preserves the metric structure of the graph domain in probability. It supplies explicit embeddings and supports efficient approximation of graph distances and complete kernel functions. The authors also provide a criterion for choosing the embedding dimension, making the tradeoff between approximation accuracy and computational cost an explicit part of using the method.

GRNF can serve as input to traditional processing methods or as a training-free input layer for a graph neural network. Its theory establishes that the underlying graph distance is a metric and can distinguish every pair of non-isomorphic graphs. That exact property of the distance should be distinguished from the probabilistic preservation offered by the vector approximation.
summary.tldr: GRNF maps graphs to vectors that preserve graph distances in probability, with an explicit accuracy–computation tradeoff.

title: Graph Random Neural Features for Distance-Preserving Graph Representations

abstract: This paper introduces kernel continual learning, a simple but effective variant of continual learning that leverages the non-parametric nature of kernel methods to tackle catastrophic forgetting. We deploy an episodic memory unit that stores a subset of samples for each task to learn task-specific classifiers based on kernel ridge regression. This does not require memory replay and systematically avoids task interference in the classifiers. We further introduce variational random features to learn a data-driven kernel for each task. To do so, we formulate kernel continual learning as a variational inference problem, where a random Fourier basis is incorporated as the latent variable. The variational posterior distribution over the random Fourier basis is inferred from the coreset of each task. In this way, we are able to generate more informative kernels specific to each task, and, more importantly, the coreset size can be reduced to achieve more compact memory, resulting in more efficient continual learning based on episodic memory. Extensive evaluation on four benchmarks demonstrates the effectiveness and promise of kernels for continual learning.

paragraphs: Continual learning must acquire new tasks while retaining knowledge of earlier ones. This paper introduces an approach based on kernel methods, using a small episodic memory of examples from each task. Those stored subsets support task-specific kernel ridge regression classifiers, avoiding memory replay and preventing interference between tasks in the classifiers.

The method also learns a kernel tailored to each task through variational random features. It formulates learning as a variational inference problem in which a random Fourier basis is a latent variable. The approximate posterior over that basis is inferred from the task’s stored subset, allowing the kernel to adapt to information in those examples.

More informative task-specific kernels allow the stored subsets to be reduced, making episodic memory more compact and the approach more efficient. Evaluations on four benchmarks demonstrate the method’s effectiveness. The contribution joins two roles for memory: retaining examples that support separate classifiers and using those same examples to learn how each task’s kernel should represent similarity.
summary.tldr: Task-specific kernel classifiers and learned random features support continual learning with compact episodic memory and no memory replay.

title: Kernel Continual Learning

abstract: We study online learning in unknown Markov games, a problem that arises in episodic multi-agent reinforcement learning where the actions of the opponents are unobservable. We show that in this challenging setting, achieving sublinear regret against the best response in hindsight is statistically hard. We then consider a weaker notion of regret by competing with the \emph{minimax value} of the game, and present an algorithm that achieves a sublinear $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(K^{2/3})$ regret after $K$ episodes. This is the first sublinear regret bound (to our knowledge) for online learning in unknown Markov games. Importantly, our regret bound is independent of the size of the opponents’ action spaces. As a result, even when the opponents’ actions are fully observable, our regret bound improves upon existing analysis (e.g., (Xie et al., 2020)) by an exponential factor in the number of opponents.

paragraphs: This paper studies episodic learning in unknown Markov games when an agent cannot observe its opponents' actions. A natural benchmark is the best response one could have selected in hindsight. The authors show that achieving sublinear regret against this benchmark is statistically hard in the setting they consider.

They then adopt a weaker benchmark: the minimax value of the game. Against this value, their algorithm achieves regret of order K^(2/3), up to logarithmic factors, after K episodes. Because this grows more slowly than the number of episodes, average regret decreases with continued interaction. The result provides a learning guarantee despite the missing information about opponents' actions.

The bound does not depend on the sizes of the opponents' action spaces. This feature also matters when those actions are observable: the authors report an exponential improvement in the number of opponents over existing analysis. The guarantee remains tied to the minimax benchmark, preserving the distinction from the harder best-response-in-hindsight comparison.
summary.tldr: An algorithm achieves sublinear regret against the minimax value in unknown Markov games without observing opponents' actions.

title: Online Learning in Unknown Markov Games

abstract: The content that a recommender system (RS) shows to users influences them. Therefore, when choosing a recommender to deploy, one is implicitly also choosing to induce specific internal states in users. Even more, systems trained via long-horizon optimization will have direct incentives to manipulate users, e.g. shift their preferences so they are easier to satisfy. We focus on induced preference shifts in users. We argue that {–} before deployment {–} system designers should: estimate the shifts a recommender would induce; evaluate whether such shifts would be undesirable; and perhaps even actively optimize to avoid problematic shifts. These steps involve two challenging ingredients: estimation requires anticipating how hypothetical policies would influence user preferences if deployed {–} we do this by using historical user interaction data to train a predictive user model which implicitly contains their preference dynamics; evaluation and optimization additionally require metrics to assess whether such influences are manipulative or otherwise unwanted {–} we use the notion of "safe shifts", that define a trust region within which behavior is safe: for instance, the natural way in which users would shift without interference from the system could be deemed "safe". In simulated experiments, we show that our learned preference dynamics model is effective in estimating user preferences and how they would respond to new recommenders. Additionally, we show that recommenders that optimize for staying in the trust region can avoid manipulative behaviors while still generating engagement.

paragraphs: Recommenders can change the preferences they are trying to satisfy. A system optimizing engagement over a long horizon may therefore have an incentive to make users easier to please. This paper proposes considering those induced changes before deployment, alongside the behavior a recommender is expected to generate.

The approach learns a predictive user model from historical interactions. That model captures preference dynamics and estimates how users would respond to hypothetical recommendation policies. To evaluate those changes, the authors define a trust region of acceptable, or safe, shifts. One possible reference is how preferences would evolve without interference from the recommender.

In simulated experiments, the learned model effectively estimates preferences and their responses to new recommenders. Systems optimized to remain within the trust region can avoid manipulative behavior while still producing engagement. The contribution combines prediction with a criterion for judging influence: forecasting a preference shift alone does not establish whether it is desirable. The reported evidence concerns simulation and the chosen notion of acceptable change.
summary.tldr: A learned preference-dynamics model and a trust region for acceptable changes help recommenders avoid manipulation in simulated experiments.

title: Estimating and Penalizing Induced Preference Shifts in Recommender Systems

abstract: Assembly of multi-part physical structures is both a valuable end product for autonomous robotics, as well as a valuable diagnostic task for open-ended training of embodied intelligent agents. We introduce a naturalistic physics-based environment with a set of connectable magnet blocks inspired by children’s toy kits. The objective is to assemble blocks into a succession of target blueprints. Despite the simplicity of this objective, the compositional nature of building diverse blueprints from a set of blocks leads to an explosion of complexity in structures that agents encounter. Furthermore, assembly stresses agents’ multi-step planning, physical reasoning, and bimanual coordination. We find that the combination of large-scale reinforcement learning and graph-based policies – surprisingly without any additional complexity – is an effective recipe for training agents that not only generalize to complex unseen blueprints in a zero-shot manner, but even operate in a reset-free setting without being trained to do so. Through extensive experiments, we highlight the importance of large-scale training, structured representations, contributions of multi-task vs. single-task learning, as well as the effects of curriculums, and discuss qualitative behaviors of trained agents. Our accompanying project webpage can be found at: https://sites.google.com/view/learning-direct-assembly/home

Through extensive experiments, we highlight the importance of large-scale training, structured representations, contributions of multi-task vs. single-task learning, as well as the effects of curriculums, and discuss qualitative behaviors of trained agents. Our accompanying project webpage can be found at: https://sites.google.com/view/learning-direct-assembly/home

paragraphs: This paper introduces a physics-based environment in which agents assemble connectable magnetic blocks into a sequence of target structures. Although the pieces and objective are simple, combining blocks into different blueprints creates a large range of possible structures. Successful assembly requires planning over multiple steps, reasoning about physical behavior, and coordinating two hands.

The training approach combines large-scale reinforcement learning with graph-based policies. Graph representations provide structure for the policy’s decisions in this assembly setting. The authors find that this combination is effective without additional complexity: trained agents can build complex blueprints they have never encountered, without further training on those targets.

The agents also operate in a reset-free setting even though they were not specifically trained for it. Extensive experiments examine the roles of training scale, structured representations, learning across multiple tasks, and curricula. The findings identify assembly as both a useful robotics objective and a diagnostic setting for studying how embodied agents acquire skills that transfer across varied construction problems.
summary.tldr: Large-scale reinforcement learning with graph-based policies produces block-assembly agents that generalize to unseen blueprints and operate without resets.

title: Blocks Assemble! Learning to Assemble with Large-Scale Structured Reinforcement Learning

abstract: In this work, we consider one-shot imitation learning for object rearrangement tasks, where an AI agent needs to watch a single expert demonstration and learn to perform the same task in different environments. To achieve a strong generalization, the AI agent must infer the spatial goal specification for the task. However, there can be multiple goal specifications that fit the given demonstration. To address this, we propose a reward learning approach, Graph-based Equivalence Mappings (GEM), that can discover spatial goal representations that are aligned with the intended goal specification, enabling successful generalization in unseen environments. Specifically, GEM represents a spatial goal specification by a reward function conditioned on i) a graph indicating important spatial relationships between objects and ii) state equivalence mappings for each edge in the graph indicating invariant properties of the corresponding relationship. GEM combines inverse reinforcement learning and active reward learning to efficiently improve the reward function by utilizing the graph structure and domain randomization enabled by the equivalence mappings. We conducted experiments with simulated oracles and with human subjects. The results show that GEM can drastically improve the generalizability of the learned goal representations over strong baselines.

paragraphs: A single demonstration of an object rearrangement task can support several interpretations of the intended goal. An agent may reproduce the demonstrated arrangement yet fail when the environment changes because it inferred the wrong spatial requirements. This paper addresses that ambiguity by learning goal representations intended to carry across environments.

Graph-based Equivalence Mappings, or GEM, represents a goal through a reward function conditioned on two components. A graph identifies important spatial relationships between objects, while mappings attached to its edges describe properties of those relationships that remain invariant. This separates which relationships matter from which changes preserve them, providing structure for learning a transferable goal.

GEM combines inverse reinforcement learning with active reward learning to refine the reward function. It uses the graph structure and domain randomization enabled by the equivalence mappings to support that refinement. Experiments with simulated oracles and human participants show that GEM can substantially improve generalization over strong baselines. The result concerns learning the intended spatial specification from ambiguous evidence, making the representation of the goal central to successful imitation.
summary.tldr: GEM learns graph-structured spatial goals from a demonstration and active feedback, improving object-rearrangement generalization in the reported experiments.

title: Discovering Generalizable Spatial Goal Representations via Graph-based Active Reward Learning

abstract: Recent years have seen the emergence of pre-trained representations as a powerful abstraction for AI applications in computer vision, natural language, and speech. However, policy learning for control is still dominated by a tabula-rasa learning paradigm, with visuo-motor policies often trained from scratch using data from deployment environments. In this context, we revisit and study the role of pre-trained visual representations for control, and in particular representations trained on large-scale computer vision datasets. Through extensive empirical evaluation in diverse control domains (Habitat, DeepMind Control, Adroit, Franka Kitchen), we isolate and study the importance of different representation training methods, data augmentations, and feature hierarchies. Overall, we find that pre-trained visual representations can be competitive or even better than ground-truth state representations to train control policies. This is in spite of using only out-of-domain data from standard vision datasets, without any in-domain data from the deployment environments.

paragraphs: Control policies that act from images are often trained with visual representations learned from scratch in their deployment environments. This paper revisits whether representations pretrained on large computer-vision datasets can provide an effective starting point. The question is whether visual knowledge acquired elsewhere can support learning to act.

The authors evaluate this idea across Habitat, DeepMind Control, Adroit, and Franka Kitchen. They examine representation-training methods, data augmentation, and feature hierarchies to understand which aspects of visual pretraining matter. This makes the study a comparison of representation choices across diverse control domains.

The reported results show that pretrained visual representations can compete with, and sometimes outperform, ground-truth state representations when training control policies. The visual pretraining uses standard vision datasets without deployment-environment data. That distinction concerns the source of the visual representation: the paper studies how those externally learned features support subsequent policy learning. Its findings establish that useful visual information for control can transfer across this substantial difference in data source.
summary.tldr: Visual representations pretrained outside deployment environments can match or exceed ground-truth state representations for learning control policies.

title: The Unsurprising Effectiveness of Pre-Trained Vision Models for Control

abstract: Recently, there is an emerging interest in adversarially training a classifier with a rejection option (also known as a selective classifier) for boosting adversarial robustness. While rejection can incur a cost in many applications, existing studies typically associate zero cost with rejecting perturbed inputs, which can result in the rejection of numerous slightly-perturbed inputs that could be correctly classified. In this work, we study adversarially-robust classification with rejection in the stratified rejection setting, where the rejection cost is modeled by rejection loss functions monotonically non-increasing in the perturbation magnitude. We theoretically analyze the stratified rejection setting and propose a novel defense method – Adversarial Training with Consistent Prediction-based Rejection (CPR) – for building a robust selective classifier. Experiments on image datasets demonstrate that the proposed method significantly outperforms existing methods under strong adaptive attacks. For instance, on CIFAR-10, CPR reduces the total robust loss (for different rejection losses) by at least 7.3% under both seen and unseen attacks.

paragraphs: A selective classifier can decline to predict when facing a potentially adversarial input. This paper argues that treating rejection of every perturbed input as cost-free can encourage rejecting many slightly altered examples that could still be classified correctly. It therefore studies robustness with an explicit cost for rejection.

In the proposed stratified setting, rejection loss is monotonically non-increasing with perturbation magnitude: declining a mildly changed input can cost more than declining a heavily changed one. The authors analyze this setting theoretically and introduce Adversarial Training with Consistent Prediction-based Rejection, or CPR, as a defense for learning robust selective classifiers.

Experiments on image datasets show substantial improvements over existing methods under strong adaptive attacks. On CIFAR-10, CPR reduces total robust loss by at least 7.3% for different rejection losses under both seen and unseen attacks. The result evaluates robustness together with the consequences of abstaining, making the rejection policy part of the measured performance rather than treating rejection as automatically successful.
summary.tldr: CPR improves adversarial classification with rejection by accounting for rejection costs that decrease as perturbations grow.

title: Stratified Adversarial Robustness with Rejection

abstract: Diffusion models recently achieved state-of-the-art in image generation. They mainly utilize the denoising framework, which leverages the Langevin dynamics process for image sampling. Recently, the guidance method has modified this process to add conditional information to achieve a controllable generator. However, the current guidance on denoising processes suffers from the trade-off between diversity, image quality, and conditional information. In this work, we propose to view this guidance sampling process from a gradient view, where image pixels are treated as parameters being optimized, and each mathematical term in the sampling process represents one update direction. This perspective reveals more insights into the conflict problems between updated directions on the pixels, which cause the trade-off as mentioned previously. We investigate the conflict problems and propose to solve them by a simple projection method. The experimental results evidently improve over different baselines on datasets with various resolutions.

paragraphs: Guided diffusion sampling introduces conditional information into image generation, allowing the output to respond to a requested condition. However, guidance creates a tradeoff among image quality, diversity, and adherence to that condition. This paper studies that tradeoff by reinterpreting the sampling process as a sequence of optimization updates to the image itself.

In the PixelAsParam view, pixels are the parameters being optimized, and each mathematical term in the sampling procedure supplies an update direction. This exposes conflicts between directions that would otherwise appear as separate parts of a denoising formula. The authors investigate these conflicts and propose a simple projection method to address them during sampling.

Experiments report improvements over different baselines on datasets with varied image resolutions. The results support the usefulness of examining how sampling updates interact, rather than considering each contribution in isolation. The paper’s central contribution is both an interpretation of guided sampling and a concrete adjustment motivated by that interpretation; it does not claim that all quality-diversity-conditioning tradeoffs disappear.
summary.tldr: PixelAsParam treats guided diffusion as pixel optimization and uses projection to address conflicting update directions.

title: PixelAsParam: A Gradient View on Diffusion Sampling with Guidance

abstract: The assumption that response and predictor belong to the same statistical unit may be violated in practice. Unbiased estimation and recovery of true label ordering based on unlabeled data are challenging tasks and have attracted increasing attentions in the recent literature. In this paper, we present a relatively complete analysis of label permutation problem for the generalized linear model with multivariate responses. The theory is established under different scenarios, with knowledge of true parameters, with partial knowledge of underlying label permutation matrix and without any knowledge. Our results remove the stringent conditions required by the current literature and are further extended to the missing observation setting which has never been considered in the field of label permutation problem. On computational side, we propose two methods, "maximum likelihood estimation" algorithm and "two-step estimation" algorithm, to accommodate for different settings. When the proportion of permuted labels is moderate, both methods work effectively. Multiple numerical experiments are provided and corroborate our theoretical findings.

paragraphs: Regression usually assumes that each response is paired with predictors from the same statistical unit. If records are mismatched, that correspondence breaks, making both parameter estimation and recovery of the correct ordering difficult. This paper analyzes the label-permutation problem for generalized linear models with multivariate responses.

The theory covers several information settings: knowing the true model parameters, knowing part of the permutation, and having neither kind of knowledge. The authors report relaxing stringent conditions from earlier work and extend their analysis to missing observations. These distinctions matter because the information available about the model or matching changes the recovery problem that must be solved.

On the computational side, the paper develops maximum-likelihood and two-step estimation algorithms for different settings. Both are reported to work effectively when the proportion of permuted labels is moderate, and numerical experiments corroborate the theory. The stated effectiveness therefore concerns a qualified mismatch regime. Together, the results connect assumptions about available information to both theoretical analysis and practical estimation procedures.
summary.tldr: The paper analyzes mismatched responses in generalized linear models and develops estimation methods effective when label permutation is moderate.

title: Regression with Label Permutation in Generalized Linear Model

abstract: Currently, applying diffusion models in pixel space of high resolution images is difficult. Instead, existing approaches focus on diffusion in lower dimensional spaces (latent diffusion), or have multiple super-resolution levels of generation referred to as cascades. The downside is that these approaches add additional complexity to the diffusion framework. This paper aims to improve denoising diffusion for high resolution images while keeping the model as simple as possible. The paper is centered around the research question: How can one train a standard denoising diffusion models on high resolution images, and still obtain performance comparable to these alternate approaches? The four main findings are: 1) the noise schedule should be adjusted for high resolution images, 2) It is sufficient to scale only a particular part of the architecture, 3) dropout should be added at specific locations in the architecture, and 4) downsampling is an effective strategy to avoid high resolution feature maps. Combining these simple yet effective techniques, we achieve state-of-the-art on image generation among diffusion models without sampling modifiers on ImageNet.

paragraphs: Generating high-resolution images directly in pixel space is difficult for diffusion models. Common alternatives use a lower-dimensional latent space or a sequence of super-resolution models, adding complexity to the generation framework. This paper asks how a standard denoising diffusion model can remain simple while achieving performance comparable to those alternatives.

The authors identify four useful changes. The noise schedule should be adjusted for high-resolution images; scaling a particular part of the architecture is sufficient; dropout should be inserted at specific locations; and downsampling can avoid high-resolution feature maps. Together, these findings address how noise, model capacity, regularization, and internal spatial resolution interact in the high-resolution setting.

Combining the techniques produces state-of-the-art ImageNet image-generation results within the stated comparison category: diffusion models without sampling modifiers. That qualification defines the scope of the performance claim. The broader contribution is evidence that targeted changes to a standard diffusion setup can make direct high-resolution generation competitive while retaining a comparatively simple overall framework.
summary.tldr: Targeted noise-schedule and architecture changes enable simple high-resolution diffusion with state-of-the-art ImageNet results among diffusion models without sampling modifiers.

title: simple diffusion: End-to-end diffusion for high resolution images

abstract: We are interested in an evaluation methodology for molecular optimization. Given a sample of molecules and their properties of our interest, we wish not only to train a generator of molecules optimized with respect to a target property but also to evaluate its performance accurately. A common practice is to train a predictor of the target property using the sample and apply it to both training and evaluating the generator. However, little is known about its statistical properties, and thus, we are not certain about whether this performance estimate is reliable or not. We theoretically investigate this evaluation methodology and show that it potentially suffers from two biases; one is due to misspecification of the predictor and the other to reusing the same finite sample for training and evaluation. We discuss bias reduction methods for each of the biases, and empirically investigate their effectiveness.

paragraphs: Molecular optimization aims to generate molecules with desirable properties, but evaluating the generator presents its own statistical problem. A common workflow learns a property predictor from a sample of molecules, uses that predictor to guide generation, and then uses it again to assess the generated molecules. The paper asks how reliable that resulting performance estimate is.

The theoretical analysis identifies two potential sources of bias. One arises when the predictor is misspecified, so its model of the target property is inadequate. The other arises from reusing the same finite sample for training and evaluation. These are distinct problems: an evaluation can be affected by the predictor’s assumptions, by the reuse of observations, or by both.

The authors discuss ways to reduce each source of bias and investigate their effectiveness empirically. Their contribution concerns the credibility of the evaluation process as well as molecular generation itself. In particular, a favorable score from the predictor used during optimization needs to be interpreted with attention to how that predictor and its evaluation data were constructed.
summary.tldr: The paper identifies two potential biases in predictor-based molecular optimization evaluation and investigates ways to reduce them.

title: Biases in Evaluation of Molecular Optimization Methods and Bias Reduction Strategies

abstract: In the graph node embedding problem, embedding spaces can vary significantly for different data types, leading to the need for different GNN model types. In this paper, we model the embedding update of a node feature as a Hamiltonian orbit over time. Since the Hamiltonian orbits generalize the exponential maps, this approach allows us to learn the underlying manifold of the graph in training, in contrast to most of the existing literature that assumes a fixed graph embedding manifold with a closed exponential map solution. Our proposed node embedding strategy can automatically learn, without extensive tuning, the underlying geometry of any given graph dataset even if it has diverse geometries. We test Hamiltonian functions of different forms and verify the performance of our approach on two graph node embedding downstream tasks: node classification and link prediction. Numerical experiments demonstrate that our approach adapts better to different types of graph datasets than popular state-of-the-art graph node embedding GNNs. The code is available at https://github.com/zknus/Hamiltonian-GNN.

paragraphs: Graph datasets can require substantially different geometries for useful node representations. Many existing approaches choose an embedding manifold in advance, which can make the model type depend on the data. This paper instead makes learning the geometry part of training the graph neural network.

The proposed method represents a node's embedding updates as a Hamiltonian orbit evolving over time. These orbits generalize exponential maps, the geometric mappings used in many fixed-manifold approaches. This allows the model to learn the underlying embedding manifold without requiring a predetermined geometry with a closed-form exponential map. The authors describe the strategy as accommodating diverse geometries without extensive tuning.

The paper investigates different Hamiltonian function forms and evaluates the resulting embeddings on node classification and link prediction. Numerical experiments show better adaptation across graph dataset types than popular state-of-the-art embedding GNNs. These findings support learning the geometry through embedding dynamics as a flexible alternative to selecting a fixed manifold beforehand, with the empirical evidence coming from the tested downstream tasks.
summary.tldr: Hamiltonian embedding dynamics let graph neural networks learn representation geometry during training.

title: Node Embedding from Neural Hamiltonian Orbits in Graph Neural Networks

abstract: We present an algorithm for learning mixtures of Markov chains and Markov decision processes (MDPs) from short unlabeled trajectories. Specifically, our method handles mixtures of Markov chains with optional control input by going through a multi-step process, involving (1) a subspace estimation step, (2) spectral clustering of trajectories using "pairwise distance estimators," along with refinement using the EM algorithm, (3) a model estimation step, and (4) a classification step for predicting labels of new trajectories. We provide end-to-end performance guarantees, where we only explicitly require the length of trajectories to be linear in the number of states and the number of trajectories to be linear in a mixing time parameter. Experimental results support these guarantees, where we attain 96.6% average accuracy on a mixture of two MDPs in gridworld, outperforming the EM algorithm with random initialization (73.2% average accuracy). We also significantly outperform the EM algorithm on real data from the LastFM song dataset.

paragraphs: The paper studies collections of short trajectories generated by several different Markov chains or Markov decision processes. The trajectories arrive without labels indicating which underlying process produced them. The goal is to recover the component models and classify new trajectories, including cases where the processes have control inputs.

The algorithm first estimates a subspace, then clusters trajectories using spectral methods and pairwise distance estimators. It refines the clustering with expectation-maximization, estimates the component models, and uses them to classify additional trajectories. This staged construction gives the clustering and model-fitting procedure an informed starting structure.

The authors provide end-to-end guarantees whose explicit requirements make trajectory length linear in the number of states and trajectory count linear in a mixing-time parameter. Experiments support the approach: on a mixture of two gridworld MDPs, average accuracy reaches 96.6 percent, compared with 73.2 percent for randomly initialized expectation-maximization. The method also substantially outperforms expectation-maximization on LastFM song data, supporting the usefulness of the structured estimation and initialization procedure.
summary.tldr: A staged spectral and expectation-maximization algorithm learns mixtures of Markov processes from short, unlabeled trajectories.

title: Learning Mixtures of Markov Chains and MDPs

abstract: We present a novel framework to regularize Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) in a few-shot setting with a geometry-aware consistency regularization. The proposed approach leverages a rendered depth map at unobserved viewpoint to warp sparse input images to the unobserved viewpoint and impose them as pseudo ground truths to facilitate learning of NeRF. By encouraging such geometry-aware consistency at a feature-level instead of using pixel-level reconstruction loss, we regularize the NeRF at semantic and structural levels while allowing for modeling view dependent radiance to account for color variations across viewpoints. We also propose an effective method to filter out erroneous warped solutions, along with training strategies to stabilize training during optimization. We show that our model achieves competitive results compared to state-of-the-art few-shot NeRF models.

The proposed approach leverages a rendered depth map at unobserved viewpoint to warp sparse input images to the unobserved viewpoint and impose them as pseudo ground truths to facilitate learning of NeRF. By encouraging such geometry-aware consistency at a feature-level instead of using pixel-level reconstruction loss, we regularize the NeRF at semantic and structural levels while allowing for modeling view dependent radiance to account for color variations across viewpoints. We also propose an effective method to filter out erroneous warped solutions, along with training strategies to stabilize training during optimization. paragraphs: GeCoNeRF addresses learning a neural radiance field from only a few input images. With sparse observations, the method supplies additional guidance at viewpoints that were not photographed. It does this through a consistency constraint that uses the scene geometry predicted during rendering.

At an unobserved viewpoint, a rendered depth map guides the warping of the available images into that view. Those warped images become provisional training targets. The method compares features rather than requiring exact pixel reconstruction, encouraging semantic and structural agreement while allowing colors to change with viewpoint. That distinction matters for representing view-dependent radiance.

Warped targets can be erroneous, so the framework includes a method for filtering incorrect warped solutions. It also introduces training strategies intended to stabilize optimization. The authors report results competitive with state-of-the-art few-shot NeRF methods. The contribution is a way to turn sparse observations into geometry-aware supervision while accommodating both imperfect warps and legitimate changes in appearance across views.
summary.tldr: GeCoNeRF uses depth-guided image warping and feature-level consistency to train competitive neural radiance fields from few views.

title: GeCoNeRF: Few-shot Neural Radiance Fields via Geometric Consistency

abstract: In model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL), policy gradients can be estimated either by derivative-free RL methods, such as likelihood ratio gradients (LR), or by backpropagating through a differentiable model via reparameterization gradients (RP). Instead of using one or the other, the Total Propagation (TP) algorithm in prior work showed that a combination of LR and RP estimators averaged using inverse variance weighting (IVW) can achieve orders of magnitude improvement over either method. However, IVW-based composite estimators have not yet been applied in modern RL tasks, as it is unclear if they can be implemented scalably. We propose a scalable method, Total Propagation X (TPX) that improves over TP by changing the node used for IVW, and employing coordinate wise weighting. We demonstrate the scalability of TPX by applying it to the state of the art visual MBRL algorithm Dreamer. The experiments showed that Dreamer fails with long simulation horizons, while our TPX works reliably for only a fraction of additional computation. One key advantage of TPX is its ease of implementation, which will enable experimenting with IVW on many tasks beyond MBRL.

However, IVW-based composite estimators have not yet been applied in modern RL tasks, as it is unclear if they can be implemented scalably. We propose a scalable method, Total Propagation X (TPX) that improves over TP by changing the node used for IVW, and employing coordinate wise weighting. We demonstrate the scalability of TPX by applying it to the state of the art visual MBRL algorithm Dreamer. The experiments showed that Dreamer fails with long simulation horizons, while our TPX works reliably for only a fraction of additional computation. One key advantage of TPX is its ease of implementation, which will enable experimenting with IVW on many tasks beyond MBRL.

paragraphs: Model-based reinforcement learning can estimate policy gradients in two ways: using likelihood-ratio estimators or differentiating through a model with reparameterization gradients. Earlier Total Propagation work combined both using inverse-variance weighting and reported large improvements. The unresolved issue was whether this combination could scale to modern reinforcement learning tasks.

The paper introduces Total Propagation X, or TPX. It changes the node at which inverse-variance weighting is performed and uses separate weights for individual coordinates. These changes make the composite estimator scalable enough to integrate with Dreamer, a visual model-based reinforcement learning algorithm. The method retains the idea of combining gradient estimates according to their variability.

In the reported experiments, Dreamer fails with long simulation horizons, while the TPX version works reliably with a modest amount of additional computation. This demonstrates the practical value of the scalable combination in a demanding setting where predictions extend over many simulated steps. The authors also emphasize ease of implementation, positioning TPX as a way to make further experiments with inverse-variance-weighted estimators more accessible.
summary.tldr: TPX scales combined policy-gradient estimators and makes Dreamer reliable at long simulation horizons in the reported experiments.

title: Model-based Reinforcement Learning with Scalable Composite Policy Gradient Estimators

abstract: We study the capabilities of speech processing systems trained simply to predict large amounts of transcripts of audio on the internet. When scaled to 680,000 hours of multilingual and multitask supervision, the resulting models generalize well to standard benchmarks and are often competitive with prior fully supervised results without the need for any dataset specific fine-tuning. When compared to humans, the models approach their accuracy and robustness. We are releasing models and inference code to serve as a foundation for further work on robust speech processing.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how far speech processing can advance by training models to predict transcripts for large quantities of internet audio. The approach centers on scaling supervision across languages and tasks. The reported training scale is 680,000 hours, allowing the authors to examine whether such broad training produces capabilities that transfer to standard speech benchmarks.

The resulting models generalize well and are often competitive with earlier fully supervised results without fine-tuning for each evaluation dataset. This is a meaningful aspect of the finding: performance transfers from the broad training procedure to benchmark tasks without requiring a separate dataset-specific adaptation step. The comparison is qualified as often competitive, rather than uniformly better across all evaluations.

The authors also report that the models approach human accuracy and robustness in their comparisons. They release models and inference code as a foundation for further research. Together, the findings support large-scale, multilingual, multitask weak supervision as a promising route to speech systems whose usefulness extends beyond a single narrowly adapted dataset.
summary.tldr: Speech models trained on 680,000 hours of multilingual, multitask supervision generalize well without dataset-specific fine-tuning and approach human performance in reported comparisons.

title: Robust Speech Recognition via Large-Scale Weak Supervision

abstract: Previous research on contrastive learning (CL) has primarily focused on pairwise views to learn representations by attracting positive samples and repelling negative ones. In this work, we aim to understand and generalize CL from a point set matching perspective, instead of the comparison between two points. Specifically, we formulate CL as a form of inverse optimal transport (IOT), which involves a bilevel optimization procedure for learning where the outter minimization aims to learn the representations and the inner is to learn the coupling (i.e. the probability of matching matrix) between the point sets. Specifically, by adjusting the relaxation degree of constraints in the inner minimization, we obtain three contrastive losses and show that the dominant contrastive loss in literature InfoNCE falls into one of these losses. This reveals a new and more general algorithmic framework for CL. Additionally, the soft matching scheme in IOT induces a uniformity penalty to enhance representation learning which is akin to the CL’s uniformity. Results on vision benchmarks show the effectiveness of our derived loss family and the new uniformity term.

paragraphs: Contrastive learning commonly trains representations by drawing positive pairs together and pushing negative pairs apart. This paper reframes the problem as matching sets of points. That perspective makes the relationships across a collection of examples part of the formulation and provides a route to deriving several contrastive objectives within one framework.

The authors formulate learning as inverse optimal transport with two nested optimization problems. The outer problem learns representations, while the inner problem learns a probabilistic matching matrix between point sets. Relaxing the inner constraints to different degrees produces three contrastive losses. InfoNCE, a widely used contrastive objective, appears as one member of this family.

The soft matching formulation also induces a uniformity penalty related to the uniformity encouraged in contrastive learning. Vision benchmark experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the derived losses and the additional penalty. The result offers both an interpretation of an established objective and a broader design framework for changing matching constraints and representation regularization.
summary.tldr: Viewing contrastive learning as inverse optimal transport unifies InfoNCE with additional losses and yields a useful uniformity penalty.

title: Understanding and Generalizing Contrastive Learning from the Inverse Optimal Transport Perspective

abstract: Image perturbation technique is widely used to generate adversarial examples to attack networks, greatly decreasing the performance of networks. Unlike the existing works, in this paper, we introduce a novel framework Deep Perturbation Learning (DPL), the new insights into understanding image perturbations, to enhance the performance of networks rather than decrease the performance. Specifically, we learn image perturbations to amend the data distribution of training set to improve the performance of networks. This optimization w.r.t data distribution is non-trivial. To approach this, we tactfully construct a differentiable optimization target w.r.t. image perturbations via minimizing the empirical risk. Then we propose an alternating optimization of the network weights and perturbations. DPL can easily be adapted to a wide spectrum of downstream tasks and backbone networks. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our DPL on 6 datasets (CIFAR-10, CIFAR100, ImageNet, MS-COCO, PASCAL VOC, and SBD) over 3 popular vision tasks (image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation) with different backbone architectures (e.g., ResNet, MobileNet, and ViT).

paragraphs: Small changes to images are often studied as a way to make neural networks fail. Deep Perturbation Learning uses learned image changes to improve network performance instead. The central idea is to adjust the training data distribution through perturbations, making the examples themselves part of the optimization process alongside the model’s weights.

Optimizing a data distribution through image changes is not straightforward. The authors construct a differentiable objective for the perturbations using empirical risk minimization. They then alternate between optimizing the network weights and optimizing the image perturbations. This gives the framework a concrete way to coordinate changes in what the network sees with changes in how it predicts.

The experiments cover image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation across six datasets, including ImageNet and MS-COCO. They also use different architectures, including ResNet, MobileNet, and ViT. The reported results support the effectiveness of learned training-image perturbations across these tested tasks and backbones, rather than confining the idea to a single vision application.
summary.tldr: Deep Perturbation Learning alternates between learning image perturbations and network weights to improve performance across several vision tasks.

title: Deep Perturbation Learning: Enhancing the Network Performance via Image Perturbations

abstract: The higher-order correlation clustering problem is an expressive model, and recently, local search heuristics have been proposed for several applications. Certifying optimality, however, is NP-hard and practically hampered already by the complexity of the problem statement. Here, we focus on establishing partial optimality conditions for the special case of complete graphs and cubic objective functions. In addition, we define and implement algorithms for testing these conditions and examine their effect numerically, on two datasets.
