paragraphs: Higher-order correlation clustering offers an expressive way to formulate clustering problems, and local search heuristics have been developed for several applications. Yet obtaining a candidate clustering and certifying its optimality are different challenges. The paper starts from the difficulty of certification, which is NP-hard and complicated in practice by the size and complexity of the problem formulation.

The authors investigate partial optimality for a restricted setting: complete graphs with cubic objective functions. The goal is to establish conditions that certify parts of an optimal solution, rather than requiring a certificate for the entire clustering. This shifts attention toward conclusions that may be available even when full optimality is difficult to establish.

The work includes algorithms for checking the proposed conditions and implementations of those algorithms. Numerical studies on two datasets examine their effect. The contribution therefore combines mathematical conditions with a practical route for testing them. Its stated scope remains the complete-graph, cubic-objective case; the abstract does not claim a general solver for all higher-order correlation clustering problems.
summary.tldr: The paper develops testable partial-optimality conditions for correlation clustering on complete graphs with cubic objectives.

title: Partial Optimality in Cubic Correlation Clustering

abstract: Datasets scraped from the internet have been critical to large-scale machine learning. Yet, its success puts the utility of future internet-derived datasets at potential risk, as model outputs begin to replace human annotations as a source of supervision. In this work, we formalize a system where interactions with one model are recorded as history and scraped as training data in the future. We then analyze its stability over time by tracking changes to a test-time bias statistic (e.g. gender bias of model predictions). We find that the degree of bias amplification is closely linked to whether the model’s outputs behave like samples from the training distribution, a behavior which we characterize and define as uniform faithfulness. Experiments in three conditional prediction scenarios – image classification, visual role-labeling, and language generation – demonstrate that models that exhibit a sampling-like behavior are more faithful and thus more stable. Based on this insight, we propose an intervention to help mitigate and stabilize unstable feedback systems.

paragraphs: When model interactions become part of future training data, today's predictions can influence tomorrow's models. This paper formalizes that feedback process: interactions are recorded as history and later scraped for training. It studies stability by following a prediction bias statistic over time, such as gender bias in model outputs.

The analysis connects bias amplification to whether outputs behave like samples from the training distribution. The authors characterize this property as uniform faithfulness. The distinction matters because a model's way of producing outputs affects the data that subsequent models encounter, and therefore how existing biases evolve through repeated feedback.

Experiments cover image classification, visual role-labeling, and language generation. Models exhibiting more sampling-like behavior are found to be more faithful and more stable in these settings. Building on that relationship, the authors propose an intervention to mitigate and stabilize unstable feedback systems. The findings concern the evolution of bias through feedback; greater stability does not itself establish that the starting distribution is unbiased.
summary.tldr: Model outputs that behave more like samples from their training distribution are associated with more stable bias under repeated data feedback.

title: Data Feedback Loops: Model-driven Amplification of Dataset Biases

abstract: The recent trend towards Personalized Federated Learning (PFL) has garnered significant attention as it allows for the training of models that are tailored to each client while maintaining data privacy. However, current PFL techniques primarily focus on modeling the conditional distribution heterogeneity (i.e. concept shift), which can result in suboptimal performance when the distribution of input data across clients diverges (i.e. covariate shift). Additionally, these techniques often lack the ability to adapt to unseen data, further limiting their effectiveness in real-world scenarios. To address these limitations, we propose a novel approach, FedGMM, which utilizes Gaussian mixture models (GMM) to effectively fit the input data distributions across diverse clients. The model parameters are estimated by maximum likelihood estimation utilizing a federated Expectation-Maximization algorithm, which is solved in closed form and does not assume gradient similarity. Furthermore, FedGMM possesses an additional advantage of adapting to new clients with minimal overhead, and it also enables uncertainty quantification. Empirical evaluations on synthetic and benchmark datasets demonstrate the superior performance of our method in both PFL classification and novel sample detection.

paragraphs: Personalized federated learning aims to fit models to individual clients while retaining the privacy-oriented benefits of federated training. This paper argues that focusing mainly on differences in the relationship between inputs and labels can overlook another source of heterogeneity: clients may also receive different kinds of inputs. That input-distribution shift can undermine personalization.

FedGMM addresses this issue by using Gaussian mixture models to fit input distributions across clients. Its parameters are estimated through maximum likelihood with a federated expectation-maximization algorithm that has a closed-form solution. The method does not assume that clients have similar gradients, which matters because the approach explicitly accommodates differences in their data.

The resulting model also supports uncertainty quantification and adaptation to new clients with minimal overhead. Experiments on synthetic data and benchmark datasets report superior performance for personalized classification and detection of novel samples. These two evaluation tasks reflect the method’s dual purpose: fitting client-specific predictions while modeling what kinds of inputs clients encounter. The contribution places input-distribution modeling at the center of personalization and adaptation.
summary.tldr: FedGMM models differing client input distributions to improve personalized federated classification, novel-sample detection, and adaptation to new clients.

title: Personalized Federated Learning under Mixture of Distributions

abstract: With recent advances in natural language processing, rationalization becomes an essential self-explaining diagram to disentangle the black box by selecting a subset of input texts to account for the major variation in prediction. Yet, existing association-based approaches on rationalization cannot identify true rationales when two or more snippets are highly inter-correlated and thus provide a similar contribution to prediction accuracy, so-called spuriousness. To address this limitation, we novelly leverage two causal desiderata, non-spuriousness and efficiency, into rationalization from the causal inference perspective. We formally define a series of probabilities of causation based on a newly proposed structural causal model of rationalization, with its theoretical identification established as the main component of learning necessary and sufficient rationales. The superior performance of the proposed causal rationalization is demonstrated on real-world review and medical datasets with extensive experiments compared to state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Text rationalization explains a prediction by selecting a subset of the input. Association-based methods can struggle when several snippets are strongly correlated and support similar predictive accuracy. In that situation, a selected snippet may appear useful without identifying the true rationale. This paper develops a causal approach to address that ambiguity.

The authors introduce a structural causal model of rationalization and use it to define probabilities of causation. They build the approach around two desired properties, non-spuriousness and efficiency, and establish theoretical identification results. Those results form the central basis for learning rationales that are necessary and sufficient within the proposed causal formulation.

Experiments on real-world review and medical datasets show superior performance compared with state-of-the-art methods. The contribution connects explanation selection to explicit causal quantities, giving the method a basis beyond predictive association alone. Its theoretical claims belong to the proposed structural model, while the experiments provide evidence that this formulation improves rationalization in the evaluated text settings.
summary.tldr: A causal model of text rationalization helps identify necessary and sufficient explanations when correlated snippets make association-based selection ambiguous.

title: Towards Trustworthy Explanation: On Causal Rationalization

abstract: Test-Time Adaptation (TTA) has recently gained significant attention as a new paradigm for tackling distribution shifts. Despite the sheer number of existing methods, the inconsistent experimental conditions and lack of standardization in prior literature make it difficult to measure their actual efficacies and progress. To address this issue, we present a large-scale open-sourced Test-Time Adaptation Benchmark, dubbed TTAB, which includes nine state-of-the-art algorithms, a diverse array of distribution shifts, and two comprehensive evaluation protocols. Through extensive experiments, we identify three common pitfalls in prior efforts: (i) choosing appropriate hyper-parameter, especially for model selection, is exceedingly difficult due to online batch dependency; (ii) the effectiveness of TTA varies greatly depending on the quality of the model being adapted; (iii) even under optimal algorithmic conditions, existing methods still systematically struggle with certain types of distribution shifts. Our findings suggest that future research in the field should be more transparent about their experimental conditions, ensure rigorous evaluations on a broader set of models and shifts, and re-examine the assumptions underlying the potential success of TTA for practical applications.

paragraphs: Test-time adaptation updates a model to cope with distribution changes encountered during deployment. Comparing methods has been difficult because studies use inconsistent experimental conditions. This paper introduces TTAB, an open benchmark containing nine leading algorithms, diverse distribution shifts, and two evaluation protocols, to make those comparisons more systematic.

The experiments identify three recurring problems. Hyperparameter choice, especially model selection, becomes difficult because online batches depend on one another. Adaptation performance also varies substantially with the quality of the starting model. Finally, some kinds of distribution shift remain difficult for existing methods even when algorithmic conditions are optimal.

These findings mean that an adaptation result needs to be interpreted alongside the starting model, the shift being tested, and the evaluation setup. The authors call for clearer reporting of experimental conditions and broader testing across models and shifts. They also argue for revisiting the assumptions behind successful practical adaptation. TTAB supplies an evaluation framework for examining those dependencies rather than assuming adaptation will reliably help across settings.
summary.tldr: TTAB reveals that test-time adaptation depends strongly on model quality, evaluation conditions, and the type of distribution shift.

title: On Pitfalls of Test-Time Adaptation

abstract: The study of behavioral diversity in Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) is a nascent yet promising field. In this context, the present work deals with the question of how to control the diversity of a multi-agent system. With no existing approaches to control diversity to a set value, current solutions focus on blindly promoting it via intrinsic rewards or additional loss functions, effectively changing the learning objective and lacking a principled measure for it. To address this, we introduce Diversity Control (DiCo), a method able to control diversity to an exact value of a given metric by representing policies as the sum of a parameter-shared component and dynamically scaled per-agent components. By applying constraints directly to the policy architecture, DiCo leaves the learning objective unchanged, enabling its applicability to any actor-critic MARL algorithm. We theoretically prove that DiCo achieves the desired diversity, and we provide several experiments, both in cooperative and competitive tasks, that show how DiCo can be employed as a novel paradigm to increase performance and sample efficiency in MARL. Multimedia results are available on the paper’s website: https://sites.google.com/view/dico-marl

paragraphs: In multi-agent reinforcement learning, encouraging agents to behave differently does not specify how different they should become. Existing approaches described in the paper reward diversity or add extra training losses, changing the learning objective without directly controlling diversity to a chosen value. This work turns that target value into an explicit design goal.

Diversity Control, or DiCo, represents each agent’s policy as a shared component plus an individual component. It dynamically scales the individual components to achieve the desired value of a given diversity metric. Because the constraint is imposed through the policy architecture, the original learning objective remains unchanged, and the method can apply to any actor-critic MARL algorithm.

The authors prove that DiCo achieves the requested diversity and test it in cooperative and competitive tasks. Their experiments show how controlling diversity can improve performance and sample efficiency. The significance is that diversity becomes an adjustable property of the agent system, with a precise metric-based target, instead of an additional incentive that merely pushes agents toward greater difference.
summary.tldr: DiCo controls multi-agent policy diversity to an exact metric value through architecture constraints while preserving the learning objective.

title: Controlling Behavioral Diversity in Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Self-supervised learning of image representations by predicting future frames is a promising direction but still remains a challenge. This is because of the under-determined nature of frame prediction; multiple potential futures can arise from a single current frame. To tackle this challenge, in this paper, we revisit the idea of stochastic video generation that learns to capture uncertainty in frame prediction and explore its effectiveness for representation learning. Specifically, we design a framework that trains a stochastic frame prediction model to learn temporal information between frames. Moreover, to learn dense information within each frame, we introduce an auxiliary masked image modeling objective along with a shared decoder architecture. We find this architecture allows for combining both objectives in a synergistic and compute-efficient manner. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework on a variety of tasks from video label propagation and vision-based robot learning domains, such as video segmentation, pose tracking, vision-based robotic locomotion, and manipulation tasks. Code is available on the project webpage: https://sites.google.com/view/2024rsp.

paragraphs: Predicting future video frames can teach a model useful visual representations, but a current image does not determine a unique future. This paper revisits stochastic frame prediction to handle that ambiguity explicitly. Its framework learns temporal relationships between frames while representing uncertainty about what may happen next, making uncertain futures part of the learning task.

The authors add a masked image modeling objective to learn dense information within individual frames. A shared decoder combines this objective with stochastic prediction, linking spatial learning inside a frame with temporal learning across frames. They find that the architecture lets the two objectives work together effectively while keeping the combination computationally efficient.

The learned representations are evaluated on video label propagation and vision-based robot learning. Tasks include video segmentation, pose tracking, robotic locomotion, and manipulation. The results demonstrate the framework's effectiveness across these settings. The contribution is the combination of uncertainty-aware temporal prediction with within-frame learning, showing that stochastic video generation can serve as a useful training signal for representations applied beyond future-frame generation itself.
summary.tldr: Stochastic future-frame prediction and masked image modeling share a decoder to learn useful visual representations for video understanding and robot learning.

title: Visual Representation Learning with Stochastic Frame Prediction

abstract: Flexible sensors hold promise for human motion capture (MoCap), offering advantages such as wearability, privacy preservation, and minimal constraints on natural movement. However, existing flexible sensor-based MoCap methods rely on deep learning and necessitate large and diverse labeled datasets for training. These data typically need to be collected in MoCap studios with specialized equipment and substantial manual labor, making them difficult and expensive to obtain at scale. Thanks to the high-linearity of flexible sensors, we address this challenge by proposing a novel Sim2Real solution for hinge joint tracking based on domain adaptation, eliminating the need for labeled data yet achieving comparable accuracy to supervised learning. Our solution relies on a novel Support-based Domain Adaptation method, namely SuDA, which aligns the supports of the predictive functions rather than the instance-dependent distributions between the source and target domains. Extensive experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our method and its superiority overstate-of-the-art distribution-based domain adaptation methods in our task.

paragraphs: Flexible sensors offer a wearable and privacy-preserving route to motion capture with few restrictions on natural movement. Training existing deep-learning systems, however, requires large, varied labeled datasets. Collecting these in specialized motion-capture studios takes equipment and manual labor, making scale difficult and expensive.

The paper proposes transferring from simulation to reality for hinge-joint tracking, drawing on the high linearity of flexible sensors. Its SuDA method aligns the supports of predictive functions across source and target domains. This changes the target of adaptation from matching instance-dependent distributions to matching the supports associated with the prediction functions.

The resulting approach eliminates the need for labeled data in the proposed tracking solution while achieving accuracy comparable to supervised learning. Extensive experiments also show an advantage over leading distribution-based domain-adaptation methods for this task. The findings support support-based alignment as a useful way to bridge simulation and real sensing in the hinge-joint setting, where the sensors’ linear behavior motivates the approach.
summary.tldr: SuDA transfers hinge-joint tracking from simulation to reality through predictive-function support alignment, reporting supervised-comparable accuracy without labeled data.

title: SuDA: Support-based Domain Adaptation for Sim2Real Hinge Joint Tracking with Flexible Sensors

abstract: LLM watermarking has attracted attention as a promising way to detect AI-generated content, with some works suggesting that current schemes may already be fit for deployment. In this work we dispute this claim, identifying watermark stealing (WS) as a fundamental vulnerability of these schemes. We show that querying the API of the watermarked LLM to approximately reverse-engineer a watermark enables practical spoofing attacks, as hypothesized in prior work, but also greatly boosts scrubbing attacks, which was previously unnoticed. We are the first to propose an automated WS algorithm and use it in the first comprehensive study of spoofing and scrubbing in realistic settings. We show that for under $50 an attacker can both spoof and scrub state-of-the-art schemes previously considered safe, with average success rate of over 80%. Our findings challenge common beliefs about LLM watermarking, stressing the need for more robust schemes. We make all our code and additional examples available at https://watermark-stealing.org.

paragraphs: Watermarks in language-model output are intended to help identify AI-generated text. This paper challenges claims that current schemes are ready for deployment by studying watermark stealing: approximately learning a watermark through queries to the API of a watermarked model. The authors identify this as a vulnerability in the schemes they examine.

The study considers two consequences. Spoofing makes text appear to carry the watermark, while scrubbing removes evidence of the watermark from generated text. The authors show that stealing a watermark enables practical spoofing and also substantially improves scrubbing. They introduce an automated watermark-stealing algorithm and evaluate both attack types in realistic settings.

For the evaluated state-of-the-art schemes, the authors report that an attacker can carry out spoofing and scrubbing for under $50, with average success exceeding 80%. These findings concern the tested schemes and conditions, rather than proving every possible watermark ineffective. They nevertheless weaken deployment-readiness claims for schemes previously considered safe and motivate watermark designs that remain robust when their behavior can be approximately inferred.
summary.tldr: Approximately learning an LLM watermark enables low-cost spoofing and scrubbing with high average success against the evaluated schemes.

title: Watermark Stealing in Large Language Models

abstract: The Gradient Descent-Ascent (GDA) algorithm, designed to solve minimax optimization problems, takes the descent and ascent steps either simultaneously (Sim-GDA) or alternately (Alt-GDA). While Alt-GDA is commonly observed to converge faster, the performance gap between the two is not yet well understood theoretically, especially in terms of global convergence rates. To address this theory-practice gap, we present fine-grained convergence analyses of both algorithms for strongly-convex-strongly-concave and Lipschitz-gradient objectives. Our new iteration complexity upper bound of Alt-GDA is strictly smaller than the lower bound of Sim-GDA; i.e., Alt-GDA is provably faster. Moreover, we propose Alternating-Extrapolation GDA (Alex-GDA), a general algorithmic framework that subsumes Sim-GDA and Alt-GDA, for which the main idea is to alternately take gradients from extrapolations of the iterates. We show that Alex-GDA satisfies a smaller iteration complexity bound, identical to that of the Extra-gradient method, while requiring less gradient computations. We also prove that Alex-GDA enjoys linear convergence for bilinear problems, for which both Sim-GDA and Alt-GDA fail to converge at all.

summary.tldr: The paper proves an advantage for alternating minimax updates under stated assumptions and introduces an extrapolation framework with stronger convergence results.

title: Fundamental Benefit of Alternating Updates in Minimax Optimization

abstract: Cross-modality transfer aims to leverage large pretrained models to complete tasks that may not belong to the modality of pretraining data. Existing works achieve certain success in extending classical finetuning to cross-modal scenarios, yet we still lack understanding about the influence of modality gap on the transfer. In this work, a series of experiments focusing on the source representation quality during transfer are conducted, revealing the connection between larger modality gap and lesser knowledge reuse which means ineffective transfer. We then formalize the gap as the knowledge misalignment between modalities using conditional distribution $P(Y|X)$. Towards this problem, we present Modality kNowledge Alignment (MoNA), a meta-learning approach that learns target data transformation to reduce the modality knowledge discrepancy ahead of the transfer. Experiments show that the approach significantly improves upon cross-modal finetuning methods, and most importantly leads to better reuse of source modality knowledge.

paragraphs: Cross-modality transfer applies a pretrained model to tasks involving a different kind of data from its original training data. Although fine-tuning can work in these settings, the authors ask how the gap between modalities affects reuse of the model's existing knowledge. Their experiments connect larger modality gaps with weaker knowledge reuse and less effective transfer.

The paper formalizes this gap through differences in the conditional distribution P(Y|X), which describes the relationship between inputs and targets. This frames the issue as knowledge misalignment between modalities. That transformation aims to reduce the knowledge discrepancy so the pretrained model can make better use of what it already learned. Experiments show significant improvements over cross-modal fine-tuning approaches and better reuse of source-modality knowledge. The contribution links an empirical diagnosis of transfer difficulty to a method that prepares target data for more effective adaptation.
summary.tldr: MoNA learns target-data transformations that reduce modality knowledge mismatch and improve reuse of pretrained knowledge during transfer.

title: Learning Modality Knowledge Alignment for Cross-Modality Transfer

abstract: The turnstile data stream model offers the most flexible framework where data can be manipulated dynamically, i.e., rows, columns, and even single entries of an input matrix can be added, deleted, or updated multiple times in a data stream. We develop a novel algorithm for sampling rows $a_i$ of a matrix $A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$, proportional to their $\ell_p$ norm, when $A$ is presented in a turnstile data stream. Our algorithm not only returns the set of sampled row indexes, it also returns slightly perturbed rows $\tilde{a}_i \approx a_i$, and approximates their sampling probabilities up to $\varepsilon$ relative error. When combined with preconditioning techniques, our algorithm extends to $\ell_p$ leverage score sampling over turnstile data streams. With these properties in place, it allows us to simulate subsampling constructions of coresets for important regression problems to operate over turnstile data streams with very little overhead compared to their respective off-line subsampling algorithms. For logistic regression, our framework yields the first algorithm that achieves a $(1+\varepsilon)$ approximation and works in a turnstile data stream using polynomial sketch/subsample size, improving over $O(1)$ approximations, or $\exp(1/\varepsilon)$ sketch size of previous work. We compare experimentally to plain oblivious sketching and plain leverage score sampling algorithms for $\ell_p$ and logistic regression.

paragraphs: Turnstile streams allow matrix data to change through additions, deletions, and repeated updates to rows, columns, or individual entries. The paper also experimentally compares the approach with plain oblivious sketching and leverage-score sampling for ℓp and logistic regression.
summary.tldr: A turnstile streaming sampler supports regression coresets and a one-plus-epsilon logistic regression approximation with polynomial sketch size.

title: Turnstile $\ell_p$ leverage score sampling with applications

abstract: A molecule’s 2D representation consists of its atoms, their attributes, and the molecule’s covalent bonds. A 3D (geometric) representation of a molecule is called a conformer and consists of its atom types and Cartesian coordinates. Every conformer has a potential energy, and the lower this energy, the more likely it occurs in nature. Most existing machine learning methods for molecular property prediction consider either 2D molecular graphs or 3D conformer structure representations in isolation. Inspired by recent work on using ensembles of conformers in conjunction with 2D graph representations, we propose E(3)-invariant molecular conformer aggregation networks. The method integrates a molecule’s 2D representation with that of multiple of its conformers. Contrary to prior work, we propose a novel 2D–3D aggregation mechanism based on a differentiable solver for the Fused Gromov-Wasserstein Barycenter problem and the use of an efficient conformer generation method based on distance geometry. We show that the proposed aggregation mechanism is E(3) invariant and propose an efficient GPU implementation. Moreover, we demonstrate that the aggregation mechanism helps to significantly outperform state-of-the-art molecule property prediction methods on established datasets.

This paper develops a molecular property predictor that combines the graph with several conformers, addressing approaches that process these representations in isolation.

The central aggregation mechanism uses a differentiable solver for the Fused Gromov-Wasserstein Barycenter problem. It integrates information from the two-dimensional structure and the collection of three-dimensional conformers. The method also uses distance geometry for efficient conformer generation and includes a GPU implementation of the aggregation procedure.

The authors prove that the aggregation is E(3)-invariant, so changing the geometric coordinate frame through Euclidean transformations does not change the aggregate representation. Experiments on established datasets show that the mechanism helps the proposed method significantly outperform state-of-the-art molecular property predictors. The contribution combines several geometric views of a molecule with its bond structure while preserving an appropriate invariance and supporting efficient computation.
summary.tldr: A differentiable, E(3)-invariant aggregation mechanism combines molecular graphs with multiple conformers to improve property prediction.

title: Structure-Aware E(3)-Invariant Molecular Conformer Aggregation Networks

abstract: Deep learning-based image restoration methods generally struggle with faithfully preserving the structures of the original image. In this work, we propose a novel Residual-Conditioned Optimal Transport (RCOT) approach, which models image restoration as an optimal transport (OT) problem for both unpaired and paired settings, introducing the transport residual as a unique degradation-specific cue for both the transport cost and the transport map. Specifically, we first formalize a Fourier residual-guided OT objective by incorporating the degradation-specific information of the residual into the transport cost. We further design the transport map as a two-pass RCOT map that comprises a base model and a refinement process, in which the transport residual is computed by the base model in the first pass and then encoded as a degradation-specific embedding to condition the second-pass restoration. By duality, the RCOT problem is transformed into a minimax optimization problem, which can be solved by adversarially training neural networks. Extensive experiments on multiple restoration tasks show that RCOT achieves competitive performance in terms of both distortion measures and perceptual quality, restoring images with more faithful structures as compared with state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Image restoration should improve an image while preserving its original structures, but learned restoration methods can struggle with that requirement. This paper formulates restoration as an optimal-transport problem in both paired and unpaired settings. Its central idea is to use the transport residual as information about the particular degradation affecting an image.

Residual-Conditioned Optimal Transport, or RCOT, uses this information in two places. A Fourier residual-guided objective incorporates it into the transport cost. A two-pass restoration map also uses it to guide prediction: a base model first produces a residual, which is encoded into a degradation-specific embedding that conditions a second refinement pass.

Using duality, the authors convert the formulation into a minimax problem that can be optimized by adversarially training neural networks. Experiments across multiple restoration tasks show competitive distortion measures and perceptual quality, with more faithful structures than state-of-the-art methods. The results support using an initial restoration’s residual as an explicit cue for both the objective and subsequent refinement.
summary.tldr: RCOT uses restoration residuals to guide an optimal-transport objective and a second refinement pass, improving structural fidelity in evaluated restoration tasks.

title: Residual-Conditioned Optimal Transport: Towards Structure-Preserving Unpaired and Paired Image Restoration

abstract: Event cameras offer promising advantages such as high dynamic range and low latency, making them well-suited for challenging lighting conditions and fast-moving scenarios. However, reconstructing 3D scenes from raw event streams is difficult because event data is sparse and does not carry absolute color information. To release its potential in 3D reconstruction, we propose the first event-based generalizable 3D reconstruction framework, which reconstructs scenes as 3D Gaussians from only event input in a feedforward manner and can generalize to unseen cases without any retraining. This framework includes a depth estimation module, an intensity reconstruction module, and a Gaussian regression module. These submodules connect in a cascading manner, and we collaboratively train them with a designed joint loss to make them mutually promote. To facilitate related studies, we build a novel event-based 3D dataset with various material objects and calibrated labels of greyscale images, depth maps, camera poses, and silhouettes. Experiments show models that have jointly trained significantly outperform those trained individually. Our approach performs better than all baselines in reconstruction quality, and depth/intensity predictions with satisfactory rendering speed.

EvGGS tackles reconstruction using only event inputs, representing the scene with three-dimensional Gaussians.

The framework connects depth estimation, intensity reconstruction, and Gaussian regression in a cascade. A joint loss trains these components collaboratively so their learning can support one another. Reconstruction happens through a feedforward process, and the framework can handle unseen cases without retraining. The authors also introduce a dataset containing objects with different materials and calibrated grayscale images, depths, camera poses, and silhouettes.

Experiments show that joint training significantly improves over training the components separately. The method also exceeds all compared baselines in reconstruction quality and depth and intensity prediction, while delivering rendering speed the authors describe as satisfactory. These findings support coordinated learning as a useful way to extract complementary scene information from event streams.
summary.tldr: EvGGS jointly learns depth, intensity, and Gaussian scene representations to reconstruct unseen scenes directly from event-camera inputs without retraining.

title: EvGGS: A Collaborative Learning Framework for Event-based Generalizable Gaussian Splatting

abstract: In this paper, we examine the time it takes for stochastic gradient descent (SGD) to reach the global minimum of a general, non-convex loss function. We approach this question through the lens of large deviations theory and randomly perturbed dynamical systems, and we provide a tight characterization of the associated hitting times of SGD with matching upper and lower bounds. Our analysis reveals that the global convergence time of SGD is dominated by the most "costly" set of obstacles that the algorithm may need to overcome in order to reach a global minimizer, coupling in this way the geometry of the underlying loss landscape with the statistics of the noise entering the process. Finally, motivated by applications to the training of deep neural networks, we provide a series of refinements and extensions of our analysis to, among others, loss functions with no spurious local minima or ones with bounded depths.

paragraphs: This paper asks how long stochastic gradient descent takes to reach a global minimum of a non-convex loss function. The target is global convergence time, which requires understanding the obstacles encountered along the route to a best solution. The authors study this question through large deviations theory and the behavior of randomly perturbed dynamical systems.

Their main result gives matching upper and lower bounds on the relevant hitting times. The analysis identifies the most costly collection of obstacles SGD may need to overcome as the dominant factor in global convergence. That cost combines the shape of the loss landscape with the statistical properties of the noise driving the updates, linking geometry and randomness in one characterization.

Motivated by neural-network training, the authors refine and extend the analysis for additional classes of losses. These include functions without spurious local minima and functions with bounded depths. The contribution provides sharp theoretical estimates of the time needed to reach a global minimizer and explains what features determine those estimates.
summary.tldr: Matching bounds characterize SGD’s global convergence time through the joint effects of landscape obstacles and update noise.

title: The Global Convergence Time of Stochastic Gradient Descent in Non-Convex Landscapes: Sharp Estimates via Large Deviations

abstract: Many applications in machine learning involve data represented as probability distributions. The emergence of such data requires radically novel techniques to design tractable gradient flows on probability distributions over this type of (infinite-dimensional) objects. For instance, being able to flow labeled datasets is a core task for applications ranging from domain adaptation to transfer learning or dataset distillation. In this setting, we propose to represent each class by the associated conditional distribution of features, and to model the dataset as a mixture distribution supported on these classes (which are themselves probability distributions), meaning that labeled datasets can be seen as probability distributions over probability distributions. We endow this space with a metric structure from optimal transport, namely the Wasserstein over Wasserstein (WoW) distance, derive a differential structure on this space, and define WoW gradient flows. The latter enables to design dynamics over this space that decrease a given objective functional. We apply our framework to transfer learning and dataset distillation tasks, leveraging our gradient flow construction as well as novel tractable functionals that take the form of Maximum Mean Discrepancies with Sliced-Wasserstein based kernels between probability distributions.

paragraphs: This paper develops a way to optimize entire labeled datasets by treating them as distributions of distributions. Each class is represented by the distribution of its features. The dataset is then represented as a mixture whose components are those class-level distributions, preserving the distinction between individual features and the classes they belong to.

The authors equip this nested space with Wasserstein over Wasserstein distance, an optimal-transport-based measure of separation. They then derive the differential structure needed to define gradient flows. These flows describe how a dataset representation can evolve in a direction that decreases a chosen objective, extending gradient-based reasoning to objects that are themselves probability distributions.

To make the framework usable, the paper introduces tractable objectives based on Maximum Mean Discrepancy, with kernels built from Sliced-Wasserstein comparisons between distributions. The authors apply these objectives and flows to transfer learning and dataset distillation. The contribution is a mathematical and computational framework for transforming structured datasets, connecting class-aware representations to a principled notion of improvement.
summary.tldr: The paper models labeled datasets as distributions of class distributions and develops optimal-transport gradient flows for transforming them.

title: Flowing Datasets with Wasserstein over Wasserstein Gradient Flows

abstract: Recently, recurrent models such as state space models and linear attention have become popular due to their linear complexity in the sequence length. Thanks to their recurrent nature, in principle they can process arbitrarily long sequences, but their performance sometimes drops considerably beyond their training context lengths—i.e. they fail to length generalize. In this work, we provide comprehensive empirical and theoretical analysis to support the unexplored states hypothesis, which posits that models fail to length generalize when during training they are only exposed to a limited subset of the distribution of all attainable states (i.e. states that would be attained if the recurrence was applied to long sequences). Furthermore, we investigate simple training interventions that aim to increase the coverage of the states that the model is trained on, e.g. by initializing the state with Gaussian noise or with the final state of a different input sequence. With only 500 post-training steps ($\sim 0.1%$ of the pre-training budget), these interventions enable length generalization for sequences that are orders of magnitude longer than the training context (e.g. $2k\longrightarrow 128k$) and show improved performance in long context tasks, thus presenting a simple and efficient way to enable robust length generalization in general recurrent models.

paragraphs: Recurrent models can process sequences with computation that grows linearly with length, yet their performance may deteriorate beyond the contexts used in training. This paper investigates why the ability to keep running does not necessarily translate into reliable long-sequence behavior. It studies state space models and linear attention through empirical and theoretical analysis.

The analysis supports the unexplored states hypothesis: training on shorter sequences exposes a model to only part of the internal-state distribution attainable on longer sequences. The authors test interventions intended to broaden that coverage. These include starting from Gaussian noise and starting from the final state produced by another input sequence.

With 500 post-training steps, approximately 0.1% of the pretraining budget, the interventions enable generalization to sequences orders of magnitude longer than the training context, including an example from 2K to 128K. They also improve long-context task performance. The results support state coverage as a useful explanation and intervention target for length generalization in the recurrent models studied.
summary.tldr: Broadening the internal states seen during training helps recurrent models handle much longer sequences with a small post-training budget.

title: Understanding and Improving Length Generalization in Recurrent Models

abstract: The Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) algorithm with a Gaussian policy has become a mainstream implementation for realizing the Maximum Entropy Reinforcement Learning (MaxEnt RL) objective, which incorporates entropy maximization to encourage exploration and enhance policy robustness. While the Gaussian policy performs well on simpler tasks, its exploration capacity and potential performance in complex multi-goal RL environments are limited by its inherent unimodality. In this paper, we employ the diffusion model, a powerful generative model capable of capturing complex multimodal distributions, as the policy representation to fulfill the MaxEnt RL objective, developing a method named MaxEnt RL with Diffusion Policy (MaxEntDP). Our method enables efficient exploration and brings the policy closer to the optimal MaxEnt policy. Experimental results on Mujoco benchmarks show that MaxEntDP outperforms the Gaussian policy and other generative models within the MaxEnt RL framework, and performs comparably to other state-of-the-art diffusion-based online RL algorithms. Our code is available at https://github.com/diffusionyes/MaxEntDP.

In this paper, we employ the diffusion model, a powerful generative model capable of capturing complex multimodal distributions, as the policy representation to fulfill the MaxEnt RL objective, developing a method named MaxEnt RL with Diffusion Policy (MaxEntDP). paragraphs: Maximum entropy reinforcement learning rewards both task success and diversity in action selection, encouraging exploration and policy robustness. A common implementation, Soft Actor-Critic, uses a Gaussian policy. The paper identifies that policy’s single-mode structure as a constraint in complex environments with multiple goals, where useful behavior may require a more varied action distribution.

MaxEntDP replaces that policy representation with a diffusion model, which can capture distributions with multiple modes. The method uses this expressive representation to pursue the maximum entropy objective. The authors state that it enables efficient exploration and brings the learned policy closer to the optimal policy for that objective.

On MuJoCo benchmarks, MaxEntDP outperforms Gaussian policies and other generative models evaluated within the maximum entropy framework. It also performs comparably to other state-of-the-art diffusion-based online reinforcement-learning algorithms. These findings support the choice of policy representation as an important part of exploration: a richer distribution can better accommodate multiple promising behaviors while remaining part of an entropy-encouraging learning objective.
summary.tldr: MaxEntDP uses a diffusion policy for maximum entropy reinforcement learning, improving exploration and outperforming tested Gaussian-policy alternatives on MuJoCo.

title: Maximum Entropy Reinforcement Learning with Diffusion Policy

abstract: Multimodal language modeling has enabled breakthroughs for representation learning, yet remains unexplored in the realm of functional brain data for clinical phenotyping. This paper pioneers EEG-language models (ELMs) trained on clinical reports and 15000 EEGs. We propose to combine multimodal alignment in this novel domain with timeseries cropping and text segmentation, enabling an extension based on multiple instance learning to alleviate misalignment between irrelevant EEG or text segments. Our multimodal models significantly improve over EEG-only models across four clinical evaluations and for the first time enable zero-shot classification as well as retrieval of both neural signals and reports. In sum, these results highlight the potential of ELMs, representing significant progress for clinical applications.
originalAbstract: Multimodal language modeling has enabled breakthroughs for representation learning, yet remains unexplored in the realm of functional brain data for clinical phenotyping. This paper pioneers EEG-language models (ELMs) trained on clinical reports and 15000 EEGs. We propose to combine multimodal alignment in this novel domain with timeseries cropping and text segmentation, enabling an extension based on multiple instance learning to alleviate misalignment between irrelevant EEG or text segments. Our multimodal models significantly improve over EEG-only models across four clinical evaluations and for the first time enable zero-shot classification as well as retrieval of both neural signals and reports. In sum, these results highlight the potential of ELMs, representing significant progress for clinical applications.

paragraphs: This paper connects EEG recordings with the language in clinical reports to learn representations for clinical phenotyping. The models are trained using 15,000 EEGs and associated reports. The motivation is to let information from both sources shape the learned representation, extending multimodal language modeling to functional brain data.

A central challenge is that a report segment and an EEG segment may describe different things or contain irrelevant information. The method combines crops of the time series with segmented report text and uses an extension based on multiple instance learning. This design aims to reduce the harm caused by treating unrelated pieces of the two sources as if they matched directly.

Across four clinical evaluations, the multimodal models significantly outperform EEG-only models. The authors also demonstrate zero-shot classification and retrieval involving both neural recordings and reports. These results show that language supervision can support useful EEG representations and additional ways to access the data, while establishing the approach’s potential for clinical applications rather than a claim of clinical deployment.
summary.tldr: Joint training on EEGs and clinical reports improves clinical evaluations and enables zero-shot classification and cross-modal retrieval.

title: EEG-Language Pretraining for Highly Label-Efficient Clinical Phenotyping

abstract: Contrastive Language-Image Pre-Training (CLIP) is highly instrumental in machine learning applications within a large variety of domains. We investigate the geometry of this embedding, which is still not well understood, and show that text and image reside on linearly separable ellipsoid shells, not centered at the origin. We explain the benefits of having this structure, allowing to better embed instances according to their uncertainty during contrastive training. Frequent concepts in the dataset yield more false negatives, inducing greater uncertainty. A new notion of conformity is introduced, which measures the average cosine similarity of an instance to any other instance within a representative data set. We show this measure can be accurately estimated by simply computing the cosine similarity to the modality mean vector. Furthermore, we find that CLIP’s modality gap optimizes the matching of the conformity distributions of image and text.

paragraphs: CLIP represents images and text in a shared embedding space, but the geometry of that space is not fully understood. This paper finds that the two modalities occupy separate ellipsoid shells whose centers are displaced from the origin. The shells are linearly separable, revealing an organized geometric difference between image and text representations.

The authors explain how this structure can represent differing levels of uncertainty during contrastive training. Frequent concepts generate more false negatives, which increases uncertainty. They introduce conformity as the average cosine similarity between an instance and other instances in a representative dataset, providing a way to describe how closely a representation aligns with the surrounding collection.

The paper shows that conformity can be estimated accurately through cosine similarity with the mean vector for the modality, avoiding the need to calculate every pairwise comparison. It also finds that CLIP’s modality gap optimizes the matching of image and text conformity distributions. These results give the separation between modalities a functional interpretation tied to uncertainty and the statistical organization of the embedding space.
summary.tldr: CLIP’s image and text embeddings form separate ellipsoid shells whose geometry relates to uncertainty and similarity distributions.

title: The Double-Ellipsoid Geometry of CLIP

abstract: Task robust adaptation is a long-standing pursuit in sequential decision-making. Some risk-averse strategies, e.g., the conditional value-at-risk principle, are incorporated in domain randomization or meta reinforcement learning to prioritize difficult tasks in optimization, which demand costly intensive evaluations. The efficiency issue prompts the development of robust active task sampling to train adaptive policies, where risk-predictive models can surrogate policy evaluation. This work characterizes robust active task sampling as a secret Markov decision process, posits theoretical and practical insights, and constitutes robustness concepts in risk-averse scenarios. Importantly, we propose an easy-to-implement method, referred to as Posterior and Diversity Synergized Task Sampling (PDTS), to accommodate fast and robust sequential decision-making. Extensive experiments show that PDTS unlocks the potential of robust active task sampling, significantly improves the zero-shot and few-shot adaptation robustness in challenging tasks, and even accelerates the learning process under certain scenarios.

paragraphs: Training an adaptive decision-maker often involves choosing among many tasks or randomized environments. Risk-averse methods emphasize difficult tasks, but identifying them through repeated policy evaluation can be expensive. This paper studies active task sampling, where a model predicts risk to help select training tasks without requiring intensive direct evaluation every time.

The authors formulate robust active task sampling as a secret Markov decision process and develop theoretical and practical insights for risk-averse settings. Their proposed method, Posterior and Diversity Synergized Task Sampling, combines posterior information with task diversity. The focus is on making task selection both useful for robustness and practical to implement, so the sampling process supports the training of adaptive policies.

Extensive experiments report stronger robustness on challenging tasks in both zero-shot and few-shot adaptation. These settings test adaptation with no task-specific examples or only a small number. PDTS also accelerates learning in certain scenarios. The speed benefit is therefore conditional, while the reported robustness improvements support actively selecting training tasks as a useful component of adaptive sequential decision-making.
summary.tldr: PDTS combines posterior information and task diversity to improve adaptation robustness, with faster learning in some tested scenarios.

title: Fast and Robust: Task Sampling with Posterior and Diversity Synergies for Adaptive Decision-Makers in Randomized Environments

abstract: We present a novel, and effective, approach to achieve optimal mesh relocation in finite element methods (FEMs). The cost and accuracy of FEMs is critically dependent on the choice of mesh points. Mesh relocation (r-adaptivity) seeks to optimise the mesh geometry to obtain the best solution accuracy at given computational budget. Classical r-adaptivity relies on the solution of a separate nonlinear “meshing” PDE to determine mesh point locations. This incurs significant cost at remeshing, and relies on estimates that relate interpolation- and FEM-error. Recent machine learning approaches have focused on the construction of fast surrogates for such classical methods. Instead, our new approach trains a graph neural network (GNN) to determine mesh point locations by directly minimising the FE solution error from the PDE system Firedrake to achieve higher solution accuracy. Our GNN architecture closely aligns the mesh solution space to that of classical meshing methodologies, thus replacing classical estimates for optimality with a learnable strategy. This allows for rapid and robust training and results in an extremely efficient and effective GNN approach to online r-adaptivity. Our method outperforms both classical, and prior ML, approaches to r-adaptive meshing. In particular, it achieves lower FE solution error, whilst retaining the significant speed-up over classical methods observed in prior ML work.

paragraphs: Finite element methods depend strongly on where mesh points are placed. Mesh relocation aims to improve solution accuracy within a fixed computational budget, but classical approaches solve an additional nonlinear meshing equation and rely on estimates linking different kinds of error. Previous machine-learning approaches have largely sought fast approximations to these classical procedures.

G-Adaptivity trains a graph neural network to place mesh points by directly minimizing the finite element solution error obtained from Firedrake. Its architecture closely matches the mesh solution space used by classical methods. This combines a structured space of possible meshes with a learned strategy driven by the accuracy of the actual numerical solution.

The authors report lower finite element solution error than both classical and earlier machine-learning approaches, while retaining the substantial speed advantage of learned mesh relocation over classical methods. They also report rapid, robust training and efficient online adaptation. The central change is the training target: optimizing the solution error directly allows the learned placement strategy to improve on merely reproducing existing meshing methods.
summary.tldr: G-Adaptivity trains a graph neural network directly on finite element solution error to improve mesh placement while retaining fast adaptation.

title: G-Adaptivity: optimised graph-based mesh relocation for finite element methods

abstract: We show that deep neural networks can achieve dimension-independent rates of convergence for learning structured densities typical of image, audio, video, and text data. For example, in images, where each pixel becomes independent of the rest of the image when conditioned on pixels at most $t$ steps away, a simple $L^2$-minimizing neural network can attain a rate of $n^{-1/((t+1)^2+4)}$, where $t$ is independent of the ambient dimension $d$, i.e. the total number of pixels. We further provide empirical evidence that, in real-world applications, $t$ is often a small constant, thus effectively circumventing the curse of dimensionality. Moreover, for sequential data (e.g., audio or text) exhibiting a similar local dependence structure, our analysis shows a rate of $n^{-1/(t+5)}$, offering further evidence of dimension independence in practical scenarios.

paragraphs: Learning a probability density becomes challenging when each example has many coordinates, such as the pixels in an image. This paper shows how deep neural networks can achieve convergence rates independent of the total number of coordinates when the density has an appropriate local dependence structure. The key condition concerns which variables remain dependent after nearby variables are known.

For images, the analysis assumes each pixel is independent of the remaining image once pixels within t steps are given. Under this structure, an L2-minimizing neural network attains the rate n raised to −1/((t+1)²+4). The exponent depends on the neighborhood radius t, which is independent of the total pixel count.

For sequential data with a similar structure, the stated rate is n raised to −1/(t+5). The authors also provide empirical evidence that t is often a small constant in real applications. Together, these results explain how local dependence can make density estimation manageable despite large ambient dimension. The dimension independence is tied to this structural condition.
summary.tldr: Under local conditional dependence assumptions, neural density estimators can achieve convergence rates governed by neighborhood size rather than total data dimension.

title: Dimension-Independent Rates for Structured Neural Density Estimation

abstract: The capability of generalization is a cornerstone for the success of modern learning systems. For non-Euclidean data, e.g., graphs, that particularly involves topological structures, one important aspect neglected by prior studies is how machine learning models generalize under topological shifts. This paper proposes AdvDIFFormer, a physics-inspired graph Transformer model designed to address this challenge. The model is derived from advective diffusion equations which describe a class of continuous message passing process with observed and latent topological structures. We show that AdvDIFFormer has provable capability for controlling generalization error with topological shifts, which in contrast cannot be guaranteed by graph diffusion models, i.e., the generalization of common graph neural networks in continuous space. Empirically, the model demonstrates superiority in various predictive tasks across information networks, molecular screening and protein interactions

paragraphs: Graph models need to generalize when the structure of connections changes, not only when individual data values change. This paper focuses on such topological shifts, an aspect the authors argue has received insufficient attention. AdvDIFFormer is a graph transformer designed around this structural generalization problem.

The model is derived from advective diffusion equations, which describe a continuous message-passing process involving both observed and latent graph structures. This physics-inspired formulation supplies the basis for the authors’ theoretical analysis. They show that AdvDIFFormer can provably control generalization error under topological shifts, a guarantee they contrast with what graph diffusion models can provide.

Experiments show superior predictive performance across information networks, molecular screening, and protein interactions. These results accompany the theoretical contribution with evidence from several graph applications. The distinction in the theory concerns the availability of an error-control guarantee; it does not mean that every diffusion-based graph model must fail on every changed graph. The paper makes changing connectivity an explicit part of model design and generalization analysis.
summary.tldr: AdvDIFFormer uses advective diffusion to improve graph prediction and provide theoretical control of generalization error under topological shifts.

title: Supercharging Graph Transformers with Advective Diffusion

abstract: Developing a better understanding of surprising or counterintuitive phenomena has constituted a significant portion of deep learning research in recent years. These include double descent, grokking, and the lottery ticket hypothesis -- among many others. Works in this area often develop *ad hoc hypotheses* attempting to explain these observed phenomena on an isolated, case-by-case basis. This position paper asserts that, in many prominent cases, there is little evidence to suggest that these phenomena appear in real-world applications and these efforts may be inefficient in driving progress in the broader field. Consequently, we argue against viewing them as isolated puzzles that require bespoke resolutions or explanations. However, despite this, we suggest that deep learning phenomena *do* still offer research value by providing unique settings in which we can refine our *broad explanatory theories* of more general deep learning principles. This position is reinforced by analyzing the research outcomes of several prominent examples of these phenomena from the recent literature.  We revisit the current norms in the research community in approaching these problems and propose practical recommendations for future research, aiming to ensure that progress on deep learning phenomena is well aligned with the ultimate pragmatic goal of progress in the broader field of deep learning.

paragraphs: This position paper asks what makes research on surprising deep-learning behavior valuable. It considers phenomena such as double descent, grokking, and the lottery ticket hypothesis. The authors argue that researchers often construct a separate explanation for each phenomenon, even when there is little evidence that the phenomenon appears in real-world applications.

Their concern is about the broader payoff of these explanations. A hypothesis tailored to one isolated observation may contribute less to general understanding than a theory that explains shared principles. The authors therefore recommend treating unusual phenomena as settings for developing and refining broader explanations of deep learning, rather than assuming every puzzle needs its own bespoke resolution.

The paper supports its position by analyzing research outcomes from prominent examples in the literature and offers recommendations for future work. It preserves a constructive role for studying unusual behavior: such cases can help sharpen theories with wider relevance. The proposed standard of value is how well an explanation advances understanding and progress across the field, not merely whether it accounts for one striking observation.
summary.tldr: Surprising deep-learning phenomena are most useful when they help refine broad theories rather than only receive isolated explanations.

title: Position: Not All Explanations for Deep Learning Phenomena Are Equally Valuable

abstract: Weight space learning aims to learn representations of neural network (NN) weights, enabling different downstream tasks. Existing approaches show promising performance, but lacking a way to shape these weight-space representations using information about the datasets the models were trained on, thus limiting downstream applications. We propose WeightCLIP, a method for learning a dataset-aligned latent space for neural networks, where datasets information is induced during training. The NNs are encoded as latent representations using an autoencoder, while dataset samples are encoded using a dataset encoder. The two representations are aligned using a contrastive objective, effectively reshaping the weight-space representations according to the datasets. We demonstrate that such representations can be used for different downstream tasks, including mapping dataset information to a weight-space representation that decode to strong models. In addition, we introduce a latent refinement process for generating models that outperforms standard fine-tuning. Overall, our results demonstrate that explicitly incorporating dataset information improves what can be achieved with weight-space representations across retrieval, generation, and refinement. Code will be available at https://github.com/HSG-AIML/WeightCLIP.

paragraphs: Weight-space learning represents entire neural networks through their parameters so those representations can support downstream tasks. WeightCLIP adds information about the datasets on which the networks were trained. The motivation is that a model representation becomes more useful when its organization reflects the data associated with that model.

The method uses an autoencoder to encode neural-network weights and a separate encoder to represent dataset samples. A contrastive objective aligns these two kinds of representation, reshaping the weight-space latent space according to dataset information. This establishes a connection between descriptions derived from data and representations that can be decoded back into model weights.

The authors demonstrate applications in retrieval, model generation, and refinement. In particular, dataset information can be mapped into a weight representation that decodes into a strong model. They also introduce a latent refinement process that outperforms standard fine-tuning in their reported results. The contribution is showing that explicitly aligning datasets and model weights expands what learned weight representations can accomplish.
summary.tldr: WeightCLIP aligns dataset and neural-network representations to improve model retrieval, generation, and latent-space refinement.

title: WeightCLIP: Aligning Datasets and Models for Weight Space Learning

abstract: Early exit neural networks, which adapt computation to input complexity, have proven effective in supervised learning but remain largely unexplored in deep reinforcement learning (DRL). In this paper, we propose Budgeted EXit Actor (BEXA), a novel actor-critic architecture that integrates early exit branches into the actor network. To ensure a mathematically principled trade-off between performance and inference expenditure, the exit decision is formulated as a constrained linear program during training, the solution of which is subsequently amortized to enable highly efficient runtime execution. BEXA is general, governed by an interpretable budget parameter, and compatible with any off-policy actor-critic method. We evaluate BEXA by integrating it with standard off-policy algorithms like SAC and TD3 on a suite of MuJoCo tasks. Our results demonstrate a substantial improvement in inference efficiency with minimal or no loss in performance. These findings highlight early exits as a promising direction for improving computational efficiency in DRL.

paragraphs: A reinforcement-learning policy need not spend the same amount of computation on every input. Budgeted EXit Actor, or BEXA, brings this idea to actor–critic learning by adding early-exit branches to the actor network. These branches allow action computation to finish before the full network is evaluated, adapting inference effort to input complexity.

The central design question is when to exit while respecting a computational budget. BEXA formulates that choice as a constrained linear program during training. It then amortizes the solution so that runtime decisions can be made efficiently. An interpretable budget parameter controls the trade-off between performance and inference expenditure, giving the method an explicit resource constraint rather than leaving computation implicit.

The architecture is presented as compatible with any off-policy actor–critic method. The authors evaluate integrations with SAC and TD3 on MuJoCo tasks and report substantial inference-efficiency improvements with minimal or no performance loss. Those results support early exits as a practical way to reduce policy-execution cost in the tested settings while maintaining task performance.
summary.tldr: BEXA adds budget-controlled early exits to actor networks, substantially reducing inference cost with minimal or no performance loss in MuJoCo evaluations.

title: Mind the Budget: Accelerating Deep Reinforcement Learning using Constrained Early Exit Neural Networks

abstract: Evaluating the robustness of Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) is essential for their continued development and responsible deployment. However, existing robustness benchmarks largely focus on hallucination or misleading textual inputs, overlooking the critical challenge posed by misleading visual inputs in assessing visual understanding. To fill this gap, we introduce MVI-Bench, the first comprehensive benchmark specially designed for evaluating how Misleading Visual Inputs undermine the robustness of LVLMs. Grounded in fundamental visual primitives, the design of MVI-Bench centers on three hierarchical levels of misleading visual inputs: Visual Concept, Visual Attribute, and Visual Relationship. Using this taxonomy, we curate six representative categories and compile 1,248 expertly annotated VQA instances. To facilitate fine-grained robustness evaluation, we further introduce MVI-Sensitivity, a novel metric that characterizes LVLM robustness. Empirical results across 18 state-of-the-art LVLMs uncover pronounced vulnerabilities to misleading visual inputs, and our in-depth analyses on MVI-Bench provide actionable insights that can guide the development of more reliable and robust LVLMs.

paragraphs: MVI-Bench examines how vision-language models respond when the image itself is misleading. The authors identify a gap in robustness evaluation: existing benchmarks emphasize hallucinations or deceptive text, leaving misleading visual inputs less thoroughly assessed. Their benchmark makes this visual challenge the central object of measurement.

The benchmark organizes misleading inputs into three levels: visual concepts, visual attributes, and visual relationships. Within this structure, the authors curate six representative categories and assemble 1,248 expertly annotated visual question-answering examples. They also introduce MVI-Sensitivity, a metric intended to support more detailed assessment of model robustness across these inputs.

Evaluating 18 leading vision-language models reveals pronounced vulnerabilities. The result indicates that strong multimodal capabilities do not, by themselves, establish robustness to misleading visual evidence in these tests. The benchmark and its taxonomy provide a structured basis for examining those weaknesses, while the accompanying analyses are intended to guide improvements in visual understanding and reliability.
summary.tldr: MVI-Bench evaluates misleading visual inputs and finds substantial robustness weaknesses across 18 vision-language models.

title: MVI-Bench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Evaluating Robustness to Misleading Visual Inputs in LVLMs

abstract: Relational deep learning (RDL) converts relational databases (RDBs) into heterogeneous graphs, but graphs derived directly from database schemas are often not well suited for how graph neural networks (GNNs) perform relational reasoning. We study what makes a relational graph suitable for deep learning and show that schema-derived graphs suffer from two systematic failures: information overload and semantic fragmentation. Through an empirical analysis on real-world databases, we find that effective graphs arise from a task-dependent balance between removing task-irrelevant structure and injecting task-aligned relational connectivity. Filtering exhibits a non-monotonic effect on performance, while structural injection is beneficial only when it reflects the logic of the downstream task. Based on these findings, we develop an end-to-end structural optimizer that applies both operations to adapt relational graphs automatically. Across 23 tasks spanning classification, regression, and recommendation, the optimized graphs consistently improve accuracy while often reducing inference cost.

paragraphs: Relational deep learning converts database tables and their relationships into graphs for graph neural networks. This paper asks whether the graph implied by a database schema is also suitable for a particular prediction task. It identifies two systematic problems with direct conversion: too much irrelevant information and fragmented semantic relationships.

An empirical study of real-world databases finds that effective graphs require a task-dependent balance between removing irrelevant structure and adding useful relational connections. More filtering does not consistently mean better performance. Likewise, adding connections helps only when they reflect the downstream task’s logic. The graph should therefore be adapted according to what the model needs to predict.

The authors build an end-to-end structural optimizer that performs both filtering and structural injection automatically. Across 23 classification, regression, and recommendation tasks, the resulting graphs consistently improve accuracy and often lower inference cost. These findings make graph construction part of the learning problem: selecting and connecting relevant relational information can improve both predictive quality and, in many tested cases, the cost of using the model.
summary.tldr: Task-aware removal and addition of graph structure improves relational prediction, with optimized graphs often reducing inference cost.

title: What Makes a Desired Graph for Relational Deep Learning?

abstract: In the field of integrated circuits, leaf cells are the basic units, serving as the fundamental building blocks (e.g., standard cells) that are widely reused in various VLSI designs, forming the basis for more complex circuits. Therefore, the design quality of leaf cell layouts significantly impacts the PPA (Power, Performance, and Area) of the final VLSI designs. To automatically design leaf cell layouts that are close to expert designs, we propose GenLeaf. GenLeaf first utilizes a supervised, performance-aware embedding model to represent layouts and automatically calculate their similarity scores. Since there are expert-designed layouts but no corresponding scripts, we implement Bayesian optimization to generate a layout-script dataset for LLM training. With subsequent supervised fine-tuning and further preference optimization, GenLeaf can generate leaf cell layouts through scripts whose performance closely resembles that designed by human engineers. Experiment results demonstrate that GenLeaf outperforms expert-designed golden layouts across key performance metrics.
