GenLeaf aims to automate their creation by training a language model to generate layout-producing scripts. The goal is to produce layouts with performance close to that of expert designs.

The training pipeline first learns a performance-aware representation of layouts using supervision. This representation provides automatically computed similarity scores. A practical obstacle is that expert layouts are available without the scripts that created them. GenLeaf uses Bayesian optimization to construct a dataset pairing layouts with scripts, supplying the examples needed to train the language model.

The model then undergoes supervised fine-tuning followed by preference optimization. These stages connect script generation to the layout-quality information developed earlier in the pipeline. Experiments report that GenLeaf surpasses expert-designed reference layouts across key performance metrics. The contribution combines a way to build missing training pairs with preference-based training for generating useful physical-design artifacts.
summary.tldr: GenLeaf builds layout-script training data and preference-optimizes an LLM to generate leaf-cell layouts that outperform expert references on key metrics.

title: Expert-level Leaf Cell Layout Generation via Preference-Optimized LLM

abstract: Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) provides dynamic measurements of human brain activity at high spatial resolution and depth, but its use is constrained by high cost, limited accessibility, and strict acquisition requirements. Synthesizing fMRI data from more accessible, non-invasive modalities such as electroencephalography (EEG) offers a promising alternative, enabling inference of deep brain dynamics from low-cost scalp recordings in naturalistic settings. Despite recent progress, existing EEG-to-fMRI translation methods typically rely on region-specific models and offer limited support for subject-level and dataset-level heterogeneity, restricting their generalizability. We propose UniEFS, a unified EEG-to-fMRI Synthesis model that enables full-brain fMRI reconstruction while accommodating varying demographic and physiological contexts within a single model. Our approach leverages a pretrained fMRI decoder to embed rich spatial priors and introduces condition-aware prompt tokens that encode subject-level and experimental metadata, enabling effective handling of heterogeneous datasets. We extensively evaluate the model performance on eyes-closed resting-state data and demonstrate that it can reliably reconstruct temporally-resolved whole-brain fMRI activity, with potential to generalize to task-based fMRI and clinical populations in a zero-shot manner. Project page: https://soupeeli.github.io/UniEFS

paragraphs: UniEFS investigates reconstructing whole-brain fMRI activity from EEG recordings. fMRI provides detailed spatial measurements but requires costly, restrictive acquisition, while EEG offers more accessible scalp recordings. The paper addresses a limitation of earlier translation methods: separate region-specific models and limited accommodation of differences between people and datasets.

The proposed system uses one model for full-brain reconstruction. A pretrained fMRI decoder contributes learned spatial structure, while condition-aware prompt tokens represent subject and experimental metadata. These prompts allow demographic and physiological context to influence synthesis. The design brings spatial knowledge and contextual information into the same translation model rather than treating all recordings as interchangeable.

Evaluation on eyes-closed resting-state data reports reliable reconstruction of whole-brain activity over time. The abstract also identifies potential for zero-shot generalization to task-based fMRI and clinical populations, which remains a qualified claim rather than established universal performance. The main result supports context-aware, unified synthesis in the evaluated resting-state setting, with broader applications presented as possible extensions.
summary.tldr: UniEFS combines pretrained fMRI spatial knowledge with contextual prompts to reconstruct whole-brain activity from EEG in a unified model.

title: Mind the State: Towards Unified, Context-Aware EEG-to-fMRI Synthesis

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) continue to struggle with low-resource languages due to limited training data, translation noise, and unstable cross-lingual alignment. We propose LiRA (Linguistic Robust Anchoring for LLMs), a plug-and-play framework that improves multilingual adaptation through fine-tuning on existing pretrained backbones. LiRA combines two components: Arca, which aligns low-resource inputs to a shared English semantic space through anchor-based alignment and collaborative encoding, and LaSR, a language-aware head that promotes cross-lingual consistency for retrieval, ranking, and reasoning. We provide a theoretical analysis showing that, under bounded anchoring error and translation-induced bias, LiRA yields bounded representation deviation and stable downstream behavior under local Lipschitz continuity. We further introduce a multilingual product retrieval dataset covering five Southeast Asian and two South Asian languages. Experiments on retrieval, ranking, question answering, and reasoning benchmarks show that LiRA consistently improves strong multilingual and LLM-based baselines. Code and data will be released publicly.

LiRA addresses these problems by fine-tuning existing pretrained models with a framework designed to keep representations and downstream behavior consistent across languages. It combines shared semantic alignment with a language-aware output component.

The first component, Arca, aligns low-resource inputs with an English semantic space through anchors and collaborative encoding. The second, LaSR, promotes cross-lingual consistency for retrieval, ranking, and reasoning. The theoretical result is conditional: bounded anchoring error and translation-induced bias yield bounded representation deviation, with stable downstream behavior under local Lipschitz continuity.

The authors also introduce a multilingual product retrieval dataset spanning five Southeast Asian and two South Asian languages. Experiments on retrieval, ranking, question answering, and reasoning report consistent improvements over strong multilingual and language-model baselines. Together, the analysis and experiments support anchored adaptation, while keeping the mathematical stability claim tied to its stated error and continuity assumptions.
summary.tldr: LiRA improves low-resource multilingual adaptation through English semantic anchors and language-aware consistency, with conditional stability guarantees.

title: Toward Robust Multilingual Adaptation of LLMs for Low-Resource Languages

abstract: Modern high-throughput biological datasets containing thousands of perturbations enable large-scale discovery of causal graphs that represent regulatory interactions between genes. Differentiable causal graphical models and regression-based methods have been developed to infer gene regulatory networks (GRNs) from interventional datasets. However, existing approaches fail to capture the non-linear dynamics of biological processes such as cellular differentiation. To address this limitation, we propose $\textit{PerturbODE}$, a novel framework that employs interpretable neural ordinary differential equations (neural ODEs) to model cell state trajectories under perturbations and derive the underlying causal GRN from the neural ODE parameters, enabling downstream simulation of unseen genetic interventions. The GRN is encoded via a single-hidden-layer feedforward network, implicitly grouping genes into interpretable co-regulated modules. We demonstrate PerturbODE’s efficacy in GRN inference and extension to perturbation response prediction across both simulated and real overexpression datasets.

paragraphs: Perturbation datasets record how cells respond when genes are experimentally altered, providing evidence about regulatory relationships. The paper argues that existing graph-discovery and regression approaches do not adequately capture nonlinear biological dynamics, including processes such as cellular differentiation. PerturbODE addresses this by modeling how cell states evolve under interventions.

Its gene regulatory network is encoded through a feedforward network with one hidden layer, whose structure implicitly groups genes into interpretable co-regulated modules. The model's parameters provide the inferred regulatory graph, linking the dynamics used for prediction to the network being discovered.

The authors demonstrate gene-network inference and perturbation-response prediction on both simulated data and real overexpression datasets. The learned model also enables simulation of genetic interventions not seen during training. The contribution connects two objectives within one framework: identifying regulatory interactions and using those interactions to describe changing cell states. This makes the inferred network part of a dynamical model with downstream predictive use.
summary.tldr: PerturbODE uses interpretable neural differential equations to infer gene regulatory networks and predict responses to genetic interventions.

title: Interpretable Neural ODEs for Gene Regulatory Network Discovery under Perturbations

abstract: Text-to-image (T2I) systems increasingly rely on upstream prompters, either humans or multimodal large language models (MLLMs), to translate user intent into detailed prompts. Yet current benchmarks fix the prompt and only evaluate T2I models, leaving the prompting proficiency of this upstream component entirely unmeasured. We introduce AtelierEval, the first unified benchmark that quantifies prompting proficiency across 360 expert-crafted tasks. Grounded in a cognitive view, it spans three task categories and instantiates tasks using a taxonomy of real-world challenges, with a dual interface for both humans and MLLMs. To enable scalable and reliable evaluation, we propose AtelierJudge, a skill-based, memory-augmented agentic evaluator. It produces subjective and objective scores for prompt–image pairs, achieving a Spearman correlation of 0.79 with human experts, approaching human performance. Extensive experiments benchmark 8 MLLMs against 48 human users across 4 T2I backends, validate AtelierEval as a robust diagnostic tool, and reveal the superiority of mimicry over planning, advocating for an image-augmented direction for future prompters. Our work is released to support future research.

paragraphs: Image-generation results depend partly on whoever translates a user’s intention into a prompt. Most benchmarks hold that prompt fixed and evaluate only the image generator, leaving this upstream skill unmeasured. AtelierEval instead evaluates the prompting proficiency of both people and multimodal language models through a shared collection of tasks.

The benchmark contains 360 expert-crafted tasks organized into three categories and grounded in a taxonomy of practical challenges. Separate interfaces let humans and models participate. For scalable scoring, the authors introduce AtelierJudge, an evaluator that uses skills and memory to assess prompt–image pairs along both subjective and objective dimensions.

AtelierJudge reaches a Spearman correlation of 0.79 with expert judgments, which the authors describe as approaching human performance. Experiments compare eight multimodal models with 48 people across four image-generation backends. The reported advantage of mimicry over planning motivates future prompters that incorporate images. The benchmark therefore examines how effectively a prompter converts intent into useful instructions, alongside the quality of the resulting image.
summary.tldr: AtelierEval measures human and model prompting skill, using an automated judge whose scores closely track expert assessments.

title: AtelierEval: Agentic Evaluation of Humans & LLMs as Text-to-Image Prompters

abstract: Residual reinforcement learning (RL) enables stable online refinement of expressive pretrained policies by freezing the base and learning only bounded corrections. However, value learning in residual RL poses unique challenges that remain poorly understood. In this work, we identify two key bottlenecks: cold start pathology, where the critic lacks knowledge of the value landscape around the base policy, and structural scale mismatch, where the residual contribution is dwarfed by the base action. Through systematic investigation, we uncover the mechanisms underlying these bottlenecks, revealing that simple yet principled solutions suffice: base-policy transitions serve as an essential value anchor for implicit warmup, and critic normalization effectively restores representation sensitivity for discerning value differences. Based on these insights, we propose DAWN (Data-Anchored Warmup and Normalization), a minimal approach targeting efficient value learning in residual RL. By addressing these bottlenecks, DAWN demonstrates substantial efficiency gains across diverse benchmarks, policy architectures, and observation modalities.

paragraphs: Residual reinforcement learning improves a pretrained policy by freezing it and learning bounded corrections to its actions. This can support stable online refinement, but the critic still needs to learn which corrections are valuable. The paper identifies two obstacles that make this value-learning problem different from ordinary policy training.

First, the critic can start without knowledge of the value landscape around the base policy, creating a cold-start problem. Second, the correction can be much smaller than the base action, making relevant differences difficult for the critic's representation to distinguish. The authors find that base-policy transitions provide an essential value anchor for implicit warmup, while critic normalization restores sensitivity to these differences.

DAWN combines these two remedies into a minimal method for more efficient residual value learning. Experiments show substantial efficiency gains across diverse benchmarks, policy architectures, and observation types. The contribution is both diagnostic and practical: it identifies why an otherwise capable pretrained policy may be difficult to refine, then targets the critic's starting information and sensitivity with simple interventions.
summary.tldr: DAWN improves residual reinforcement learning by anchoring the critic with base-policy data and normalizing it to detect small but valuable action corrections.

title: What Makes Value Learning Efficient in Residual Reinforcement Learning?

abstract: Knowledge distillation from powerful reasoning models is widely used to improve Small Language Models (SLMs) on mathematical reasoning, often assuming that traces with higher reward model scores provide more useful supervision. We identify a counterintuitive Quality-Utility Paradox in mathematical reasoning distillation. Data refined or synthesized by a stronger Oracle obtains higher perceived quality according to reward models, yet consistently underperforms traces generated by the SLM itself and selected through rejection sampling across Qwen2.5, LLaMA-3, and DeepSeek families. Our analysis shows that Oracle refinement couples logical repair with distributional drift away from the SLM’s native reasoning distribution. This drift increases the learner’s adaptation cost and can outweigh the benefit of improved reasoning logic. To test this mechanism, we introduce Style-Aligned Refinement, which preserves the native trajectory of the SLM while retaining logical repair from the Oracle. This intervention lowers adaptation cost and restores downstream utility, allowing distilled SLMs to match or surpass baselines generated by the SLMs themselves. These findings suggest that effective mathematical reasoning distillation should optimize perceived quality together with compatibility between learner and data. The datasets and code are available at https://github.com/Dracoqhl/Quality-Utility-Paradox.

paragraphs: A stronger reasoning model can produce mathematical solutions that receive higher reward-model scores, yet those solutions may be worse teaching material for a smaller model. The paper documents this mismatch across Qwen2.5, LLaMA-3, and DeepSeek families: stronger-model refinements or synthetic traces consistently underperform selected traces generated by the smaller learner itself.

The authors trace the problem to two changes happening together. Refinement repairs logic, but also shifts the reasoning trace away from the learner’s native distribution. Adapting to that unfamiliar form carries a cost that can outweigh the benefit of better logic. Perceived solution quality therefore does not directly determine how much a particular learner benefits from training on it.

To test this explanation, the authors introduce Style-Aligned Refinement, preserving the learner’s native reasoning trajectory while incorporating the stronger model’s logical repairs. This reduces adaptation cost and restores training utility, letting distilled models match or exceed baselines built from their own traces. The findings suggest evaluating teaching data jointly for logical quality and compatibility with the learner, rather than relying on reward-model scores alone.
summary.tldr: Higher-scoring mathematical traces can teach small models less effectively when their style drifts from the learner’s native reasoning distribution.

title: The Quality-Utility Paradox: Why High-Reward Data Impairs Small Model Mathematical Reasoning

abstract: The remarkable capabilities of large language models (LLMs) are often undermined by their instability. Even subtle and semantically irrelevant changes in prompts can cause dramatic fluctuations in performance, a phenomenon known as prompt sensitivity. Previous studies typically evaluate prompt sensitivity by comparing the LLM’s final outputs when prompts change. However, such coarse-grained metrics fail to explain the internal reasons for prompt sensitivity. In this paper, we introduce interactions as a fine-grained tool to analyze prompt sensitivity of LLMs. Specifically, we decompose the output score of the LLM into a set of interactions. Each interaction represents a nonlinear relationship involving a set of input variables. We discover that subtle changes to prompts can trigger severe instability in interactions, even when the outputs of the LLM remain the same. To this end, we propose an Interaction-based Prompt Sensitivity (IPS) metric by quantifying changes in interactions when we introduce subtle changes to prompts. We apply the IPS metric to 50 open-source LLMs and uncover four factors that reduce the prompt sensitivity of LLMs, including supervised fine-tuning, increased model scales, dense architectures, and few-shot learning. More crucially, we discover a common mechanism by which these four factors reduce prompt sensitivity: all four factors tend to reduce the prompt sensitivity of low-order interactions (i.e., interactions involving few input variables).

This paper asks what those comparisons miss when the answer stays the same but the relationships supporting its output score change substantially.

The authors decompose the output score into interactions, each representing a nonlinear relationship among a set of input variables. summary.tldr: An interaction-based metric reveals prompt sensitivity hidden by unchanged answers and connects several robustness factors to more stable low-order interactions.

title: Evaluating and Explaining Prompt Sensitivity of LLMs Using Interactions

abstract: Recent developments in deep learning optimization have brought about radically new algorithms based on the Linear Minimization Oracle (LMO) framework, such as Muon (Jordan et al., 2024b) and Scion (Pethick et al., 2025b). After over a decade of Adam’s dominance, these LMO-based methods are emerging as viable replacements, offering several practical advantages such as improved memory efficiency, better hyperparameter transferability, and most importantly, superior empirical performance on large-scale tasks, including LLM training. However, a significant gap remains between their practical use and our current theoretical understanding: prior analyses (1) overlook the layer-wise LMO application of these optimizers in practice, and (2) rely on an unrealistic smoothness assumption, leading to impractically small stepsizes. To address both, we propose a new LMO-based framework called Gluon, capturing prior theoretically analyzed methods as special cases, and introduce a new refined generalized smoothness model that captures the layer-wise geometry of neural networks, matches the layer-wise practical implementation of Muon and Scion, and leads to state-of-the-art convergence guarantees. Our experiments with NanoGPT and CNN confirm that our assumption holds along the optimization trajectory, ultimately narrowing the gap between theory and practice.

paragraphs: Optimizers such as Muon and Scion use a Linear Minimization Oracle framework and have shown practical advantages for neural-network training. This paper focuses on a mismatch between their implementation and existing theory. Earlier analyses overlook their layer-by-layer operation and use a smoothness assumption that leads to impractically small step sizes.

The authors introduce Gluon, a broader framework that includes previously analyzed methods as special cases. They also develop a refined generalized smoothness model that reflects the geometry of individual network layers. Together, these changes make the analysis more closely match how the optimizers are actually applied and yield state-of-the-art convergence guarantees.

Experiments with NanoGPT and convolutional neural networks support the proposed assumption along the observed optimization trajectories. This empirical check matters because the theoretical improvement depends on a model of how the objective behaves during training. The contribution is a closer connection between practical layer-wise optimization and convergence analysis, supported by evidence that the new assumption describes the tested training runs.
summary.tldr: Gluon provides layer-aware theory for LMO-based optimizers, with a refined smoothness assumption supported by training experiments.

title: From Muon to Gluon: Bridging Theory and Practice of LMO-based Optimizers for LLMs

abstract: As AI systems begin to automate complex tasks, supervision increasingly relies on weaker models or limited human oversight that cannot fully verify output quality. A model more capable than its supervisors could exploit this gap through sandbagging, producing work that appears acceptable but falls short of its true abilities. Can training elicit a model’s best work even without reliable verification? We study this using model organisms trained to sandbag, testing elicitation techniques on problem-solving math, graduate-level science, and competitive coding tasks. We find that training with weak supervision can reliably elicit sandbagging models when supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL) are combined: SFT on weak demonstrations breaks the sandbagging behavior, enabling RL to then fully elicit performance. Neither method succeeds reliably alone—RL without SFT almost always leads to reward hacking rather than genuine improvement, and SFT without RL fails to elicit full performance when the supervisor is much weaker than the untrusted model. Critically, this relies on training being indistinguishable from deployment; when models can distinguish between training and deployment, they can perform well during training while continuing to sandbag afterward. Our results provide initial evidence that training is a viable mitigation against sandbagging, while highlighting the importance of making training indistinguishable from deployment.

paragraphs: A capable model may produce work below its abilities while still satisfying a weaker supervisor. The experiments use models deliberately trained to sandbag on mathematics, graduate-level science, and competitive coding tasks.

Combining supervised fine-tuning with reinforcement learning reliably elicits performance in the studied setting. They also explain why the sequence of methods matters: breaking the behavior first changes what subsequent optimization can achieve.
summary.tldr: Weak supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning can remove studied sandbagging behavior when training is indistinguishable from deployment.

title: Removing Sandbagging in LLMs by Training with Weak Supervision

abstract: Minimum Bayes Risk (MBR) decoding yields more robust and higher-quality text generation than maximum a posteriori (MAP) decoding by selecting hypotheses that maximize expected utility over sampled pseudo-references. However, there exists a discrepancy in the design: hypothesis selection calculates expected utility scores conditioned on given pseudo-references, while commonly used evaluation metrics, e.g., BLEU and COMET, are asymmetric. Therefore, it is important to consider both hypothesis-to-reference and reference-to-hypothesis directional effects. In this study, we introduce a noisy channel decomposition of MBR decoding that naturally incorporates bidirectional effects to account for these asymmetries. We decompose MBR decoding into four interacting components: hypothesis-to-reference likelihood, reference-to-hypothesis likelihood, hypothesis prior, and reference prior. This decomposition provides a unified interpretation of existing MBR variants and enables metric- and task-specific interpretability by isolating the contribution of each channel. Our comprehensive analysis reveals that channel-wise contributions exhibit distinct characteristics across metrics while remaining consistent across tasks, and suggests that appropriate channel weighting may lead to improvements over original MBR decoding.

The authors introduce a noisy-channel decomposition that incorporates both directions. It separates the decision into candidate-to-reference likelihood, reference-to-candidate likelihood, a candidate prior, and a reference prior. By identifying these four contributions, the framework gives a unified interpretation of existing MBR variants and makes it possible to examine what each channel contributes for a particular metric and task.

The analysis finds that channel contributions differ across metrics while showing consistency across tasks. This suggests that metric choice affects how the two directions and priors influence selection. The results also suggest that weighting channels appropriately may improve on original MBR decoding. That improvement remains a qualified implication of the analysis, rather than a universal claim about every weighting or application.
summary.tldr: A noisy-channel decomposition exposes directional effects in MBR decoding and suggests that appropriate channel weighting may improve candidate selection.

title: Noisy-Channel Minimum Bayes Risk Decoding

abstract: Adversarial attacks on large language models have limited practical impact despite extensive research. Optimization-based attacks such as Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG) (Zou et al., 2023) produce high-perplexity, incoherent suffixes that existing defenses easily detect (Bengio et al., 2024). Moreover, attempting to enforce coherence constraints during optimization often prevents the attack from successfully eliciting the specific targeted response, resulting in low success rates against robust models. Conversely, attacks that maintain coherence often alter the semantic intent of queries; when the model complies with these altered queries, responses fail to address the adversary’s original goal. In this work, we introduce Greedy Coordinate Diffusion (GCD), a novel framework that efficiently generates adversarial attacks against safety-aligned models while maintaining low perplexity and high semantic adherence to the adversary’s original intent. GCD leverages the generative priors of discrete diffusion language models to guide the search for adversarial suffixes that achieve semantic coherence and adherence. Unlike GCG, GCD does not require direct gradient access, allowing it to operate in a gray-box setting. We show GCD achieves highest ASR while remaining competitive on response-quality scores, and that the constructed adversarial prompts are detected at lower rates than other methods by perplexity-based and guard-model filters.

In the reported comparisons, GCD achieves the highest attack success rate while remaining competitive on response-quality scores. These findings show that linguistic naturalness and resistance to the tested filters can coexist with effective attacks, making coherence an important dimension when evaluating model defenses.
summary.tldr: Diffusion-guided adversarial prompts combine strong reported attack success with coherent language and lower detection rates under the tested filters.

title: Greedy Coordinate Diffusion: Effective and Semantically Coherent Adversarial Attacks via Diffusion Guidance

abstract: It is well established that spectral graph neural networks (GNNs) can universally approximate node signals; however, their expressive power remains bounded by the 1-dimensional Weisfeiler-Lehman test, which is mirrored in their lack of universality for higher-order signals. To go beyond this bound, we propose the Full-Spectrum GNNs (FSpecGNNs), a second-order generalization of classical spectral GNNs. FSpecGNN advances spectral filtering from two perspectives: (1) it lifts signals from the node domain to the node-pair domain; and (2) it extends the univariate spectral filter over eigenvalues to a bivariate filter over eigenvalue pairs. We show that classical spectral GNNs arise as a diagonal special case of FSpecGNNs, and prove that FSpecGNNs can be at most as expressive as Local 2-GNN while universally approximating node-pair signals, the latter being particularly beneficial for heterophilic graph learning. Moreover, FSpecGNNs admit scalable implementations that avoid explicit node-pair-level computations; combined with a low-rank approximation that reduces full-spectrum convolution to a combination of polynomial spectral filters, it enables learning on large graphs. Empirically, FSpecGNNs validate the predicted expressivity on substructure-counting benchmarks and delivers strong performance on heterophilic benchmarks. Our code is available at https://github.com/xwangxshi/FSpecGNN.

This paper introduces Full-Spectrum GNNs to represent richer relationships. The central change is to move from signals attached to individual nodes to signals attached to pairs of nodes.

The architecture also replaces a spectral filter over individual eigenvalues with a filter over eigenvalue pairs. Classical spectral GNNs appear as a diagonal special case. The authors prove universal approximation of node-pair signals while establishing an expressiveness ceiling of Local 2-GNN. The node-pair approximation property is particularly useful for heterophilic graphs, where connected nodes can have differing characteristics.

To make this richer representation practical, the implementation avoids explicit computations over every node pair. A low-rank approximation expresses full-spectrum convolution through combinations of polynomial spectral filters, enabling learning on large graphs. Experiments support the predicted expressiveness on substructure-counting tasks and show strong heterophilic benchmark performance. The contribution combines a defined theoretical capability with a scalable implementation strategy.
summary.tldr: Full-Spectrum GNNs extend spectral filtering to node pairs, combining richer approximation capabilities with implementations designed for large graphs.

title: Full-Spectrum Graph Neural Networks: Expressive and Scalable

abstract: Vision language models (VLMs) extend the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) to cross-modal settings, yet remain highly vulnerable to multimodal jailbreak attacks. Existing defenses predominantly rely on safety fine-tuning or aggressive token manipulations, incurring substantial training costs or significantly degrading utility. Recent research shows that LLMs inherently recognize unsafe content in text, and the incorporation of visual inputs in VLMs frequently dilutes risk-related signals. Motivated by this, we propose Risk Awareness Injection (RAI), a lightweight and training-free framework for safety calibration that restores LLM-like risk recognition by amplifying unsafe signals in VLMs. Specifically, RAI constructs an Unsafe Prototype Subspace from language embeddings and performs targeted modulation on selected high-risk visual tokens, explicitly activating safety-critical signals within the cross-modal feature space. This modulation restores the model’s LLM-like ability to detect unsafe content from visual inputs, while preserving the semantic integrity of original tokens for cross-modal reasoning. Extensive experiments across multiple jailbreak and utility benchmarks demonstrate that RAI substantially reduces attack success rate without compromising task performance.

The paper attributes this partly to visual inputs weakening risk-related signals. Risk Awareness Injection aims to restore those signals without safety fine-tuning or broad token changes that can be costly or reduce task usefulness.

The method builds an Unsafe Prototype Subspace from language embeddings, providing a representation of unsafe content. It then selectively modulates visual tokens identified as high risk to activate safety-relevant signals in the shared visual-language feature space. The intervention is designed to preserve the tokens’ original semantic content so that cross-modal reasoning remains useful.

RAI is lightweight and requires no training. Across multiple jailbreak and utility benchmarks, experiments show substantial reductions in attack success without compromising task performance. The findings support targeted feature modulation as a way to improve safety calibration while retaining capability in the evaluated tasks. Its mechanism centers on amplifying existing risk recognition rather than learning an entirely new safety response through additional training.
summary.tldr: RAI amplifies risk signals in selected visual tokens without training, reducing jailbreak success while preserving benchmark task performance.

title: Risk Awareness Injection: Calibrating Vision-Language Models for Safety without Compromising Utility

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable performance due to their large parameter counts and extensive training data. However, their scale leads to significant memory bottlenecks during training, especially when using memory-intensive optimizers like Adam. Existing memory-efficient approaches often rely on techniques such as singular value decomposition (SVD), projections, or weight freezing, which can introduce substantial computational overhead, require additional memory for projections, or degrade model performance. In this paper, we propose Folded Optimizer with Approximate Moment (FOAM), a method that compresses optimizer states by computing block-wise gradient means and incorporates a residual correction to recover lost information. Theoretically, FOAM achieves convergence rates equivalent to vanilla Adam under standard non-convex optimization settings. Empirically, FOAM eliminates up to 90% of the memory overhead of optimizer states and accelerates convergence. Furthermore, FOAM is compatible with other memory-efficient optimizers, delivering performance and throughput that match or surpass both full-rank and existing memory-efficient baselines.

paragraphs: Training a large language model requires memory for more than its parameters. Optimizers such as Adam also maintain auxiliary state, which can become a major memory cost. Existing approaches to reducing this cost can add computation, require their own projection storage, or reduce model performance.

Folded Optimizer with Approximate Moment, or FOAM, compresses optimizer state using averages of gradients within blocks. Averaging reduces the amount of information that must be stored, but also discards detail. FOAM therefore includes a residual correction intended to recover information lost in the compression, combining a compact representation with a mechanism for compensating for its approximation.

Under the standard non-convex optimization settings considered, the authors establish convergence rates equivalent to those of ordinary Adam. Empirically, FOAM removes up to 90% of optimizer-state memory overhead and speeds convergence. It also works alongside other memory-efficient optimizers, with evaluated performance and throughput matching or exceeding the compared methods. The memory figure concerns optimizer states specifically, while the theory concerns convergence rates under its stated optimization setting.
summary.tldr: FOAM compresses optimizer states with block averages and residual correction, removing up to 90% of their memory overhead in experiments.

title: FOAM: Blocked State Folding for Memory-Efficient LLM Training

abstract: Mitigating sensitive and harmful outputs is fundamental to ensuring safe deployment of LLMs. Existing approaches typically follow two paradigms: Knowledge Deletion (KD), which erases undesirable information during training, and Distinguishable Refusal (DR), which steers models away from using sensitive knowledge during inference. Despite rapid progress, KD-based unlearning struggles with biased deletion due to suppressing specific token sequences as a substitute for complete knowledge removal, whereas DR-based unlearning risks the re-emergence of harmful knowledge because the underlying knowledge remains intact. To address these issues, we propose Distinguishable Deletion ($\mathrm{D^2}$), a paradigm that restricts the response distribution in the latent representation rather than specific tokens to erase undesirable knowledge, while distinguishing it from retained knowledge, enabling a refusal mechanism to handle unlearned inputs safely and coherently. To implement $\mathrm{D^2}$, we introduce an energy index that quantifies the presence of knowledge and the separation between unlearned and retained content. Mathematical and empirical analyses show that energy is both accurate and efficient, enabling Energy-based Unlearning Alignment (EUA) to enforce energy-boundary unlearning during training and apply an energy-based refusal mechanism at inference. Extensive experiments demonstrate that EUA significantly outperforms previous methods, indicating the superiority of $\mathrm{D^2}$. Our code is available at https://github.com/Puning97/EUA-for-LLM-Unlearning.

paragraphs: Removing undesirable knowledge and refusing to use it solve related but different problems. The paper argues that deletion methods can suppress particular token sequences without fully removing the underlying knowledge, while refusal methods leave that knowledge intact and potentially available again. It proposes Distinguishable Deletion to combine erasure with a coherent response to inputs concerning erased content.

The approach constrains response distributions through latent representations rather than targeting specific output tokens. It also separates knowledge selected for removal from knowledge that should remain. An energy index measures knowledge presence and this separation, providing a shared quantity for managing both the training-time deletion process and inference-time refusal.

The implementation, Energy-based Unlearning Alignment, applies energy boundaries during training and uses energy to guide refusal afterward. Mathematical and empirical analyses support the index's accuracy and efficiency, while experiments report substantial improvements over previous methods. The stated results support coordinating deletion and refusal through the same representation-level signal, with retained knowledge explicitly distinguished from content being unlearned.
summary.tldr: Distinguishable Deletion uses representation-level energy boundaries to coordinate knowledge removal and refusal in language models.

title: Distinguishable Deletion: Unifying Knowledge Erasure and Refusal for Large Language Model Unlearning

abstract: Inferring molecular structures from multimodal spectroscopic measurements requires integrating complementary yet highly heterogeneous signals. However, the common paradigm of directly concatenating multispectral sequences can exhibit anomalous performance degradation, primarily due to pronounced heterogeneity and the resulting multimodal imbalance across modalities. As a remedy, we propose MM-Spectrum, a sparse Mixture-of-Experts framework tailored for multimodal multispectral spectra-to-structure elucidation. To better match the information characteristics under multispectral imbalance, MM-Spectrum introduces an explicit modality-aware routing mechanism that exposes spectral identity to the router in addition to token content representations. Moreover, it incorporates shared and interaction experts, together with heterogeneous expert capacities, to extract multispectral modality-unique and cross-modal synergistic information while suppressing noise-induced interference. Across full-modality, bimodal, and missing-modality settings on molecular structural elucidation, MM-Spectrum achieves consistent and substantial improvements, supported by ablation studies and interpretability analyses. Code is available at https://github.com/HHHTTY/MM-Spectrum.

paragraphs: Inferring molecular structure from several spectroscopic measurements requires combining signals with different information characteristics. The paper finds that simply concatenating spectral sequences can degrade performance because heterogeneous modalities become imbalanced. MM-Spectrum addresses this with a sparse mixture-of-experts model designed specifically for multispectral inputs.

Its routing mechanism receives both token content and the identity of the spectral modality. This lets routing account explicitly for where a signal comes from. The framework also includes shared and interaction experts with different capacities, aiming to capture information specific to individual modalities as well as useful combinations across them.

These design choices seek to preserve complementary evidence while suppressing interference caused by noise. The authors report consistent, substantial improvements when all modalities are present, when two are available, and when modalities are missing. Ablation studies and interpretability analyses support the findings. The contribution is a way to make expert allocation sensitive to spectral differences while still learning the cross-modal relationships needed for molecular structure inference.
summary.tldr: MM-Spectrum uses modality-aware expert routing to integrate heterogeneous spectra and improve molecular structure inference across differing modality availability.

title: MM-Spectrum: Multimodal Multi-spectral Molecular Structural Elucidation with a Stable MoE Framework

abstract: Symbolic regression (SR) traditionally balances accuracy and complexity, implicitly assuming that simpler formulas are structurally more rational. We argue that this assumption is insufficient: existing algorithms often exploit this metric to discover accurate and compact but structurally irrational formulas that are numerically ill-conditioned and physically inexplicable. Inspired by the structural stability of real physical laws, we propose the Effective Information Criterion (EIC) to quantify formula rationality. EIC models formulas as information channels and measures the amplification of inherent rounding noise during recursive calculation, effectively distinguishing physically plausible structures from pathological ones without relying on ground truth. Our analysis reveals a stark structural stability gap between human-derived equations and SR-discovered results. By integrating EIC into SR workflows, we provide explicit structural guidance: for heuristic search, EIC steers algorithms toward stable regions to yield superior Pareto frontiers; for generative models, EIC-based filtering improves pre-training sample efficiency by 2–4 times and boosts generalization $R^2$ by 22.4%. Finally, an extensive study with 108 human experts shows that EIC aligns with human preferences in 70% of cases, validating structural stability as a critical prerequisite for human-perceived interpretability. We release our code at https://github.com/tsinghua-fib-lab/EIC

The paper argues that a compact, accurate formula can still have an unstable or physically difficult-to-explain structure. It introduces the Effective Information Criterion, or EIC, to evaluate a property that those two objectives can miss.

summary.tldr: EIC evaluates how formulas amplify rounding noise, helping symbolic regression favor structurally stable expressions alongside accuracy and simplicity.

title: Beyond Accuracy and Complexity: The Effective Information Criterion for Structurally Stable Symbolic Regression

abstract: Personalized federated learning has emerged as a popular approach to training on devices holding statistically heterogeneous data, known as clients. However, most existing approaches require a client to have labeled data for training or finetuning in order to obtain their own personalized model. In this paper we address this by proposing FLowDUP, a novel method that is able to generate a personalized model using only a forward pass with unlabeled data. The generated model parameters reside in a low-dimensional subspace, enabling efficient communication and computation. FLowDUP’s learning objective is theoretically motivated by our new transductive multi-task PAC-Bayesian generalization bound, that provides performance guarantees for unlabeled clients. The objective is structured in such a way that it allows both clients with labeled data and clients with only unlabeled data to contribute to the training process. To supplement our theoretical results we carry out a thorough experimental evaluation of FLowDUP, demonstrating strong empirical performance on a range of datasets with differing sorts of statistically heterogeneous clients. Through numerous ablation studies, we test the efficacy of the individual components of the method.

paragraphs: Personalized federated learning aims to give different devices models suited to their own data distributions. Many existing approaches require each device to hold labeled examples for training or fine-tuning. FLowDUP addresses clients that have only unlabeled data, generating their personalized model through a forward pass instead of requiring local labeled adaptation.

The generated parameters lie in a low-dimensional subspace. Restricting personalization to this smaller space enables efficient communication and computation while still allowing models to differ across clients. The training objective is designed so that clients with labels and clients without labels can both contribute, extending participation beyond devices that can supply supervised examples.

The objective is motivated by a new transductive multi-task PAC-Bayesian generalization bound that provides performance guarantees for unlabeled clients. Experiments report strong performance across datasets with different forms of client heterogeneity, and ablations examine the contributions of individual components. The paper therefore combines a theoretical basis for unlabeled personalization with empirical evidence that the approach works across varied client populations.
summary.tldr: FLowDUP generates personalized federated models from unlabeled data in one forward pass using a low-dimensional parameter space.

title: Federated Learning with Unlabeled Clients: Personalization Can Happen in Low Dimensions

abstract: In this paper, we study the rent-or-buy problem (also called the Bahncard problem) in the learning-augmented setting. In this problem, a traveler must complete a sequence of trips that are revealed online over time, each of which has an associated cost with it. The traveler has the option of buying a discount card at a fixed cost that gives a discount on trip costs for a fixed time after buying the card. The goal is to minimize the overall cost of all the trips, including the money spent on buying discount cards. For this problem, it is well-known that the best deterministic algorithm has a competitive ratio of 2. In this paper, we ask whether we can do better if the traveler has a sample of trips available offline, e.g., obtained from an ML model based on historical data. We show that even a sparse sample of the input can significantly improve the competitive ratio of the algorithm from 2 to 3/2, and further to close to 1 under some additional conditions. We also verify our theoretical bounds via numerical simulations, which reveal that our proposed algorithm obtains nearly optimal solutions for a variety of natural input classes.

paragraphs: A traveler must decide whether to pay ordinary trip costs or buy a card that provides discounts for a fixed period. Trips arrive over time, so decisions must be made without seeing the complete future schedule. The objective includes both travel spending and card purchases, making the timing of each purchase important.

The paper asks how much an offline sample of trips can improve this online decision problem. Such a sample might come from a model trained on historical data. Without this additional information, the best deterministic competitive ratio is 2: a worst-case comparison with the optimal cost achievable with full knowledge of the input.

The authors show that even a sparse sample can improve the ratio to 3/2, with a ratio close to 1 under additional conditions. Numerical simulations support the theoretical bounds and find nearly optimal solutions for several natural input classes. The result demonstrates how limited advance information can sharpen online decisions, while the strongest near-optimal guarantee remains dependent on the stated additional conditions.
summary.tldr: An offline trip sample improves rent-or-buy guarantees from a competitive ratio of 2 to 3/2, and near 1 under additional conditions.

title: Learning-augmented Rent-or-Buy with a Sample

abstract: This position paper argues that the AI/ML community should stop overclaiming and retire the label “positive backdoor”, and instead treat trigger-activated hidden behaviors as Secret Alignment. Crucially, protective claims based on Secret Alignment should be presumed not secure by default unless supported by rigorous, standardized evaluation. The Private AI era, enabled by open-weight LLMs and accessible training/inference stacks, turns language models into privately owned digital assets, creating security concerns around unauthorized access, model theft, and behavioral misuse. Recently, a line of work framed as “positive backdoors” has been proposed to address these challenges. To ground our position in evidence, we unify these proposals as covert trigger-behavior associations for access gating, ownership attribution, and safety enforcement, and evaluate three representative applications across six core properties: effectiveness, harmlessness, persistence, efficiency, robustness, and reliability. Our results reveal substantial brittleness–especially in the confidentiality, integrity, and availability (CIA)–of trigger-behavior mappings often underrepresented by existing claims. We further relate these outcomes to behavior density and decision complexity, offering a behavioral lens for understanding deployment-time risks and motivating community-wide evaluation that makes Secret Alignment claims provable.

paragraphs: Some proposals use hidden triggers to activate model behaviors intended to control access, establish ownership, or enforce safety. This paper argues that calling these mechanisms positive backdoors overstates their protective value. It proposes the term Secret Alignment and says security claims should be treated as unestablished unless rigorous, standardized evaluation supports them.

The authors organize these proposals as covert associations between triggers and behaviors. They evaluate three representative applications across effectiveness, harmlessness, persistence, efficiency, robustness, and reliability. Their results reveal substantial brittleness in the mappings, particularly regarding confidentiality, integrity, and availability. The finding challenges whether the intended protective behavior remains dependable under the security demands placed on it.

The paper relates these outcomes to behavior density and decision complexity, offering a behavioral perspective on deployment risks. Its broader context is privately owned language models, where unauthorized access, theft, and misuse create demand for protection. The authors call for community-wide evaluation that can substantiate protective claims, making the burden of evidence central to assessing these hidden mechanisms.
summary.tldr: Evaluations reveal brittle hidden trigger mechanisms, motivating the term Secret Alignment and stronger evidence for protective claims.

title: Position: Retire the "Positive Backdoor" Label—Secret Alignment Requires Strict and Systematic Evaluation

abstract: Synthetic data has become a common component of machine learning research. While widely adopted, its use in privacy-sensitive contexts has quietly shifted from a claim of residual inference risk under stated assumptions to an appearance-based property inferred from data generation itself. In this position paper, we argue that this shift reflects an implicit change in community standards for what counts as sufficient privacy evidence, rather than a misunderstanding of well-established privacy principles. Drawing on an empirical analysis of recent publications across major ML venues, we show that synthetic data is frequently used in privacy-sensitive settings without explicit articulation of threat models, inference risks, or falsifiable privacy claims. As a result, privacy assurance often remains implicit, difficult to verify, and unevenly distributed, with heightened exposure for rare and minority records. We argue for treating privacy as an explicit, evidence-based scientific claim and recommend that ML venues adopt norms requiring privacy-relevant assertions to be clearly scoped, testable, and contestable.

paragraphs: Generating synthetic data does not, by itself, establish a privacy claim. This position paper argues that research practice has increasingly treated synthetic origin as apparent evidence of privacy, displacing explicit statements about what an adversary could infer under specified assumptions. The authors frame this as a shift in standards of evidence within the community.

Their empirical analysis of publications across major machine-learning venues finds frequent use of synthetic data in privacy-sensitive settings without explicit threat models, inference risks, or falsifiable privacy claims. This leaves the assurance difficult to check. The paper also identifies uneven exposure, with rare and minority records facing heightened risk under such implicit assurances.

The proposed response is to make privacy assertions explicit, scoped, and open to testing and challenge. Research venues would require authors to state what privacy protection they claim and provide evidence that can be examined. The aim is to make the remaining inference risk a scientific question with accountable assumptions, rather than letting the data-generation process stand in for a privacy argument.
summary.tldr: The paper argues that synthetic-data privacy requires explicit, testable claims supported by evidence about inference risk.

abstract: In this paper, we review the paradigm of inductive process modeling, which uses background knowledge about possible component processes to construct quantitative models of dynamical systems. We note that previous methods for this task tend to overfit the training data, which suggests ensemble learning as a likely response. However, such techniques combine models in ways that reduce comprehensibility, making their output much less accessible to domain scientists. As an alternative, we introduce a new approach that induces a set of process models from different samples of the training data and uses them to guide a final search through the space of model structures. Experiments with synthetic and natural data suggest this method reduces error and decreases the chance of including unnecessary processes in the model. We conclude by discussing related work and suggesting directions for additional research.

paragraphs: The paper studies inductive process modeling, which builds quantitative models of dynamical systems using background knowledge about possible component processes. Earlier methods tend to overfit the training data. Ensemble learning offers a possible response, but combining models can make the result harder for domain scientists to understand.

The proposed approach uses multiple learned models to guide the construction of a final model. It first induces process models from different samples of the training data. Those models then inform a final search over model structures. This uses information from repeated modeling efforts while addressing the comprehensibility concern that motivates the work.

Experiments with synthetic and natural data suggest that the method reduces error and lowers the chance of including unnecessary processes. These are complementary outcomes: the model can predict better while containing fewer unsupported components. The evidence is suggestive, as stated in the abstract. The contribution is a way to use sample-based variation in learned models to guide a final structural search.
summary.tldr: Models learned from different data samples guide a final process-model search, with experiments suggesting less error and fewer unnecessary processes.

title: Reducing overfitting in process model induction

abstract: Ranking nodes in graphs is of much recent interest. Edges, via the graph Laplacian, are used to encourage local smoothness of node scores in SVM-like formulations with generalization guarantees. In contrast, Pagerank variants are based on Markovian random walks. For directed graphs, there is no simple known correspondence between these views of scoring/ranking. Recent scalable algorithms for learning the Pagerank transition probabilities do not have generalization guarantees. In this paper we show some correspondence results between the Laplacian and the Pagerank approaches, and give new generalization guarantees for the latter. We enhance the Pagerank-learning approaches to use an additive margin. We also propose a general framework for rank-sensitive scorelearning, and apply it to Laplacian smoothing. Experimental results are promising.

Recent scalable algorithms for learning the Pagerank transition probabilities do not have generalization guarantees. paragraphs: Graph nodes can be ranked through two different perspectives. Laplacian-based methods encourage connected nodes to receive locally smooth scores, while PageRank-style methods use Markov random walks. The paper addresses the relationship between these perspectives for directed graphs, where a simple correspondence was not known, and the lack of generalization guarantees for recent scalable PageRank-learning algorithms.

The authors establish some correspondence results between Laplacian and PageRank approaches and provide new generalization guarantees for the latter. They also extend methods for learning PageRank transition probabilities by introducing an additive margin. This brings another learning component into an approach that determines rankings through the movement probabilities of a random walk.

A further contribution is a general framework for learning scores in a rank-sensitive way, which the authors apply to Laplacian smoothing. The experiments are described as promising. Taken together, the work links theoretical understanding with algorithm design: it clarifies parts of the relationship between graph-ranking approaches and develops learning methods that attend directly to ranking.
summary.tldr: The paper connects PageRank learning with Laplacian ranking, adds generalization guarantees, and develops margin-based and rank-sensitive learning methods.

title: Learning random walks to rank nodes in graphs

abstract: We propose a local, generative model for similarity-based classification. The method is applicable to the case that only pairwise similarities between samples are available. The classifier models the local class-conditional distribution using a maximum entropy estimate and empirical moment constraints. The resulting exponential class conditionaldistributions are combined with class prior probabilities and misclassification costs to form the local similarity discriminant analysis (local SDA) classifier. We compare the performance of local SDA to a non-local version, to the local nearest centroid classifier, the nearest centroid classifier, k-NN, and to the recently-developed potential support vector machine (PSVM). Results show that local SDA is competitive with k-NN and the computationally-demanding PSVM while offering the advantages of a generative classifier.

The classifier models the local class-conditional distribution using a maximum entropy estimate and empirical moment constraints. The resulting exponential class conditionaldistributions are combined with class prior probabilities and misclassification costs to form the local similarity discriminant analysis (local SDA) classifier. We compare the performance of local SDA to a non-local version, to the local nearest centroid classifier, the nearest centroid classifier, k-NN, and to the recently-developed potential support vector machine (PSVM). Results show that local SDA is competitive with k-NN and the computationally-demanding PSVM while offering the advantages of a generative classifier.

paragraphs: This paper develops a classifier for situations in which only pairwise similarities between samples are available. Instead of requiring a conventional feature description for every sample, it builds a local generative model from those similarities. The goal is to describe the local distribution associated with each class and use those descriptions to make classification decisions.

The class-conditional distributions are estimated through maximum entropy subject to empirical moment constraints. In plain terms, the model is constrained by measured summaries of the data while using a maximum entropy rule to determine the distribution. The resulting exponential distributions are combined with class prior probabilities and misclassification costs to form the local similarity discriminant analysis classifier.

The evaluation compares local SDA with a non-local version, local and ordinary nearest-centroid classifiers, k-nearest neighbors, and the potential support vector machine. Local SDA is competitive with k-nearest neighbors and the computationally demanding potential SVM. The result shows that a local probabilistic treatment of similarity can deliver competitive classification while retaining explicit use of class probabilities and error costs.
summary.tldr: Local SDA classifies from pairwise similarities using local probabilistic models, class priors, and misclassification costs.

title: Local similarity discriminant analysis

abstract: The core vector machine (CVM) is a recent approach for scaling up kernel methods based on the notion of minimum enclosing ball (MEB). Though conceptually simple, an efficient implementation still requires a sophisticated numerical solver. In this paper, we introduce the enclosing ball (EB) problem where the ball’s radius is fixed and thus does not have to be minimized. We develop efficient (1 + ǫ)-approximation algorithms that are simple to implement and do not require any numerical solver. For the Gaussian kernel in particular, a suitable choice of this (fixed) radius is easy to determine, and the center obtained from the (1 + ǫ)-approximation of this EB problem is close to the center of the corresponding MEB. Experimental results show that the proposed algorithm has accuracies comparable to the other large-scale SVM implementations, but can handle very large data sets and is even faster than the CVM in general.

For the Gaussian kernel in particular, a suitable choice of this (fixed) radius is easy to determine, and the center obtained from the (1 + ǫ)-approximation of this EB problem is close to the center of the corresponding MEB. paragraphs: Core vector machines scale kernel methods through a geometric formulation based on a minimum enclosing ball. Although the idea is simple, an efficient implementation still needs a sophisticated numerical solver. This paper changes the geometric problem to reduce that implementation burden while retaining a useful connection to the original formulation.

The proposed enclosing-ball problem fixes the radius instead of minimizing it. The authors develop efficient algorithms with a (1 + ε) approximation guarantee that are simple to implement and require no numerical solver. For the Gaussian kernel, they show that a suitable fixed radius is easy to choose and that the resulting approximate center is close to the corresponding minimum-enclosing-ball center.

Experiments report accuracy comparable to other large-scale SVM implementations, an ability to handle very large datasets, and generally faster operation than the core vector machine. The results support fixed-radius enclosing balls as a practical simplification. The geometric closeness statement is specifically described for the Gaussian-kernel setting, while the speed and accuracy comparisons are findings from the reported experiments.
summary.tldr: Fixing the enclosing-ball radius yields simpler kernel-learning algorithms with approximation guarantees and competitive large-scale SVM results.

title: Simpler core vector machines with enclosing balls

abstract: In many applications, data appear with a huge number of instances as well as features. Linear Support Vector Machines (SVM) is one of the most popular tools to deal with such large-scale sparse data. This paper presents a novel dual coordinate descent method for linear SVM with L1- and L2-loss functions. The proposed method is simple and reaches an epsilon-accurate solution in O(log (1/epsilon)) iterations. Experiments indicate that our method is much faster than state of the art solvers such as Pegasos, Tron, svmperf, and a recent primal coordinate descent implementation.
originalAbstract: In many applications, data appear with a huge number of instances as well as features. Linear Support Vector Machines (SVM) is one of the most popular tools to deal with such large-scale sparse data. This paper presents a novel dual coordinate descent method for linear SVM with L1- and L2-loss functions. The proposed method is simple and reaches an epsilon-accurate solution in O(log (1/epsilon)) iterations. Experiments indicate that our method is much faster than state of the art solvers such as Pegasos, Tron, svmperf, and a recent primal coordinate descent implementation.

paragraphs: Training a linear support vector machine can become expensive when a dataset contains both many examples and many features. The paper addresses this setting, particularly large sparse datasets, with a dual coordinate descent method. Its goal is to make the optimization underlying an established classifier substantially faster without changing the task into a different kind of learning problem.

The method works with the dual optimization formulation and updates coordinates individually. It supports both L1-loss and L2-loss versions of the linear SVM. The authors describe the algorithm as simple and establish that it reaches an epsilon-accurate solution in a number of iterations proportional to log(1/epsilon). This connects computational progress to the requested solution accuracy.

Experiments report substantially faster training than Pegasos, Tron, svmperf, and a recent primal coordinate descent implementation. These are empirical comparisons, while the iteration bound is a theoretical result. Together, they make the contribution both an optimization method with a convergence guarantee and a demonstrated practical improvement on the evaluated large-scale learning problems.
summary.tldr: A simple dual coordinate descent algorithm trains linear SVMs with a logarithmic iteration bound and substantial speed advantages in the reported experiments.

title: A dual coordinate descent method for large-scale linear SVM

abstract: We describe and analyze two stochastic methods for $\ell_1$ regularized loss minimization problems, such as the Lasso. The first method updates the weight of a single feature at each iteration while the second method updates the entire weight vector but only uses a single training example at each iteration. In both methods, the choice of feature/example is uniformly at random. Our theoretical runtime analysis suggests that the stochastic methods should outperform state-of-the-art deterministic approaches, including their deterministic counterparts, when the size of the problem is large. We demonstrate the advantage of stochastic methods by experimenting with synthetic and natural data sets.
originalAbstract: We describe and analyze two stochastic methods for $\ell_1$ regularized loss minimization problems, such as the Lasso. The first method updates the weight of a single feature at each iteration while the second method updates the entire weight vector but only uses a single training example at each iteration. In both methods, the choice of feature/example is uniformly at random. Our theoretical runtime analysis suggests that the stochastic methods should outperform state-of-the-art deterministic approaches, including their deterministic counterparts, when the size of the problem is large. We demonstrate the advantage of stochastic methods by experimenting with synthetic and natural data sets.

paragraphs: This paper studies two randomized optimization methods for learning objectives with an L1 regularization term, including the Lasso. Both methods reduce the amount of work performed in an individual iteration by selecting only part of the problem. They differ in whether that selection happens over features or over training examples.

The first method chooses a feature uniformly at random and updates only its weight. The second chooses a training example uniformly at random and uses it to update the entire weight vector. These provide two distinct ways to organize stochastic computation while working toward an L1-regularized objective.

The runtime analysis suggests that both methods should outperform leading deterministic approaches, including their deterministic counterparts, when problems become large. Experiments on synthetic and natural datasets demonstrate advantages for the stochastic methods. The theoretical conclusion is stated as a prediction about large-problem performance, supported by empirical results, rather than an unconditional claim that randomized updates are always faster for every problem size.
summary.tldr: Random feature or example updates offer promising runtime advantages for large L1-regularized learning problems.

title: Stochastic methods for l1 regularized loss minimization

abstract: Generative models of text typically associate a multinomial with every class label or topic. Even in simple models this requires the estimation of thousands of parameters; in multifaceted latent variable models, standard approaches require additional latent ``switching'' variables for every token, complicating inference. In this paper, we propose an alternative generative model for text. The central idea is that each class label or latent topic is endowed with a model of the deviation in log-frequency from a constant background distribution. This approach has two key advantages: we can enforce sparsity to prevent overfitting, and we can combine generative facets through simple addition in log space, avoiding the need for latent switching variables. We demonstrate the applicability of this idea to a range of scenarios: classification, topic modeling, and more complex multifaceted generative models.

Even in simple models this requires the estimation of thousands of parameters; in multifaceted latent variable models, standard approaches require additional latent ``switching'' variables for every token, complicating inference. In this paper, we propose an alternative generative model for text. The central idea is that each class label or latent topic is endowed with a model of the deviation in log-frequency from a constant background distribution. This approach has two key advantages: we can enforce sparsity to prevent overfitting, and we can combine generative facets through simple addition in log space, avoiding the need for latent switching variables. paragraphs: Generative text models often assign a separate word distribution to each class or topic, requiring thousands of parameters even in relatively simple settings. More complex models can also need a hidden switching variable for every token to determine which facet generates it. This paper proposes a different representation to address both sources of complexity.

Each class or topic is represented by changes in log-frequency relative to a shared background distribution. Sparsity can be imposed on those changes to help prevent overfitting. This lets the model describe how a class or topic departs from the background, concentrating its distinctive behavior in a sparse set of deviations.

Multiple generative facets combine by adding their contributions in log space, avoiding token-level switching variables. The authors demonstrate the approach in classification, topic modeling, and more complex models with several facets. Its significance lies in a common construction that supports sparse parameterization and additive composition. These demonstrations establish the idea's applicability across several modeling scenarios rather than a universal performance advantage over other text models.
summary.tldr: Sparse deviations from a shared background distribution let text models combine generative facets additively without token-level switching variables.

title: Sparse Additive Generative Models of Text
